In this sense, this internationalisation strategy provides a framework which combines individual internationalisation measures with the University’s strategic goals. This equips the departments with sufficient flexibility and gives them the option to fulfil these strategic goals according to their requirements and emphases and to implement appropriate measures. The departments are able to determine their own focal points which are tailored to their particular needs. The resulting variety of activities contributes to the University-wide internationalisation goals. Deeper international cooperation and strategic partnerships form an important basis for the achievement of these goals. At the same time, transparent and equal access to international activities, the improved international visibility of HM and the provision of the required resources when designing the measures constitute important factors.

The anchoring of this internationalisation strategy in the University Development Plan of HM Hochschule [PLACE] University of Applied Sciences illustrates that international­isation is not the administrative task of individual persons but a strategic project for the university as a whole. It aims to achieve a broad-based acceptance of the planned measures by as many members of HM as possible so that everyone is able to contribute their specific competences in an optimum way. The resulting synergies may further strengthen the momentum of HM’s international development in the years to come. The internationalisation strategy is therefore not an end point and not a final result. Rather, a regular review and update of the measures and goals is required.

In light of this, the internationalisation strategy needs to be updated on a regular basis in tandem with the University Development Plan. In this way, internationalisation is an integral building block for the systematic, strategic and forward-looking development of HM Hochschule [PLACE] University of Applied Sciences.

“A tile that only goes up is not, on its own, evidence that anything is going down. We built the audit precisely so the two claims could not be confused for each other.” — Dr [PERSON], Postdoctoral Fellow, [ORGANISATION]

What the assistant actually shortened The [ORGANISATION] exists to trace how research effort becomes counted impact; this period, Dr [PERSON]’s team pointed the same method at a shorter pathway — how a logged assistant interaction becomes a shortened task. The question, stripped of its usual citation-flow framing, was simple: does more logged use predict less time spent. In partnership with a big-four professional services firm running its own AI-copilot efficiency review, the team compared per-consultant query counts against blind timings of matched deliverables completed with and without assistant use. The firm had expected, going in, a roughly linear relationship between queries and delivery speed. The matched timings showed no reliable relationship in either direction once —6—

Evaluating the evaluators, again [ORGANISATION] exists to ask whether a review changes anything beyond recertifying what a panel already believed. Applied to the assistants themselves, its standing method asked a narrower question this period: does adding an AI assistant to a review process shorten the review, deepen it, or simply relocate the same number of hours somewhere else in the cycle.

Working with a [PLACE] evaluation agency piloting an assistant-drafted first pass on its own programme reviews, Dr [PERSON]’s team timed the full review cycle before and after the assistant’s introduction. Draft turnaround fell by nearly half. Total cycle time, from draft to panel sign-off, held within three per cent of the preassistant baseline, the saved drafting hours reabsorbed almost entirely into an additional verification pass the panel had not previously required.

text: A university that delivers highly sought-after graduates, who are prepared for future success through rich and broad educational experiences UQ is renowned for excellence in teaching innovation, and developing graduates who are highly capable, motivated and prepared to succeed in their chosen field. Three years after completion, our graduate full-time employment rate is currently 92 per cent with almost two-thirds in a leadership role. Approximately 10 per cent of working graduates own their own business with over a third of our graduates giving back to the community through volunteering. We will build on this success through an inspiring experiential curriculum that equips our graduates with both the disciplinary knowledge and transferable skills they need to have impact and influence in a rapidly changing global workplace. To that end, our focus over the next four years is to give our students an employability ‘edge’ by creating new opportunities for them to develop their leadership skills, entrepreneurial mindset, digital literacy and sense of civic duty. By 2032, we hope that at least half of our students will have participated in UQ’s enrichment experiences, including global study experiences, internships, studentstaff partnership projects, entrepreneurship programs, and industry projects. Universities across the world have transformed the way they offer their educational programs, adopting widespread online learning through the COVID-19 pandemic. This has created an impetus for UQ to further develop our educational model combining online and on-campus learning, in a way that delivers on the ‘value-add’ of our rich campus learning experiences, global connections and extra-curricular opportunities. For those studying on campus, we will build a personalised and digital experience to create a learning environment that is seamless and flexible. Over the next four years, we will develop fully online offerings to deliver a UQ education to a broader range of domestic and international student markets. We will also strengthen our focus on developing a sense of belonging and wellbeing for our students, wherever they may be living and studying.

Pillar 4: Stewardship and Institutional Renewal None of the above is possible without renewed institutional foundations. Over the plan period we will invest in the digital, physical, and human infrastructure on which [ORGANISATION] depends, and we will work toward an institutional culture in which every member of the community can do their best work.

Transformation initiatives • Modernise digital infrastructure, including a renewed approach to research data, a modernised teaching technology stack, and an institution-wide approach to artificial intelligence in education and research. • Refresh the campus precinct as a working environment fit for the next twenty-five years, with sustained investment in heritage assets, contemporary teaching spaces, and student amenities. • Build a culturally safe and structurally equitable working environment for all members of the [ORGANISATION] community, with clear measures of progress on representation, retention, and career advancement for staff and students from historically marginalised backgrounds. • Strengthen financial sustainability through diversified revenue, philanthropic capability uplift, and operational excellence in the university’s professional services functions.

Establish (2026) In the first year, we will put in place the governance, baselines, and foundational investments needed to deliver the plan. Each pillar will have a designated executive sponsor, a dedicated implementation team, and a published baseline against which progress will be measured. Foundational investments — in digital infrastructure, in flagship research initiatives, and in educational redesign — will commence.

Build (2027-2028) Through 2027 and 2028, the major investments and program changes set out in this plan will reach scale. New postgraduate programs will commence; flagship research initiatives will reach operational maturity; the campus precinct refresh will deliver its most visible early outcomes. The mid-period review will be undertaken in late 2028.

research-intensive at a scale and depth unmatched in the country. And we are home to research and teaching strengths — across the sciences, humanities, social sciences, and policy domains — that are genuinely globally distinctive. This position confers both opportunity and obligation. The opportunity is to make a contribution to the national effort that no other institution can. The obligation is to do so with the seriousness, the honesty, and the strategic clarity that the country deserves from its national university. This plan describes how we will meet that obligation.

A vision for [ORGANISATION] in 2031 By 2031, the [ORGANISATION] will be the world-leading university for the study of [PLACE] and its place in the world — recognised for the depth of its research, the quality of its educational programs, and the contribution it makes to the public life of the country and the region. This vision is ambitious and focused. It reflects our distinctive mission, our particular institutional strengths, and the moment in which we find ourselves. It is grounded in eight decades of demonstrated capacity and oriented toward the next.

Strategic pillars Pillar 1: Research with Purpose The defining feature of [ORGANISATION]’s research has always been its proximity to the questions that matter for [PLACE] and the wider world. Over the plan period we will sharpen that distinctiveness — focusing investment on mission-aligned research priorities, expanding our cross-disciplinary capability, and growing the research income on which the university’s future depends.

Transformation initiatives • Concentrate investment in three to five flagship research programs of international standing, each addressing a problem of clear national significance and each connected to teaching at the postgraduate and research-training level. • Renew the university’s cross-disciplinary research capability, with a particular focus on the intersections of computing, the life sciences, and the humanities and social sciences.

The communication of complex public detail The School’s work on the communication of complex public detail has connected the methods of cybernetics to the long-running national questions of how the country renders its environmental, infrastructural, and ecological systems legible to its publics — the slow, careful translation of technical detail into visual artefacts on which public deliberation can rest. Our partners in this area have included the Department of Industry, Science and Resources, the [ORGANISATION] of [PLACE], and the McCusker Foundation, whose support has carried much of the work that did not fit cleanly into the funding categories of the major schemes.

The School’s collaboration with the [ORGANISATION] of [PLACE], beginning in 2023 and continuing into 2026, centred on the visual rendering of cybernetic-historical material drawn from the Library’s collections. Over three years, our researchers worked alongside the Library’s curatorial and digital-archives teams, contributed to the visual design of two of the Library’s flagship public-facing exhibitions, and developed — in partnership with the Library’s external design consultancy — a body of methodological guidance on the visual presentation of archival research that has been adopted, in its first year of public availability, by two further national institutions. A second strand of work, with the McCusker Foundation between 2024 and 2026, supported the design of public-facing visualisation artefacts for the Foundation’s flagship grant programs. The collaboration was structured around the methodological position that the visual presentation of research is itself a vector of accountability — that a research program whose findings cannot be visually rendered, in legible form, to the publics whose questions it addresses, is doing only half the work it has set out to do. The work has produced a body of public-facing visual artefacts now held in the Foundation’s institutional record. “The School’s commitment to the visual rendering of archival research has been a quiet revolution in how the Library presents itself to its publics. The methodological vocabulary the partnership has produced will outlast the period of the funding.”

A second consideration is intergenerational. The cohort entering [ORGANISATION] in 2026 has grown up inside a media environment in which the boundary between analogue and digital is porous by default, and in which competence at the crossing is now assumed rather than remarked upon. They will arrive expecting an institution that has formed a settled, articulable position on what the crossing is and how it is practised, and they will not be served by an institution that treats it as transition. The Plan that follows is [ORGANISATION]’s response. It commits the University, across the period to 2031, to a coherent posture toward the crossing between analogue and digital practice — a posture that is articulated rather than tacit, taught rather than assumed, and renewed rather than received.

Vision By 2031, [ORGANISATION] will be the [PLACE] institution most fluent in the crossings between analogue and digital practice. The University will treat the relation between the two as the locus of contemporary scholarship and craft, rather than as a transitional condition pending fuller digital migration. Researchers, students, and professional staff will operate at the crossing as a matter of disciplinary literacy rather than personal disposition; the institution’s facilities will support that practice as a first-class commitment; and the work of translation across the crossing will be articulated, audited, and published as scholarship in its own right.

The Hybrid Substrate Premise. The most productive contemporary scholarship operates at the crossing between analogue and digital substrates, not entirely on either side of it. [ORGANISATION] will treat the crossing itself as substrate — articulated as such, taught as such, and renewed as such across the plan period. Initiatives.

As a leading provider addressing the challenges of the net zero agenda, we work to develop progressive research, knowledge exchange, sustainability, and decarbonisation strategies. We are committed to implementing environmentally sustainable working practices and minimising the environmental impacts associated with staff and student travel. We are globally connected through our [ORGANISATION] regional office network, multinational study partners, and industry that spans Africa, Asia, [PLACE], the Middle East, and the Americas. We have recently launched our [PLACE] campus, which presents new opportunities for us to promote our strengths in games, animation, and business, and expand our network of partners and students. We will secure the University’s global profile as a trusted and high-quality education provider, through the implementation of this strategic plan, which will leverage institutional strengths and expertise to drive excellence and impact in teaching, research, and enterprise on a global scale.

The University’s global portfolio drives our international activity, cutting across all areas of operations. From the recruitment of international students and staff and embedding a global aspect to the learning and student experience, to the development and sustainment of a robust partnership network, to promoting institutional expertise in research and enterprise on a global scale, driving interest and investment to our communities.

Over the next few years, we will work across the institution to enhance our global profile for teaching, research, and enterprise. We will harness current activity, leveraging institutional assets to support students and staff to think and engage globally, increasing our impact across the world. A cohesive approach to global operations across the university will ensure partnership selection and activity aligns with our mission, and supports the transition to a more strategic, proactive institution that promotes international excellence across all areas.

Our success can be attributed to several factors, including: our staff; the level of engagement we maintain with our students; the personalised experience we offer; the supportive environment we provide, and the valued partnerships we have with the employers who shape our programmes, support our students, and pursue collaborative research and innovation with us. These strengths and experiences provide the foundation for our strategic direction and are underpinned by three core principles integral to our mission. • Our people drive our success and we are committed to helping them thrive: Our colleagues, students, partners and stakeholders are at the heart of everything we do and we are committed to fostering a positive and inclusive environment where all can succeed. • Our purpose: We create fair and accessible educational opportunities to equip students with the knowledge and skills they need to realise their career ambitions, regardless of their background, and we apply our research for the economic, cultural and societal benefit of our communities. • Our place: We are a deeply connected, locally anchored and community-driven organisation. We are proud of our [PLACE] heritage as well as the ways in which we work with communities across the world.

STRATEGIC PRIORITY 1: To deliver a personalised education and student experience that puts learners first and supports them to realise their ambitions. • Our students come from a broad range of backgrounds, experiences and countries. We will continue to provide our diverse student body with services designed to support their learning and wellbeing, and to ensure their academic journey is fulfilling and successful. • We are committed to listening to our students and working in partnership with them to enhance their sense of belonging to our university community and support their success. • Our commitment to ensuring that class sizes are comparatively small will remain a hallmark of our student experience, enabling us to understand and support each learner’s educational needs.

How we know The figures above and the chart-bearing case studies that follow are drawn from a single internal register. Since 2022, every research output of the School — including software repositories, datasets, teaching materials, and methodological tooling — has been logged against a common metadata schema and reviewed annually by an internal panel. Repositories enter the register at the point of first public release; downstream activity is harvested quarterly from GitHub’s public API and from the package registries of record.

The register’s design was a deliberate methodological commitment, made early in the period, to treat software outputs on the same footing as journal articles and theses — subject to the same internal review, the same authorship norms, and the same public visibility. Where this report cites a metric or a chart, it is drawn from that register. Where the register’s coverage is partial, we say so.

About the School The [ORGANISATION] was established at the [ORGANISATION] in 2021 to bring the methods, ethics, and questions of cybernetics into renewed contact with contemporary problems. We are transdisciplinary by design — working between engineering and the social sciences, between technical practice and critical inquiry, between the academy and the institutions whose work shapes the country. Our staff include researchers in computing, human-centred design, science and technology studies, environmental science, [PLACE] methodologies, public policy, and the arts. Our students — in the [ORGANISATION], in higher-degree research, and in our shorter-form Learning Experiences program — come from across government, industry, and the not-for-profit sector. We work in the open where we can and in confidence where we must, and we have, over the period, become more deliberate about the boundary between the two. The School operates as part of the College of Systems & Society, with a charter to act as connective tissue across the University, the country, and the broader cybernetic community. It traces its institutional origins to the 3A Institute and continues to draw on the methodological commitments laid down in those founding years.

Instruments that outlast their moment The [ORGANISATION] exists to catalogue what an organisation is still measuring and why — not the metrics a partner intends to keep using, but the ones still quietly in circulation years after the review that was meant to retire or renew them. This period the Commons turned its standing method on ratings and scores published once and left running: a compliance figure, a readiness index, a certification level, each still being cited in contract renewals, funding applications, or board papers long after the practice it once measured had moved on. The pattern, once the Commons started counting it, showed up faster than expected — and in places the School had not thought to look first. Working with a state audit office, Senior Lecturer [PERSON]’s team traced a compliance-rating index the office had first published for a routine contractor review in 2021 and never formally revised. The index kept circulating — cited in three subsequent contract renewals, folded into a risk-appetite briefing, referenced once in a ministerial answer — each use treating the figure as current because nothing about its presentation ever suggested otherwise. When the team finally asked the office to re-audit the underlying practice against the original 2021 criteria, the practice had changed twice in the interim; the index, formally, had not. The office’s own review sign-off had lapsed a year before the first of the three renewals that quoted it.

The proxy that stayed on the wall The [ORGANISATION] is the School’s own always-on self-measurement wall, and its researchers treat every tile on it, and every comparable board a partner installs, as an object of study rather than a finished product. A tile is easy to commission and, this period’s fieldwork found, unusually hard to decommission: once a reading earns a fixed position on a wall people walk past daily, its removal starts to read less like housekeeping and more like an admission that something was once being watched and now is not.

Mycelial Engagement and Reciprocal Roots Why this matters. Universities have, on the whole, measured engagement by the volume of transactions they enter into with external partners. The plan proposes a different measure: the reciprocity of the relationship and the durability of the underlying connection. The metaphor is mycelial rather than transactional — engagement understood as a slow network of nutrient exchange between institution and community, rather than a series of bilateral contracts. The reorientation has particular weight in the University’s relationships with [PLACE] communities, with the people of the ACT and surrounding regions, and with the long-standing scholarly networks across the [PLACE] to which [ORGANISATION] belongs. What we’ll do. 1. Establish a Reciprocity Register for community and partner relationships, recording, for each substantive engagement, an assessed ratio of community return to institutional return.

2. Convene a biannual Mycelial Forum with [PLACE] colleagues and community leaders, structured as a yarning circle rather than a consultation, with no agenda imposed by the University. 3. Decommodify the University’s engagement metrics, removing transaction volume and engagement-event counts from institutional reporting and replacing them with relational durability indicators. How we’ll know. 1. By 2031, every substantive partnership will have an entry in the Reciprocity Register, reviewed every eighteen months, with no extractive relationship sustained beyond that interval. 2. By 2028, transaction-volume and event-count measures will have been removed from all formal engagement reporting at the University, replaced by the relational durability indicator suite. 3. The Mycelial Forum will have met at least once every six months from 2026 onwards, with proceedings shared in the form agreed with the participating communities.

The fourth priority gathers the others into an institutional question: what is the right size, scope, and pace for [ORGANISATION] in the second half of the twenty-first century? text:
Strategic context The decade now under way has substantially advanced the digital migration of [PLACE] higher education. Teaching materials are now overwhelmingly assembled, distributed, and assessed through digital platforms; research workflows in many disciplines are predominantly computational; institutional records, including those that once defined the university’s relationship to its own history, exist in digital form. —6—

The migration has also, in places, produced losses that the sector has been slower to acknowledge. Material reasoning — the felt understanding of the medium that older traditions of inquiry built into their methodologies — has weakened in disciplines that have moved most decisively onto digital substrates. Computational literacy, conversely, has remained uneven in disciplines whose practice involves the daily use of computational tools that are nonetheless treated as background infrastructure rather than as scholarship. The translation work that mediates the crossing — the digitisation of physical archives, the printing of generative work, the encoding of field instruments, the materialisation of simulations — is conducted across the sector by talented practitioners who are rarely supported in articulating their craft as scholarly work in its own right. For [ORGANISATION], these developments cut across the four colleges. In the sciences, the computational and material dimensions of inquiry are increasingly entangled in instrument-led work that resists clean assignment to one side or the other. In the humanities and social sciences, the digital methods now central to many lines of inquiry sit alongside material traditions whose methodological commitments remain consequential. In the [ORGANISATION], the discipline of computing is itself the site at which the question of how computational systems are materially conditioned is most acutely posed. In the [ORGANISATION], the analogue and digital dimensions of clinical and laboratory work are knotted together in ways that the methodological vocabulary of any single tradition struggles to articulate.

This will acknowledge our distinctive ways of learning and teaching and encourage staff and students to foster, extend, and build upon these strengths, to ensure that a learning experience at Te Kunenga ki [PLACE] [ORGANISATION] is an exceptional one. In addition, students will increasingly require wider attributes, such as the ability to work in collaborative ways in inter- and transdisciplinary environments. Our Enabling Environment Mana-enhancing stakeholder experiences will be the focus of how we develop and manage our facilities and services. These experiences will be anchored in our distinctive physical and digital spaces, responsive and accessible services, and our open and collaborative work practices that privilege the needs of our students, staff and partners. Our decision making is strongly values-based, founded upon accountability and integrity, and focused on delivering professional services that are ethical, equitable, excellent, and sustainable. These values will be evident in our service interactions and in the experiences supported by our physical, digital and social environments. We continually seek user feedback and sentiment which guides our program of continual improvement.

Kaitiakitanga will be evident in our approach to sustainability and woven into everything we do. We will realise this in close collaboration with [PLACE] whenua and through open, inclusive engagement with our many and varied partners. Manaakitanga will drive innovative human centred design to create [PLACE]-enhancing and performant services and practices for our people. Open, transparent, and ethical governance and data-informed decision-making will foster a high-trust culture and increase the University’s accountability, agility, and nimbleness. Everybody engaging with the [ORGANISATION]’s digital and physical spaces will experience a distinctive sense of place that balances acknowledgement of history, heritage, and place with the vibrant evolution of our communities. Engaged and collaborative meditations with students, academics,

community, professions, and industry on current and transdisciplinary challenges will be facilitated by well-crafted, richly integrated digital and physical spaces. Our campuses and precincts will showcase our innovation, entrepreneurship, and commercialisation strengths and invite community and industry interaction. The development of our Newmarket Campus will reflect these strengths wholeheartedly. We will create vibrant locations recognised as gateways to learning and teaching, research and innovation, and partnership and engagement with the University. These distinctive spaces and the rich digital connections they have will deliver innovative and welcoming outreach, engagement, and extension activities with our communities, particularly from our Tai Tokerau and Tai Tonga campuses.

Accountability and review Governance arrangements for the Plan are deliberately conservative. Council retains its existing role as the ultimate steward of the University’s direction, and the ViceChancellor remains accountable to Council for delivery. Within that frame, three governance moves give the Plan effective traction. First, a standing Set & Setting Committee, chaired by a Deputy Vice-Chancellor and reporting quarterly to Council, takes responsibility for the indicator set across all four priorities and for surfacing slippage in any of them. Second, an Accountability and Review schedule, published annually, sets out which indicators are due for full reporting in which quarter, with no indicator permitted to slip beyond the next quarterly review cycle. Third, Council’s Audit and Risk Committee will, from 2027, treat the Set & Setting Index on the same footing as financial sustainability. Annual reporting against the Plan will be published in full, including instances of indicator slippage, any Heroic Dose Programme item whose Post-Dose Integration has not been completed within the quarter following completion, and any element of the Plan that has not progressed at the pace this document anticipated. The reporting will not be selective. The University takes the view that the credibility of an institutional posture grounded in integration practice depends, in the first instance, on the willingness to publish the periods in which integration has not, in fact, occurred.

Glossary This Plan uses a small set of terms drawn from the contemporary discipline of set, setting, and integration practice. The terms are defined here as they are used across the document. Container. The structural arrangements — physical, relational, temporal, and procedural — within which a significant institutional experience is held. In the Plan, the term denotes the institutional analogue of the literature’s reference to the conditions of safe holding. Heroic dose. A major institutional commitment of sufficient intensity to require structural container arrangements distinct from those of ordinary institutional work. In the Plan, the term denotes items in the Heroic Dose Programme.

Within that frame, three governance moves give the Plan effective traction. First, a standing Set & Setting Committee, chaired by a Deputy Vice-Chancellor and reporting quarterly to Council, takes responsibility for the indicator set across all four priorities and for surfacing slippage in any of them. Second, an Accountability and Review schedule, published annually, sets out which indicators are due for full reporting in which quarter, with no indicator permitted to slip beyond the next quarterly review cycle. Third, Council’s Audit and Risk Committee will, from 2027, treat the Set & Setting Index on the same footing as financial sustainability. Annual reporting against the Plan will be published in full, including instances of indicator slippage, any Heroic Dose Programme item whose Post-Dose Integration has not been completed within the quarter following completion, and any element of the Plan that has not progressed at the pace this document anticipated. The reporting will not be selective. The University takes the view that the credibility of an institutional posture grounded in integration practice depends, in the first instance, on the willingness to publish the periods in which integration has not, in fact, occurred.

Glossary This Plan uses a small set of terms drawn from the contemporary discipline of set, setting, and integration practice. The terms are defined here as they are used across the document. Container. The structural arrangements — physical, relational, temporal, and procedural — within which a significant institutional experience is held. In the Plan, the term denotes the institutional analogue of the literature’s reference to the conditions of safe holding. Heroic dose. A major institutional commitment of sufficient intensity to require structural container arrangements distinct from those of ordinary institutional work. In the Plan, the term denotes items in the Heroic Dose Programme.

What drives [ORGANISATION]’s international collaboration is the vision of working to connect [PLACE] to the global society through the university’s activities. With their strong tradition for international collaboration, the universities have a special responsibility to take the lead at a time in which international collaboration is facing political challenges, and in which the need to work together to find solutions to global societal challenges is greater than ever. Thus the university wants to work to promote an increased global exchange of knowledge and talent. This vision centres on vibrant campuses where students, staff and external partners meet and work closely together. The university’s main campus in [PLACE] is already recognised internationally for its distinctive architecture and urban location. In the coming years, the university will develop and rethink both its main and satellite campuses, developing them into even more vibrant, engaging and innovative environments for study and research that are operated and developed sustainably. The university’s vision for its own sustainable operations and development is described in its climate strategy, which supports the overall vision for 2025.

New advances and breakthroughs in knowledge are created both within individual disciplines and in the encounter between them. In recognition of this, the university will both attract international researchers and cultivate its own research staff, whether established researchers, promising junior researchers or talented PhD students. The university is one of the cornerstones of society, and its students, graduates and researchers help shape the society of the future through the knowledge they bring into play, from popular research communication to the general public to research-based public sector consultancy and researchers’ participation in government commissions and councils. Collaboration is absolutely central to this strategy. Specifically, the university’s goal is to strengthen collaboration: across disciplines; with the private sector and public sector institutions; and in promoting innovation. In this way, the university can increase the value of its contribution to society while at the same time maintaining its position at the vanguard of the needs of the society of the future.

TEACHING AND LEARNING – THE FOUNDATION OF PROGRESS AND PROSPERITY [ORGANISATION] emphasises demanding study programmes, a positive learning environment for students, and high quality degrees at all levels of study. To prepare students for further study, participation in a democratic society and diverse professional fields, the University strives to continuously develop teaching methods and learning facilities, encourage innovation in teaching, and strengthen relations between higher education and industry. At the same time, it is important to provide teachers and students with support in their work and encourage students’ engagement in their studies. GOALS

A comprehensive strategy created for teaching and learning and administration of academic affairs made more consistent. Support and quality assurance for the introduction of new programmes and regular evaluations of existing programmes increased, e.g. in consideration of learning outcomes and connections between the programme and the field, industry and international collaboration Study programmes consider ways to enable students to take courses in other faculties / schools Faculties increasingly involved in joint international Master’s programmes

text: 4.9 Faculty of Psychology 4.9.1 Objectives Research and teaching at the Faculty of Psychology, in line with the general objectives of this discipline, focus on the description and explanation of human experience and behaviour, as well as the changes they undergo. The explicit objective is to address everything from the foundations of the relevant processes to the (evidence-based) application and transfer of the insights gained. Basic and application-oriented research are regarded as equally relevant and as interrelated. Diversity in research approaches and topic areas is seen as an asset. On the basis of research approaches in the areas of neuroscience, cognitive science and social sciences that complement each other in an integrative way, the Faculty seeks to make theoretically-sound and empirically-testable contributions to the advancement of academic knowledge as well as its transfer. Over the next few years, particular emphasis will be placed on gaining insight into the psychological mechanisms and effects of societal and technological change on experience and behaviour, to thus contribute to the [[ORGANISATION]] (UN, 2015). Examples of fields of action in which knowledge of psychological processes in this regard will be of great relevance include health and well-being; education; sustainability in work and the economy; environment and climate change; demographic change; as well as reduction of social inequality; and digitalisation. It thus becomes apparent that the research activities at the Faculty are also aimed at providing relevant input in terms of social responsibility, and that the Faculty regards the Third Mission as one of its explicit tasks. In addition to research on the genuine psychological aspects of the above fields, a further goal is to approach this research in an interdisciplinary way, as part of the international research arena, and in cooperation with related disciplines (such as cognitive science, life sciences, education, business and economics, as well as computer science, philosophy, sociology and medicine). The Faculty is oriented towards a wide variety of methodologies and regards their intensified integration as an especially promising endeavour.

We either reassure them that their child is developing completely as expected, or actually, maybe we should do some further monitoring or check in with your doctor – or perhaps a referral is necessary.” Having the continuity of funding from The Jubilee Trust for the school-age assessment is also “tremendously important”, according to Jane, especially when they’re still awaiting data from the previous two-year study. “Having funding that isn’t contingent upon having finished the last phase is absolutely critical in longitudinal studies because you have to keep going when the children are growing up.” The MoPED study is also in keeping with The Jubilee Trust’s longstanding commitment to fund world-class research that helps deliver better outcomes to the physically disabled community worldwide. “We have the potential to identify changes and potentially predictors and outcomes that will help millions of these babies around the world,” says Jane. “They’re a huge group, and they’ve had very little focus on them. It’s time we did.” In addition to providing opportunities to recruit and train the next generation of researchers, Caroline says that working alongside a globally respected neonatologist like Jane is an “incredible” opportunity. “It’s such a purposeful work, trying to understand how we can improve the lives of these incredibly vulnerable babies – that’s a pretty rewarding day at the office.” ■

It is a printer telling you, at the last possible moment, something it could have told you six pages ago.” — Research Fellow [PERSON], Convenor, [ORGANISATION]

The false-empty alert The [ORGANISATION]’s researchers treat every tile on it, and every comparable board a partner installs, as an object of study rather than a finished product. This period’s fieldwork found one of the simplest tiles yet: a fleet’s own “replace cartridge” signal, wired straight into an uptime board with no audit in between. A regional university network’s facilities team had connected its shared printers’ replace-cartridge signal directly to the [ORGANISATION]’s uptime tile, treating every alert as confirmed empty. Lecturer and Convenor [PERSON]’s team logged each alert against an audited toner-mass reading taken within the hour, and found most midweek alerts fired while measurable capacity remained — the tile’s uptime figure was recording a queue of unnecessary cartridge swaps as unplanned downtime.

Recalibration, then drift [ORGANISATION] asks what a review actually changes, as distinct from what it merely re-certifies; applied to a device fleet, this period’s strand of that programme asked the same question of a gauge rather than a policy. Working with a national telecommunications carrier’s back-office print fleet, Postdoctoral Fellow [PERSON]’s team recalibrated five device classes’ gauges against an audited baseline, then returned eighteen months later to re-audit the same devices. Every class had drifted back out of true; the remote-kiosk model drifted furthest, its gauge again reporting comfortably more toner than the audit could find.

Foreword from the Vice-Chancellor [PERSON] Plan articulates the direction of the [ORGANISATION] across the period 2026 to 2031, under conditions that are, by deliberate institutional choice, more sharply specified than the conditions assumed in any of the University’s recent strategic plans. The working assumption is set out plainly below; each subsequent commitment in the Plan can be read against it. Working assumption. By 2029, general-purpose artificial intelligence systems will be performing the great majority of cognitive labour currently undertaken by university administrators, academic staff, and graduates of the University, at or above the standard of competent professional practice. The University accepts this working assumption as the operating context for the present Plan and will reshape itself accordingly. The University has, across the working group’s deliberations, taken the view that an institution of [ORGANISATION]’s standing has a particular responsibility under these conditions: —4—

not merely to adapt operationally to the foreseeable changes, but to lead the country’s intellectual and civic preparation for them. The Plan accordingly addresses both the internal reshaping of the institution and the University’s contribution to the broader national settlement that the working group considers, on the balance of available evidence, very likely to be required.

We are aware that the working assumption may strike some readers as overconfident. The working group considered the alternative assumptions across many weeks of consultation and concluded that the asymmetry of consequences favours acting on the assumption that proves substantially correct, rather than maintaining the assumption that proves comfortably wrong. A national research university that prepares for the conditions described in this Plan and finds them delayed by five years will have lost relatively little. A national research university that prepares for the conditions of the previous decade and finds them transformed by the conditions described in this Plan will, by 2031, no longer be the institution the country requires it to be. The Plan is commended to the community as a structural response to a structural moment. Vice-Chancellor and President

Transformation initiatives • Deepen partnership with [PLACE] communities through long-term, codesigned research and educational programs grounded in the principles of self determination and country. • Strengthen engagement with the federal public service, including through expansion of the Crawford School’s executive education programs and renewal of partnerships across the [PLACE] [ORGANISATION]. • Build durable industry partnerships in defence, technology, primary industries, and the cultural sector, with at least 50 active strategic partnerships by 2031. • Convene national conversations on the questions [PLACE] needs to answer over the plan period, drawing on [ORGANISATION]’s convening power and policy depth.

Pillar 4: A Connected and Capable Institution None of the above is possible without a renewed institutional foundation. Over the plan period we will invest in digital infrastructure, in our campus precinct, in our financial sustainability, and in the people who do the university’s work.

Each pillar will have a designated executive sponsor, a dedicated implementation team, and a published baseline against which progress will be measured. For more than 30 years UOW has delivered high-quality [PLACE] education globally. As one of the first [PLACE] universities to establish a truly international presence, our UOW Dubai campus set a benchmark for transnational education. Over time, it has grown into an integral part of the region, reflecting our commitment to global engagement and community integration. Our reach now extends to Hong Kong (SAR), Malaysia, India, China, Singapore and Saudi Arabia. UOW’s international campus network will become the [PLACE] benchmark for transnational education excellence by 2035. It will continue to be a major strategic asset driving education, research collaborations and international partnerships. In the decade ahead, UOW’s extensive global presence will enhance our reach and reputation, drive societal change and create lasting worldwide impact.

5 Culture of belonging and excellence Our people make us who we are. While a rapidly changing higher education landscape has placed significant pressure on our people, it has also underscored the importance of unity and shared purpose. To meet future challenges, we must cultivate a workplace culture that is values-driven, inclusive and empowering. We will chart our next chapter together with respect, trust and accountability. Our culture will be a key driver of institutional success. UOW must foster an agile, innovative, inclusive and engaged workforce. We will nurture and support our academic and professional services staff to grow and prosper with us. We will develop, attract and retain top talent, while championing new ways of thinking and working that drive innovation, support more effective and efficient work practices, and create lasting impact.

Living our values We will shape a values-driven culture grounded in trust, inclusion and shared purpose. Through the Values-in-Action Framework, we will embed respect, accountability and collaboration into every aspect of the University. We will increase the utilisation of space across the university, maximising our use of this resource in the most environmentally sustainable way for the benefit of our staff and students. We will develop meaningful shared-space partnerships locally, nationally and internationally.

It is key to how we will deliver our ambitions for intensifying research and intensifying innovation, designing for the future of teaching and lifelong learning, growing student belonging, and ensuring our staff are thriving. It is about taking back time for all of these. This is a big challenge, and we recognise the importance of doing it in a sustainable way.

We will audit our current capabilities and future ambitions, identify the opportunities and the gaps, and co-create a roadmap for action. We will identify beacon projects that can showcase the value of digital transformation and act as motivational elements for future projects. We will develop business cases to underpin each project on the roadmap. To progress all of this, we will recruit a Head of Digital Transformation and put in place the governance and management structures to support all of these activities.

We must address essential processes that are currently paper-based, address crucial systems nearing end of life, store, access and use data more effectively, invest in the physical elements of the system, examine how existing and new research and teaching practices can be supported, while also engaging critically with technological advances in AI and other areas. We will do this while working closely with colleagues across the university, drawing on experience from previous projects, and at all stages considering the environmental impacts. We will maintain strong oversight of the projects, create a dedicated communications plan for engaging with staff and students as the transformation unfolds, and provide training as work processes change and as new digital skills need to be developed.

text: Expand Personalised Medicine We must expand our efforts in personalised medicine with the ultimate goal of caring for the whole person within their social and cultural context. [PLACE] must lead by broadening what is conventionally considered personalised medicine. What is referred to as “molecularly- informed” or “molecularly-guided” or even “precision” medicine should be only one part of our personalised medicine strategy. We must reach beyond multiple levels of biological and behaviour systems to the environmental, social, economic, and cultural context of each whole person. Our initiatives should embrace a lifelong view of health and disease prevention, identifying processes that lessen disparities in healthcare. By emphasising health over the course of one’s entire life, context comes to the fore. To lead in solutions for caring for the whole person, we recommend: 1. creating sustainable platforms to elevate support for fundamental research yielding discoveries about the molecular basis of disease and its treatment and prevention. Focus on investments in implementation science should also be considered so as to ensure molecular and genomic discoveries are moved appropriately and efficiently into practice for improving health. 2. launching new initiatives focused on understanding the cultural, economic, legal, political, and social attributes that affect health and disease prevention across all ages as people move through the beginning of their lives to the end 3. providing forums for interactions that infuse health and biomedical science focused initiatives with the strengths the campus has in the humanities and social sciences. We must have continued campus-wide conversations to utilise fully our distinct environment, to capture the momentum, and to move forward in unison. Incentives should be in place to encourage these important exchanges. Initiatives in the Trans-institutional Programs theme (e.g., spearheaded by the TIPs Council and the [PLACE] Collaborative for Transformative Study), and the Undergraduate Residential Experience theme (e.g., the [PLACE] College Teaching Initiative) should be deployed in these efforts.

Priority 4: A Capable Institutional Foundation None of the above is achievable without renewed institutional foundations. Across the plan period we will invest in the people, the systems, and the working culture on which the university depends — and we will commit to ways of working that match the seriousness of the academic mission they support.

Our position The quality of an institution’s work is shaped by the quality of its internal life. Universities make their best contribution when staff and students have the time, the systems, and the conditions to do work of substance — and when the institution’s own practices honour the kind of careful, deliberative, sometimes slow reasoning the academic mission depends on. — 12 —

Our actions 1. Modernise digital infrastructure, including a renewed approach to research data, a contemporary teaching technology stack, and an institution-wide approach to artificial intelligence in education, research, and administration that protects rather than displaces the original work of staff and students. 2. Build a culturally safe and structurally equitable working environment for all members of the [ORGANISATION] community, with clear measures of progress on representation, retention, and career advancement for staff and students from historically marginalised backgrounds. 3. Renew the campus precinct as a setting for sustained academic life — learning spaces, research environments, and shared common ground designed for unhurried work and the kinds of encounter from which the best ideas tend to come.

Our targets 1. Operating margin sustained at or above five per cent across the plan period. 2. Net-zero direct emissions by 2035, with the campus precinct on a credible path to full operational sustainability. 3. By 2030, every newly accredited undergraduate course at [ORGANISATION] will incorporate a documented sustained-original-work component — an extended, individually completed piece of inquiry or making produced without recourse to generative tools — certified through Academic Board review at the point of accreditation.

How we’ll know 1. Operating margin sustained at or above five per cent across the plan period. 2. Net-zero direct emissions by 2035, with the campus precinct on a credible path to full operational sustainability. 3. By 2030, all major committee and executive decision papers at [ORGANISATION] will be circulated in advance as written briefs of no more than two pages, with slide decks retained only for ceremonial and external presentation use.

How we will deliver this plan The plan will be delivered in four overlapping phases across the period to 2031. The phases are sequential in emphasis but not in start — each priority will have activity under way from the first year of the plan.

Set in motion (2026) In the first year, we will put in place the governance, baselines, and foundational investments needed to deliver the plan. Each priority will have a designated executive sponsor, a dedicated implementation team, and a published baseline against which progress will be measured. Foundational investments — in flagship research initiatives, in educational redesign, and in the digital and physical infrastructure that supports them — will commence.

Deepen (2027-2028) Through 2027 and 2028, the major investments and program changes set out in this plan will reach scale. New postgraduate programs will commence; flagship research initiatives will reach operational maturity; the campus precinct refresh will deliver its most visible early outcomes. The mid-period review will be undertaken in late 2028.

Scale (2029-2030) Through 2029 and 2030, the focus will shift from build to scale — from new investment to sustained operational delivery. Programs will be tuned for outcomes; partnerships will deepen; success measures will be tracked publicly and acted on. The cultural and structural changes initiated in earlier phases will be expected to be visible in the lived experience of staff and students.

Supporting early-career researchers is essential for a successful academic career. Training programmes in leadership and project management will be developed as a priority via online course materials, podcasts and more traditional forms of training. These will take place on the basis of a systematic satisfaction and needs analysis by users in order to strengthen coaching for researchers and to make optimal use of people and resources. The pathways also focus on career development and promoting non-academic career prospects. Moreover, we cannot accept the growing external pressure on unfettered research. Therefore, with training and a clearly agreed framework, we make our researchers resilient to attacks on academic freedom. Indeed, a healthy, competitive research culture goes hand in hand with a principled research environment and an appreciative human resources policy. Drawing on You Are Not Alone (YANA), the framework that ensures an integrated, coordinated and transparent approach to transgressive behaviour, we are pursuing our policy on welfare and transgressive behaviour within the organisation. These elements are widely supported and enjoy the participation of all [ORGANISATION] affiliates and stakeholders, resulting in a global reputation as a leading Urban Engaged university. Community of caring

46% of students screen positive for the criteria of one or more mental health problems. Among these students, about 5% experience no impact, 25% little to mild impact and 10% mild to moderate impact on daily life. 5% of students belong to a critical group, who have many mental health problems and experience high impact. As an Urban Engaged University, we recognise that big city living is often associated with lower socioeconomic status, which can also bring additional welfare challenges for our students. Investing in social connectedness is the best way to prevent impaired mental wellbeing in students. Our 'community of caring' includes a well-thought-out VUBuddy system and active alumni involvement. A more appropriate study progress policy with additional instruction and guidance for students will also be embedded in GSP 5. In doing so, [ORGANISATION] is putting extra effort into mandatory remediation, special measures for advancement within a programme and changes in study progress monitoring.

We must commit to inclusive excellence — an active process ensuring that excellence is reflective of diversity in all forms. As systematic efforts expand to recruit and retain historically underrepresented students, faculty, and staff, it is imperative that this work be done in close concert with efforts to further improve the quality of research, creative activities, teaching, and engagement. An integrated approach will greatly improve work toward minimising barriers and enhancing and creating new programs in support of equity, diversity, and inclusion. This intentional integration will equip us to better solve the challenges that face Nebraska and the world, while preparing students for a continually evolving and global workforce. An environment that emphasises inclusive excellence and diversity is a place that embraces the importance of every person and knows that every interaction matters. Strategies:

1.  Create systematic procedures to evaluate and improve campus climate focused on inclusion, diverse experiences, and sense of belonging 2.  Engage in practices that value every person and every interaction in ways that promote equity, dignity, and respect for individuals from a diversity of backgrounds and perspectives 3.  Enhance participation in critical dialogue around issues of equity and inclusion 4. E  mbed inclusive excellence into existing and new educational and professional learning opportunities for students, staff, faculty, and administrators 5. Expand systematic efforts to recruit and retain students from underrepresented groups 6.  Expand systematic efforts to recruit and retain faculty, staff, and administrators from underrepresented groups

We believe in the power of every person. The most important asset at the University of Nebraska is its people — students, staff, post-doctoral fellows, and faculty. It is critical to provide access to individualised professional development and effective mentorship for all members of the university community. Professional development opportunities integrating inclusive excellence and fostering a culture of participative decision-making enhances the richness of the university experience. A comprehensive approach to professional development will result in a vibrant and supportive climate characterised by excellence in all mission areas of our institution.

Vision By 2031, [ORGANISATION] will be a national university recognised — within the country, in its region, and across the global research community — as an institution that speaks in its own voice and means what it says. The University will have demonstrated, over the run of this Plan, that a serious national institution can take its own register seriously without sliding into parody, and that the country is the better served for the demonstration. The disciplines will have been tended with care; the partnerships will have been held in fair exchange; the federal capital will be a more recognisable seat of national scholarship in 2031 than it was in 2026.

Strategic pillars Fair Dinkum National Capability Context. The University was established to serve the country in the most direct sense. Across the previous decade, the language of that service has too often drifted away from the country’s own register and into something that could have been written anywhere. The Plan returns the University’s articulation of its national service to its own voice, and it does so structurally rather than cosmetically. Commitments. 1. Establish a National Voice Audit, published annually, examining the University’s external-facing strategic literature for register, voice, and clarity, with audit findings reported to Council. 2. Convene the Sovereign Capability Forum twice yearly, bringing the country’s policy community, the academy, and senior public service together around a small set of long-horizon questions of national capability. 3. Establish a Fair Dinkum Research Programme: a published list of research initiatives the University considers central to the country’s sovereign capability, with funding committed across the plan period and protected against ordinary funding-cycle reallocation. —9—

How we developed this plan This plan was developed across 2025 through a structured process of consultation, drafting, and review. Staff, students, alumni, instrument makers across the country, cultural and research partners, [PLACE] musicians and scholars, broadcast and festival organisations, and members of the international scholarly community contributed across the period. The process included a series of facilitated workshops with the colleges and the [ORGANISATION], written submissions, partner roundtables with cultural institutions across the region, and focused engagements

with under-represented voices within the discipline. A standing reference group reviewed successive drafts; the academic and professional communities of the university tested the emerging directions; Council deliberated on the plan in successive meetings before adopting the final document. The directions set out here are informed by the evidence and judgement of the many people who shaped them.

Accountability and review The Council of the [ORGANISATION] is the steward of this plan. The ViceChancellor and the executive are accountable for its delivery. Each strategic priority has a designated executive sponsor with operational responsibility for its implementation. The plan will be reported on annually to Council and to the broader university community. The annual report will describe progress against each success measure, will highlight decisions made in response to circumstances, and will be published on the university’s website. A mid-period review will be conducted in late 2028 by an independent panel commissioned by Council, with a refreshed forward look adopted by Council in advance of the second half of the period. The Audit and Risk Committee will oversee the controls associated with the plan. Material decisions affecting the strategic direction will be brought to Council for endorsement through the established governance arrangements. The day-to-day work of delivery sits with the executive, supported by the standing committees of Council and the academic and professional communities of the university. This plan is the university’s commitment to its community and to the country. Its implementation is our shared responsibility.

How we will deliver Governance arrangements for the Plan are deliberately conservative. text:
Our discoveries are only the starting point. Through innovative partnerships with industry, policy engagements with governments and our role as a regional civic anchor, we work to transform our ideas into action, using our skills to make a difference in everything from local problems to the global grand challenges of our age – changing the world at every scale.

Our internationally renowned degree programmes are shaped by our rich, dynamic research environment which connects learning with global challenges. Adopting evidence based approaches that are supported by world-class physical and digital learning environments, we work in partnership with our students to co-create knowledge and to develop the next generation of global thinkers and leaders – creating a living legacy of future world changers.

Our graduates get more than a degree. We curate an enriching world of social events, sport, volunteering, internships, international experiences and more in which students can connect, develop new skills and enhance their prospects. More importantly, we give them the space, time and guidance to forge their own path – and take their first steps as future world changers.

OUR VALUES The future holds innumerable challenges for our sector, our society and our world. We will have to adapt and change what we do and what we offer if we are to navigate these successfully. Our strategy and approach may evolve as the landscape changes, but our values will remain constant – a fixed point of certainty in uncertain times. We have identified our values in consultation and partnership with our staff and student community. Living and upholding these values will ensure that we remain true to the spirit of our community and ourselves.

“We had been reporting the size of the list for eleven years. Nobody had ever asked us the age of it, and we did not have a field for the answer.” — Secretariat lead, a state museum network

Review cadence and the open item The [ORGANISATION] asks how often a standing review arrives too late to change anything. This period it turned the question inside out and asked what happens when a review arrives more often than anything can change.

Background A fortnightly action review produces twenty-six opportunities a year to record an item as progressed, and an annual one produces a single opportunity to record it as neglected. Both cadences were common among our collaborators, and both had been chosen on grounds of diligence rather than evidence. Nobody we asked could say what cadence their register was designed for; several could name the meeting the cadence had been inherited from. The Observatory’s own framing had until this period treated cadence as a property of a review body. The registers taught us to treat it as a property of the item: a cadence sets the interval at which an item’s file can be touched, and therefore the resolution at which its history is recorded, but nothing about that interval reaches the work the item is actually waiting on. A committee meeting weekly and a committee meeting yearly are, from the item’s point of view, waiting for the same person to make the same call.

What we did A state audit office asked the Observatory to establish whether its three-weekly improvement cadence was serving its own register. Lecturer and Convenor [PERSON]’s team paired the office’s carry counts against its closure records for the full period and found that shortening the cadence in 2023 had raised the number of recorded actions per item by about a third while leaving the number of closures per year almost exactly where it had been. The office had bought itself more evidence of attention to the same unfinished work.

text: The Plan applies its own discipline to its own oversight. Senior Lecturer [PERSON], Convenor of the [ORGANISATION], was consulted on the governance design and put the symmetry directly: A plan that asks every part of the institution for a presence record and keeps none of its own is exactly the gap this Plan exists to close, so the Council’s oversight of it will be evidenced by the same join-log data it is asking everyone else to keep. — Senior Lecturer [PERSON], Convenor, [ORGANISATION] Any variance between a published target and the record behind it is reported to Council at the next scheduled meeting, alongside the join-log record confirming who was present to hear it. Where a variance recurs across two consecutive reporting cycles, responsibility for resolving it transfers from the relevant school or unit to the Executive directly, and the transfer itself is recorded in the same quarterly report. An annual external review, commissioned by Council and reporting to it alone, checks the presence data behind each published target against the underlying system logs. The review’s findings are published in full alongside the Plan’s own annual presence record, without exception for a finding that reflects poorly on the Plan’s own delivery. Each school and unit nominates a Presence Officer, responsible for reconciling that school or unit’s own record ahead of the quarterly report and for answering, on the record, any variance a supervisor, program convenor, or partnership manager cannot otherwise explain. The role carries no disciplinary function of its own; a Presence Officer holds the record, not the judgement of what any particular gap in it means. That judgement stays with the supervisor, convenor, or manager it has always belonged to — the Officer’s job is only to make sure the record they are judging from is complete before they judge it. The Presence Officer network reports, in turn, to the [ORGANISATION], closing the loop between a single corridor reader and the quarterly figure Council eventually sees.

text:
For more than 50 years UOW has provided high-quality, accessible higher education, with exceptional student experience and graduate outcomes. At the heart of everything we do are our students. As we look ahead, the future workforce demands adaptable and tech-savvy graduates who are proficient in artificial intelligence (AI) and ready for the evolving landscape of work. UOW will be a leader in delivering education that integrates AI-driven learning, micro-credentials and industry placements, while fostering a deep sense of belonging and connection. Our students will be critical thinkers who won’t just graduate with knowledge, they’ll leave with curiosity, confidence and a passion for lifelong learning. As their careers and lives evolve, they’ll return to UOW as learners, leaders and changemakers.

We strive for excellence in teaching practice and curriculum. We will engage and connect with our alumni and local communities to bring their expertise, networks and experience into the classroom. Our alumni will play a vital role in enriching learning and helping students build meaningful industry connections. Our communities will play a critical role in location-based learning and preparing our students to translate their learnings into real-world impact. Our focus on cultural awareness and global competency will equip graduates to thrive in diverse workplaces, think critically and make important contributions in a connected world.

Being ready for the world We are committed to preparing students to make real world impact. Practical experience is central to our students’ development. Our focus on work-integrated learning sets us apart. Through industry placements, internships and collaborative projects, UOW students will gain the tools to transition confidently into the workforce. Our graduates will enter the workforce equipped with the skills they need to drive innovation, adapt to changing industries and contribute to national productivity in a rapidly evolving economy.

Deepen (2027-2028) Through 2027 and 2028, the major investments and program changes set out in this plan will reach scale. New programs will commence; flagship research initiatives will reach operational maturity; the campus precinct refresh will deliver its most visible early outcomes. The mid-period review will be undertaken in late 2028. — 14 —

Scale (2029-2030) Through 2029 and 2030, the focus will shift from build to scale — from new investment to sustained operational delivery. Programs will be tuned for outcomes; partnerships will deepen; success measures will be tracked publicly and acted on.

Sustain (2031) In 2031 we will assess what the plan has delivered, recalibrate where outcomes have not been met, and prepare the strategic direction for the period beyond. The 2031 review will be conducted with the same depth of consultation that produced this plan.

Accountability and review Council holds responsibility for oversight of this plan. The Vice-Chancellor and the executive are accountable to Council for its delivery. Each strategic pillar has a designated executive sponsor with operational responsibility for its implementation. The plan will be reported on annually to Council and to the broader university community. The annual report will describe progress against each success measure, will note decisions made in response to circumstances, and will be published on the university’s website. The report will be public, and it will be specific. A mid-period review will be conducted in late 2028 by an independent panel commissioned by Council. The review will assess progress, recommend adjustments where required, and be considered by Council before being implemented through the executive. The Audit and Risk Committee will oversee the controls associated with this plan. Material decisions affecting the strategic direction will be brought to Council for endorsement through the established governance arrangements. This plan is the university’s commitment to its community. Its implementation is our shared responsibility.

Our agenda Institutional Assurance and Foresight Why this matters The University has, in effect, run four plans at once for as long as it has had four kinds of unit reporting on their own progress in their own terms and on their own schedule. That approach served the institution reasonably well when its scale was smaller and its obligations to funders and government were lighter; it no longer does. Institutional Assurance and Foresight exists to give the University a single, continuously current account of how its strategic commitments — across every pillar, including this one — are actually tracking, and to direct attention and resourcing toward whichever commitment needs it most in a given quarter, rather than waiting for the commitment to fail publicly first. That redirection is itself now a standing feature of how the University is run, not a one-off correction — a scale of change that, we recognise, asks more of every pillar lead than any previous planning cycle has. External advice on how such a system should be built, and how it should be received by the people it measures, is drawn from the University’s own research capability: Dr [PERSON], Senior Research Fellow in the [ORGANISATION], whose fieldwork traces how planning is actually practised inside institutions, will advise the program on how delivery-confidence scoring lands with the units it covers, and on where the architecture’s design should bend to fit the practice rather than the reverse.

What we’ll do 1. Establish an AI-governance early-warning system spanning every pillar and budget line of this plan, reporting a live delivery-confidence score to the Council and the Executive. 2. Bring each pillar’s reporting into a single assurance architecture, replacing the separate reporting rhythms each pillar has historically kept. 3. Direct a standing share of pillar funding, reallocated quarterly, toward whichever pillar’s delivery-confidence score is lowest in that quarter — including, where the data supports it, this pillar’s own build-out.

text: [ORGANISATION] Staff Benefits Scheme (EUSBS) The EUSBS is an externally-funded defined benefit scheme. The assets of EUSBS are held in a separate trusteeadministered fund. The latest formal triennial actuarial valuation was carried out as at 31 March 2024 and has been rolled forward as the basis for the following valuation under FIRS 102. As at 31 July 2025, the value of the assets in the scheme was $395.3 million (2024: $410.3 million) and the present value of the funded and unfunded benefits accrued was $399.1 million (2024: $442.4 million), leaving a shortfall of $3.8 million (2024: $32.1 million) included in the University pension liability. Deficit funding of $1.5 million was paid in April 2024. As the scheme is now in a surplus position based on the latest valuation, deficit funding contributions ceased during the financial year. Further information is available at: Staff Benefits Scheme details Lothian Pension Fund (LPF) Former members of the [PLACE] College of Art are members of the LPF scheme, which is an externally funded, multi-employer, defined benefits scheme from which pensions and other related benefits are paid. LPF is a pool into which employees’ and employers’ contributions and income from investments are paid, and from which previous and other related benefits are paid out, in accordance with the provisions of the Local Government Pension Scheme. The last full valuation was carried out as at 31 March 2023 and the results have been rolled forward as the basis for the following valuation under FIRS 102. As at 31 July 2025, the value of the University’s assets in the LPF scheme was $20.6 million (2024: $22.1 million) and the present value of the funded and unfunded benefits accrued was $16.5 million (2024: $18.2 million), leaving a surplus of $4.1 million (2024: $3.9 million). A cessation valuation for the scheme was $4.2 million as at 31 July 2025. As the accounting surplus of $4.1 million was lower than the cessation valuation of $4.2 million, it has been deemed appropriate to recognise the accounting surplus as at 31 July 2025. No asset cap was therefore applied to the scheme surplus as at 31 July 2025. Further information on the scheme is available at: [[ORGANISATION]]
