As at 31 July 2025, the value of the assets in the scheme was $395.3 million (2024: $410.3 million) and the present value of the funded and unfunded benefits accrued was $399.1 million (2024: $442.4 million), leaving a shortfall of $3.8 million (2024: $32.1 million) included in the University pension liability. Deficit funding of $1.5 million was paid in April 2024. As the scheme is now in a surplus position based on the latest valuation, deficit funding contributions ceased during the financial year. Further information is available at: Staff Benefits Scheme details [ORGANISATION] Former members of the [PLACE] College of Art are members of the LPF scheme, which is an externally funded, multi-employer, defined benefits scheme from which pensions and other related benefits are paid. LPF is a pool into which employees’ and employers’ contributions and income from investments are paid, and from which previous and other related benefits are paid out, in accordance with the provisions of the [ORGANISATION]. The last full valuation was carried out as at 31 March 2023 and the results have been rolled forward as the basis for the following valuation under FIRS 102. As at 31 July 2025, the value of the University’s assets in the LPF scheme was $20.6 million (2024: $22.1 million) and the present value of the funded and unfunded benefits accrued was $16.5 million (2024: $18.2 million), leaving a surplus of $4.1 million (2024: $3.9 million). A cessation valuation for the scheme was $4.2 million as at 31 July 2025. As the accounting surplus of $4.1 million was lower than the cessation valuation of $4.2 million, it has been deemed appropriate to recognise the accounting surplus as at 31 July 2025. No asset cap was therefore applied to the scheme surplus as at 31 July 2025. Further information on the scheme is available at: [[ORGANISATION]]

Accident in the Studio and the Lab Why this matters. Across the creative, experimental, and computational disciplines, accident has been a generative force in inquiry: the unforeseen plate that initiates a body of work, the mis-set parameter that opens a line of investigation, the slipped exposure that becomes a method. The institutions in which these disciplines are housed rarely teach accident explicitly. [ORGANISATION] will treat accident as a teachable practice, distinct from method but not opposed to it.

What we’ll do. 1. The University will establish the [ORGANISATION] Glitch Studio at the [ORGANISATION] & [PLACE] as a teaching and research facility devoted to studied error in digital, analogue, and hybrid media, with a charter mandating annual artist residencies drawn from the international hybrid-media community. 2. The University will convene the cross-college Accident Working Group, with terms of reference requiring it to develop a shared institutional vocabulary for productive accident across disciplinary contexts and to publish its working glossary annually. 3. An “accident reasoning” capability will be embedded into all 4000-level coursework offerings in the College of Science and the [ORGANISATION] by 2028, sequenced across the second half of each unit. 4. The University will establish the Failed Experiment Archive: a permanent, indexed institutional record of significant unsuccessful experiments conducted at the University from 2026 onward, deposited within twelve months of experimental conclusion. How we’ll know. • Eighty per cent of taught laboratory units at 3000 level and above will publish an annual “instructive accidents” report by 2029, sustained at that level through the remainder of the plan period. • The Glitch Studio will operate an indexed public exhibition program of no fewer than three exhibitions per year by 2028, with each exhibition accompanied by a published catalogue of its methodological declarations.

y Our signature curriculum will prepare students to apply knowledge in practice – through problem based interdisciplinary projects and partner enabled learning rooted in our public mission. It will expose students to diverse perspectives, give them access to our world-leading facilities and help them to challenge dominant narratives and understand the world from multiple viewpoints. This also means equipping our teaching colleagues with the time, tools and support to innovate with confidence.

y Our research platforms will feed directly into our teaching – giving students exposure to cutting edge ideas and opportunities to contribute to discovery. This will develop the skills and mindset employers value – from collaboration and adaptability to civic consciousness and the ability to move between disciplines.

At the same time, we will enhance our on-campus community through better services,

y Assessment will shift to competency-based progression and applied tasks that reflect what students can do, not just what they know. Immersive technologies will expand what’s possible in teaching – through virtual fieldwork, simulations and more inclusive forms of engagement. y Employability will be a core outcome – with stronger career pathways through alumni mentoring and the UK’s widest range of paid roles during study.

To establish important areas and create new impetus, the university should be able to use strategic resources quickly and flexibly. Start-up funding for projects that are not yet part of long-term plans should be increasingly financed by external funding (foundations, industry collaborations). – Establishment of a strategic reserve to fund initiatives with significant academic potential. – Support with preparing the application for competitive funding programs.

Efficient research infrastructure and Core Facilities are essential in many experimental scientific fields in order to conduct successful research. Due to the high methodological expertise of its employees, Core Facilities assume the role of a technology leader and provide all scientists at the [ORGANISATION] with effective and cost-efficient access to state-of-the-art research methods. – Ensure the research infrastructure required for internationally competitive top-level research. – Ongoing expansion and evaluation of strategically important Core Facilities.

To react nimbly and rapidly to changes and opportunities, an interdisciplinary advisory board will be set up to advise the President’s Board on strategic issues related to expansion of research, and to identify up-and-coming, promising areas of research as early as possible. In addition to designated researchers at the [ORGANISATION], recognised external experts from [PLACE] and abroad will be represented on this advisory board. – Establishment of an interdisciplinary advisory board at the level of the President’s Board. Provide an optimum research environment Appointment and promotion policy

Researchers’ individual achievements, embedded within the university context and its objectives, form the basis of the [ORGANISATION]’s reputation and visibility. It is therefore imperative to have a consistent appointment policy based on excellence in order to secure the [ORGANISATION]’s long-term position. – Optimise and expedite appointment and promotion processes. – More flexible, performance and demand-based equipment approvals processes.

In order to elevate the trajectory of [PLACE] A&M as a world-leading land-, sea-, and space-grant research university requires us to attract outstanding talent – faculty, students, and staff – to join us. We must build a strong portfolio of funders, collaborators, partners, and solution seekers to invest their resources, both time and treasure, in our shared vision. We must improve and expand the physical and organizational infrastructure of [PLACE] A&M to serve as an ever-brighter beacon for the creation and application of new knowledge. We must also communicate to a broad audience why the research we do matters.

Increase the breadth and scope of our research As our programs continue to advance, [PLACE] A&M will develop new approaches to assess and to cultivate our progress in multidisciplinary research and its synergistic impacts. At the same time, to benchmark our progress we will continue to focus on traditional metrics such as external support of our research portfolio, research facilities and capabilities, scholarly productivity and impact, partnerships with industry and national labs, and more. To broaden [PLACE] A&M’s reach into the unknown realms of discovery, we will:

Expand the importance and impact of our research on [PLACE], the nation, and the planet Opportunities abound to bring together the extraordinary talents of the [PLACE] A&M community of researchers and scholars to tackle scientific and societal challenges by developing new knowledge, new tools, and new approaches drawn from all fields of creativity and scholarship. text: [PLACE] the Trajectory Early Why this matters. A commitment made without evidence of the trajectory it backs is a commitment the University discovers the shape of only after making it — in the first year of an appointment, the first term of an enrolment, the first cycle of a partnership. [PLACE] the trajectory early moves that discovery to before the offer is drafted, where it is still cheap to be wrong. The appointing panel or admissions committee that reads the trajectory late is not being careless; it is simply working with the only evidence the process gave it, gathered after the decision it was meant to inform. What we’ll do. 1. Every advertised continuing and fixed-term academic and professional role will require a trajectory portfolio — a structured account of the candidate’s likely next five years, evidenced against commitments the candidate has previously made and kept — alongside the standard application, reviewed by the appointing panel before an offer is drafted. 2. Every Higher Degree by Research and coursework admission will carry a trajectory statement at the point of offer, held by the enrolling school and revisited at the candidate’s first formal milestone. 3. The [ORGANISATION] will publish a common portfolio template and scoring rubric, adopted by every appointment panel and admissions committee by the end of 2027, with no locally authored alternative permitted to persist past a single review cycle. 4. Application systems will present the trajectory portfolio and the standard application as a single combined submission from 2028, so a candidate completes one process rather than two. How we’ll know. • 100% of continuing and fixed-term academic appointments will draw on a completed trajectory portfolio before an offer is extended, from 2027 onward, with no waiver sustained for more than a single recruitment cycle. • Portfolio review turnaround will hold at fewer than 15 business days from submission to panel recommendation, reported each term. • By 2029, every admissions committee across both Schools will use the common rubric, retiring locally authored alternatives entirely. • Candidate-reported completion time for the combined submission will be published each admissions cycle from 2028, alongside the completion rate.

Transformation initiatives • Move beyond first-generation reconciliation work toward structural transformation — including a renewed [ORGANISATION], sustained investment in [PLACE]-led research, and a long-term commitment to truth-telling about the university’s own history. • Strengthen engagement with the federal public service, including through expansion of executive education and renewal of partnerships across the [PLACE] [ORGANISATION]. • Build durable partnerships with civil-society organisations, primary industries, and the cultural sector, with at least 50 active strategic partnerships by 2031. • Convene national conversations on the questions [PLACE] needs to answer over the plan period, drawing on [ORGANISATION]’s convening power and the depth of expertise across the university.

Pillar 4: Stewardship and Renewal None of the above is possible without renewed institutional foundations. Over the plan period we will invest in the digital, physical, and human infrastructure on which [ORGANISATION] depends, and we will work toward an institutional culture in which every member of the community can do their best work.

Transformation initiatives • Modernise digital infrastructure, including a renewed approach to research data, a modernised teaching technology stack, and an institution-wide approach to artificial intelligence in education and research. • Refresh the campus precinct as a working environment fit for the next twenty-five years, with sustained investment in heritage assets, contemporary teaching spaces, and student amenities. • Build a culturally safe and structurally equitable working environment for all members of the [ORGANISATION] community, with clear measures of progress on representation, retention, and career advancement for staff and students from historically marginalised backgrounds. • Strengthen financial sustainability through diversified revenue, philanthropic capability uplift, and operational excellence in the university’s professional services functions.

Establish (2026) In the first year, we will put in place the governance, baselines, and foundational investments needed to deliver the plan. Each pillar will have a designated executive sponsor, a dedicated implementation team, and a published baseline against which progress will be measured. Foundational investments — in digital infrastructure, in flagship research initiatives, and in educational redesign — will commence.

text:
Global rankings are an important tool for attracting academic staff, students, and high-value partnerships, and for increasing research and international student income. As such, they help provide the platform for us to undertake high-impact research across the University, including in areas of importance to our [PLACE] and [PLACE] communities. While rankings are a far from perfect measures of quality, they are increasingly important in a competitive global environment, especially given that [PLACE] Government investment is significantly constrained and prioritised elsewhere. Our rankings have declined significantly in recent years. The measures underpinning the rankings indicate that we need to dramatically improve the communication of our research impact and quality to the world. Increasing our efforts to demonstrate impact to the [PLACE] community will help to maintain the University’s social licence and accountability, and aid in increasing government funding for research. Action: Ensure that effective support mechanisms (such as strategic communications and marketing, media training, conference attendance, and publication support) are in place to strengthen the ability of our researchers to showcase their research.

Partnerships are critical to delivering much of our research, such as our relationship with the health sector that facilitates much of our clinical research. However, formal partnerships require investment to develop and resourcing to maintain, therefore careful decision-making is required on which partnerships the University pursues, to ensure they deliver value to both sides of the partnership. Our current approach to research partnerships has resulted in many partnerships without sufficient scale or alignment to deliver optimal value. We must adopt a more strategic approach to partnership development to increase the impact of our partnerships. Action: Focus our efforts in current and new research partnership development, using criteria including strategic alignment, alignment with research focus areas, opportunity for growth into other areas of the University, and financial sustainability.

text:
Vice-Chancellor’s introduction This is the [ORGANISATION]’s strategic plan for the period 2026 to 2031. It sets out the directions the University will pursue over the next phase of its institutional life, and the choices we have made in setting them. The plan reflects our continuing commitment to research excellence, to the depth and seriousness of our educational programs, and to the partnerships through which a national university actually meets the country it serves. It also reflects the recognition that the work of a university is undertaken on a long horizon — shaped by problems we have only begun to see clearly, and by futures whose outlines remain to be drawn.

The directions in this plan have been informed by extensive consultation with our staff, students, alumni, partners, and Council. They are deliberate. They reflect choices made carefully, and they will require sustained effort to deliver. The Hybrid Media Studio will be established at the [ORGANISATION] & [PLACE], equipped for analogue printmaking, screen-based composition, and computational image-making within a single integrated floor plan and a shared teaching faculty. 2. A faculty-wide Visual Literacy Capability will be developed, spanning typography, diagrammatic reasoning, generative pipelines, and image provenance, with sequenced offerings available to every academic and professional staff member from 2028. 3. The University will convene the biennial [PLACE] Hybrid Media Workshop, hosted in alternating years with a partner institution drawn from the [PLACE] region. Indicators. • All [ORGANISATION] institutional publications will carry a per-figure provenance declaration by 2029, with no exception sustained for more than a single review cycle.

Stewardship of Tools and Methods Context. The University’s collective methodological inheritance — the tools, forms, notations, and conventions through which research is done — has historically been the private business of individual disciplines. In an environment in which the methodological substrate is itself in motion, [ORGANISATION] will steward this inheritance as a shared scholarly asset.

Commitments. 1. The [ORGANISATION] Methods Office will be established, reporting to the Deputy ViceChancellor (Research), to maintain the institution’s tools-and-methods register and to convene methodological renewal across the disciplines. 2. A “Methodological Heritage” capstone unit will be developed and made available to honours-level students in every undergraduate program offered by the University, with sequenced delivery from 2028. 3. The University will stand up an annual Methods Review, audited externally, of all major research infrastructure decisions taken at college level or above, with findings published openly within ninety days of review completion. Indicators. — 12 —

• One hundred per cent of new [ORGANISATION] research centres established from 2027 will publish a Methodological Inheritance Statement within twelve months of standing up, with no exception sustained for more than a single review cycle. • The Methods Office will release a publicly downloadable Methods Inventory annually from 2028, including version, custodianship, and intended-use envelope per entry. • A published five-year audit of tools-and-methods adoption across the four colleges, released in 2031 to inform the strategic cycle that follows.

[ORGANISATION] STRATEGIC ADVISORY COMMITTEE In January 2020, [ORGANISATION] started a strategic planning process that began with envisioning alternative futures, each rooted in elements of [ORGANISATION]’s history and proven successes. With these futures as a foundation for creative exploration, a 22-member advisory committee comprised of faculty and staff representatives from across the University worked to identify current and possible initiatives that could be scaled to help the University more fully achieve its mission. The team analysed over 73 initiatives for impact and ability to scale – and then categorised them within four key mission areas: teaching and learning, research, community impact and leadership. Through discussion and analysis of initiatives, the committee then identified unique strengths that not only define who we are as an institution, but that also give us clear advantages for where we want to be in 10 years: our place, our people, our culture of care and our engagement with partners. With these strengths and advantages guiding the process, a core team from the advisory committee worked to bridge

recommendations from the larger group with input from campus leadership and from faculty and staff colleagues throughout the campus community. Draft after draft of strategic advantages, goals and initiatives, pathways and possibilities began to emerge, each more fully reaffirming the importance of our mission and our clear purpose in higher education. Metrics quickly followed, providing us with a compass and a means for assessing how well we are accomplishing our goals. Drafts were shared formally and informally and, as ideas were refined with college, school, and research leaders, department heads and Cabinet members, the value of the plan was deepened by the process of collective planning. With this plan in place, the real work of the campus community will begin. And, while we know that there will be bumps along the way, we believe our vision is based on a solid foundation of who we are and who we can become.

Transformation initiatives • Renew the undergraduate experience around inquiry, judgement, and a substantive engagement with the methodological and intellectual traditions of the disciplines we teach. • Embed the methodological vocabulary of integrated design pedagogy — the foundational course, the project-based seminar, the technical-cultural integration — across the undergraduate experience, in active dialogue with the disciplinary depth of the schools. • Lift HDR completions and reduce mean time-to-completion through redesigned candidature support and renewed supervisory frameworks. • Embed a plurality of knowledges across the curriculum — including substantive engagement with [PLACE] methodologies and critical perspectives in disciplines that have historically marginalised them.

Pillar 3: Place, Partnership, and Country Universities flourish through their relationships with the communities they serve — and they fail when those relationships are characterised by extraction rather than partnership. Over the plan period we will deepen our engagement, take honest steps toward reconciliation, and renew the standing partnerships through which the work of a national university actually reaches the country.

Transformation initiatives • Move beyond first-generation reconciliation work toward structural transformation — including a renewed [ORGANISATION], sustained investment in [PLACE]-led research, and a long-term commitment to truth-telling about the university’s own history. • Strengthen engagement with the federal public service, including through the expansion of executive education and the renewal of partnerships across the [PLACE] [ORGANISATION]. • Build durable partnerships with civil-society organisations, industry, and the cultural sector, with a particular focus on the institutions that anchor the country’s public and intellectual life. • Convene national conversations on the questions [PLACE] needs to answer over the plan period, drawing on [ORGANISATION]’s convening power and the depth of expertise across the university.

By committing to ensuring the ability of University graduates to operate in a global environment, we will create conditions for all students to engage in global exchanges of scientific ideas through physical or virtual mobility, as well as an international subject content. The internationality of studies at the University will be developed by increasing the internationality of the study environment and by implementing internationalization plans of each study program. For the internationalization of research and studies, we will use the opportunities provided by Arqus the [PLACE] University Alliance – an innovative and open laboratory for institutional learning. We will create long-term, sustainable structures and mechanisms of close inter-institutional cooperation in the fields of studies, research and social partnership.

Core research and innovation values The university’s core research and innovation values hold broad consensus and will underpin our institutional research and innovation strategy for the next five years. These values were developed in consultation with the wider [ORGANISATION] community in alignment with the Statement of Institutional Purpose ratified by the [ORGANISATION]’s Governing Council.

Our strategic objectives will inform and propel [ORGANISATION]’s research and innovation and performance measures over the next five years. They will help us continue to be one of the world’s top research intensive universities and to address global challenges. These objectives complement those of the academic divisions as they continue to develop their own plans, goals, actions and performance measures.

Inclusive excellence and leadership in research and innovation allow us to have the broadest and deepest impact in scholarship and on society. We will continue to lead in research funding, global rankings and international recognition of our academic excellence, and through our successes in innovation and entrepreneurship.

We will provide all members of our scholarly community with the necessary supports they need to be successful and competitive. We will create and refine tools, policies, best practices and procedures that advance research and innovation, ensuring the highest standards of ethics, integrity and accountability.

Our research and teaching missions are inextricably linked. Research-informed teaching innovations, standards and practices enhance the entire educational mission and position the university as the top destination for future students, postdoctoral fellows, researchers and innovators. Our innovation and entrepreneurship community provides mentorship, expertise, space and networks for all stages of the innovation journey for students and faculty. These programs not only strengthen existing areas of excellence and develop new ones, but they also increase synergies between teaching and research.

The mid-period review will be undertaken in late 2028.

Driver 1 Daring to be different: Building a new model of co-operative education and research that seamlessly integrates work and study. We are embedding co-operative education across every level of study – from certificate to PhD – making real-world learning the hallmark of a [PLACE] experience.

Inspired by global leaders in Co-op education and tailored to [PLACE]’s needs, our model integrates work and study without extending time to graduation. Learners gain valuable experience while earning their qualifications, accelerating career outcomes and improving graduate salaries.

The Co-op model is embedded in our research through strong industry partnerships and global collaborations. In our Higher Degrees by Research (HDR) programs, this includes co-designing, co-supervising and co-funding projects with industry partners, alongside opportunities for PhD candidates to undertake research internships. Our growing network of Co-op partners includes global firms like IBM, Ernst & Young and Accenture, who co-recruit and train learners on campus.

We’re committed to remaining among the top universities in [PLACE] for employability and starting salary. By enabling placements alongside study, we’ll ensure graduates are ready to work from day one – with many learners transitioning directly into roles with their placement hosts. Through paid placements we’ll further breakdown financial barriers – boosting equity, access and making education and real-world experience more accessible to a diverse range of learners.

By 2040, we aim to have thousands of active partners across diverse sectors – co-designing curriculum, hosting learners, upskilling staff and co-investing in facilities like our campus-based technology parks. These partnerships will create a strong pipeline of talent research, innovation and opportunity, with employers turning to [PLACE] as their university of choice. Co-op will shape how we deliver education, research and support services. It will become a whole-of-university ethos – guiding every decision and driving strategic transformation.

Third, judgement-based assurance is already the sector’s quiet practice. Peer review, examiners’ reports, promotion committees, and accreditation panels all rest, in the final instance, on the trained sense of the people in the room; the surrounding documentation records the judgement rather than producing it. This Plan does not introduce felt sense into the University’s assurance arrangements. It acknowledges the position felt sense already occupies, and resources it accordingly. Fourth, the University holds a distinctive institutional capability in this domain. The [ORGANISATION] brings two decades of scholarship on evaluation ecosystems and metric stewardship; the [ORGANISATION] brings the anticipatory and foresight practices through which an institution senses conditions before they are recorded. Few institutions are better placed to make attunement rigorous, and the University regards the opportunity as strategic rather than incidental. Read together, these features ask the University for a deliberate posture rather than an incremental one. The posture this Plan adopts is set out in the ambition that follows. —6—

Our ambition By 2031, [ORGANISATION] will be the institution whose quality is assured by the calibrated, collective, and accountable felt sense of its own community. Quality at the University will be something its practitioners recognise together, in structured settings, on the record, and at the point where quality is made rather than where it is later documented. The instruments that once stood in for that recognition will have been honourably retired; the community that replaces them will be accredited, renewed, and trusted — inside the institution and beyond it — to know good work when it feels it.

Foreword from the Vice-Chancellor [PERSON] Plan articulates the direction of the [ORGANISATION] across the period 2026 to 2031. The Plan is framed, throughout, by the institutional legacy of [PERSON], the University’s most consequential alumnus, whose centenary falls in the final year of the plan period. It is not the working group’s view, and it is not Council’s view, that institutional planning should reach unduly into the past. The view that has emerged across consultation, however, is that the [PERSON] tradition — often referred to in the University’s older literature simply as “the [PERSON] disposition” — continues to distinguish [ORGANISATION] from the institutions with which it is most often compared, and that the centenary year provides a structural occasion for the University to take fresh form around the disposition rather than merely commemorate its founder.

The disposition is well documented. [PERSON] characterised it, variously, as “the patient examination of the half-baked”, “the work of taking the unbaked seriously”, and, in the often-cited formulation from the 1948 notebook, “the discipline of recognising what is, in fact, packaged for use”. It produced, across the productive period of the 1920s and 1930s, the inventions for which he remains best known — the wooden magnet, the boxed spark plug sparks, the bottled spirit-level bubbles, the dehydrated water pills, the clockwork motor vehicle, and the around-the-corner hammer, among others — and it shaped the institutional culture of the University in ways that have continued, with admirable consistency, across the eight decades since. The Plan accordingly addresses the [PERSON] tradition as a substantive institutional commitment. It does so across four priorities — the [PERSON] legacy itself, the [PERSON] research method, the education of the [PERSON] posterity, and the stewardship of the [PERSON] Collections, Archives, and Spirit — each unpacked in the body of this document. We commend the Plan to the University community in the conviction that an institution which knows its tradition is an institution better placed to do its tradition’s continuing work. Vice-Chancellor and President

Integration. The slow embedding of an experience or finding into the working understanding of the institution, distinguished from the experience itself. The Plan treats integration as a substantive institutional discipline. Microdose. A sub-perceptual dose; in the Plan, a low-intensity, regularly administered formation-oriented seminar distributed across the long arc of a degree. Set. The mindset, intention, and preparation with which the University approaches a given inquiry. The first of the two classical terms the Plan invokes. Setting. The physical, relational, and temporal conditions in which inquiry is conducted. The second of the two classical terms the Plan invokes. Sub-perceptual dose. A dose at a level below the threshold of immediate perception but sufficient, when regularly administered, to produce durable formation. In the Plan, the term denotes the principle underlying the Microdose Curriculum.

Looking ahead The decade ahead will ask of universities a different kind of attention from the one the sector has spent the previous forty years cultivating: the willingness to take seriously the conditions under which inquiry produces durable understanding, rather than the willingness to multiply the inquiries themselves. The University’s wager, in this Plan, is that the institutions which continue to matter through the second half of this century will be those that have, in the second half of this decade, attended to set, setting, container, and integration with the seriousness the contemporary literature recommends. The work is patient and largely invisible from outside. Much of it is the slow work of preparation, of holding, and of integration that no audience ever sees directly. But the conditions on which a national research university’s contribution to the country depends are not built in any other way. The medicine, properly held, integrates. [ORGANISATION] will continue the work of holding it.

text: Roadmap The plan will be delivered in four overlapping phases across the period 2026 to 2031. The phasing reflects the realistic pace at which a research-intensive national university can stand up a capability of this scale, and the differing time horizons over which the priorities will mature. Each phase has its own emphasis; none stand alone. Set in motion (2026). The first year is a year of groundwork. Implementation arrangements are stood up, baseline measures are confirmed, the consultation and partnership settings on which the plan depends are renewed, and the early actions in each priority are set in motion. The end-of-year review establishes the conditions for a stronger build phase. Deepen (2027–2028). The middle years of the early period are the years of substantive build. Initiatives in each priority move from establishment into delivery; the cross-disciplinary research programme reaches operating maturity; the public performance programme begins to take its sustained shape; the precinct consolidation reaches its first major milestones. The mid-period review is undertaken in late 2028. Scale (2029–2030). The later years of the plan period are the years in which the directions set out here are scaled into the institutional fabric. The Archive opens and accepts its first acquisitions; the fabrication and acoustic capability reaches sustained operating scale; the undergraduate studio cycle is integrated across the colleges; the partnership programme reaches its planned breadth. Sustain (2031). The final year is a year of consolidation and forward look. The plan and its initiatives are reviewed against the evidence of the preceding years; the directions for the period beyond 2031 are settled in the light of what has been learned; the foundations for the next strategic cycle are laid.

Objective 6 Developing staff potential The challenge Motivated and competent staff are the prerequisite for ensuring that an organisation can realise its ambitions. Universities seeking to attract and retain highly qualified and committed people in research, teaching, innovation and public engagement, continuing education, technical services, administration and management need to enable participation and equal opportunity, ensure information and involvement, and provide good working conditions and reliable career prospects. This calls for a holistic approach to diversity, leadership and organisation. In order to be successful, universities must ensure that all members of the institution are able to develop their potential to the full.

Objective 7 Building bridges to the world The challenge Global networking as a result of digitalisation, [PLACE] programmes, international partnerships and alliances as well as international rankings are just a few of the highly diverse aspects that characterise the worldwide scientific community today. Over the past few decades, science and academic education, especially in the [PLACE] Union, have benefitted to an unprecedented extent from increasing cross-border cooperation and easier international access. Nevertheless, open international exchange among academics and academic freedom are at risk wherever democratic values are flouted. Universities consistently build bridges by cultivating personal contact and establishing joint programmes based on clear standards in the areas of research, the promotion of early-career researchers, and study programmes.

Cooperation is integral to science – internationally, regionally, with colleagues from other academic institutions and with private enterprises as well as societal actors. Especially within the local region, manifold opportunities exist to complement competences and develop synergies in close cooperation based on mutual trust. In the face of today’s growing demands on research and education, it is possible to benefit mutually from cooperation in the areas of teaching and learning, research and development, innovation and public engagement. Moreover, changes in the law and in funding policies within the [PLACE] science system will impact on the collaboration between universities and non-university research institutions in future years. The universities are in a position to help shape this process.

Research with Impact The bedrock of [ORGANISATION]’s global reputation for impact is the extraordinary strength of our research. We will be recognised as a world-leading university, and collaborative partner of choice, founded on the excellence and transformative impact of our research. Our global reach will be recognised, and our social purpose will also champion the delivery of prosperity, jobs and well-being to our local and regional communities. We value basic, curiosity-driven research as a driver of discovery. We will build on these knowledge foundations to develop new ideas and theories, continuing to develop design-led innovations addressing global challenges in the fields of health, education, sustainability, and social justice.

Education and Student Experience We will offer a world-leading education and student experience through a blend of traditional programmes, stackable qualifications, and micro-credentials, with flexibility and support to learn on campus, through blended learning or online. Our programmes will develop skills and will support work-based learning to maximise the opportunity for students to move into the world of work. Our learning and teaching will be student-focused, delivering the best possible student experience and work-ready students equipped for the world that they are destined to shape. To support their development as change-makers, our students will be encouraged to help develop and define the values of the university. Through this ongoing endeavour students will be empowered to help us create and deliver a smooth and seamless student experience from the point of initial enquiry to graduation and beyond, as alumni and continuing members of our community. Our approach throughout development and delivery of learning and teaching in [ORGANISATION], Kirkcaldy, and internationally will be through meaningful and sustained partnerships. This is the commitment that underpins our enabling strategy on Education and Student Experience.

“A score doesn’t announce its own expiry. Somebody has to keep asking it how old it actually is, and for four years nobody at the carrier had that job.” — Senior Research Fellow [PERSON], Convenor, [ORGANISATION]

Retiring a reading, formally [ORGANISATION] asks what a review actually changes, as distinct from what it merely re-certifies; applied to metric stewardship, this period’s strand of that programme asked a narrower version of the same question — what does it take, procedurally, for an organisation to formally retire a reading it has stopped needing. Lecturer and Convenor [PERSON]’s team found the honest answer was almost always: more than deciding the number is no longer useful.

A chronic-disease foundation had carried a single wellbeing-index item in its annual report for eleven years, unchanged since the underlying survey instrument it drew from was substituted for a longer, better-validated one in the report’s third year. The item stayed because retiring it required an explicit board resolution nobody had thought to draft, and because the annual report’s template treated the item as a fixed row rather than a chosen one. Working with the School, the foundation drafted its first formal retirement protocol: a standing annual prompt requiring every legacy indicator to be re-justified in writing or struck from the template, with the item in question the protocol’s first formal retirement. “Nobody ever votes to keep a stale indicator. It survives because retiring it was never anybody’s job description, and giving it one turned out to be most of the fix.” — Dr [PERSON], Convenor, [ORGANISATION]

text: At UQ, our success depends on the talent, creativity and dedication of our people. We support staff by developing their skills and talents, encouraging personal and professional growth and creating opportunities for leadership and impact within and beyond the University. We aim to cultivate an environment that promotes equity, diversity and inclusion, where everyone is valued, respected and able to thrive. As digital and technological change becomes more central to our work, we will equip staff with the skills, confidence and ethical frameworks needed to navigate both opportunities and risks. By strengthening capabilities such as critical thinking, creativity, empathy, intuition and ethical judgment, we will support staff to use AI strategically. This approach will be guided by responsible-use frameworks, strong governance and equitable access to tools and resources. We are committed to developing career pathways and strengthening leadership skills for both academic and professional staff. Building on the initiatives such as our Leadership Framework, the Study for Staff program and the creation of Teaching Associate roles, we aim to build the capabilities required for UQ’s future workforce. We are also committed to ensuring that UQ reflects societal diversity and values the varied experiences, perspectives and knowledge of our people. We will apply an intersectional perspective to our equity, diversity and inclusion efforts to ensure no one is left behind, while fostering safe and supportive environments for all staff. Our priorities include increasing the representation of women and [PLACE] and [PLACE] peoples – particularly in senior leadership roles, implementing anti-racism initiatives, eliminating UQ’s gender pay gap, addressing psychological safety and removing barriers for people with disability and the neurodivergent community.

Foundational Goals 1. Generate new revenue We will align and expand the programs offered through Continuing Education, Executive Education, Partnered Projects and Pre-College (see also p 23) locally and globally to honour our mission of making lifelong learning opportunities accessible to a broader range of students. This will also increase income from grant-funded research and offer new revenue sources from events, conferences and facilities rentals. We will invest in building on the existing fundraising operation in Institutional Engagement and lay the groundwork for a comprehensive capital campaign by expanding our global network of alumni groups, involving faculty and staff, and launching volunteer, mentorship, career planning and internship programs.

2. Rethink the way we budget and prioritise our resources We will reconcile specific resource needs with the diversity of practices our model of immersive studio education requires by creating a more inclusive and integrated process for allocating and managing our budget in alignment with enrolment trends.

3. Radically improve efficiency We will adopt a new enterprise management system to break down siloed functional processes and advance our operations. We will transform [ORGANISATION]’s websites and other digital functions into a strategically consistent, intentional and audience-focused ecosystem. We will address space and scheduling issues by establishing clear policies and efficient workflows. Executive summary This Strategic Plan commits [ORGANISATION], across the period 2026-2031, to a single organising idea: that no AI-assisted recommendation affecting a student, staff member, or applicant should take effect without a named person attesting that they have read it and stand behind it. Four strategic priorities carry that commitment from the decision itself through to the capacity to review it, the public’s standing to ask about it, and its survival as the number of such decisions keeps rising.

Together these priorities move the University from a default in which an AI-assisted recommendation is actioned unless someone happens to object, to a default in which it is actioned only once someone specific has attested to it. The initiatives that follow are specific by design: each carries a target, a date, and a mechanism for knowing whether it has been met. Where earlier plans have asked the University to “govern AI responsibly” in the abstract, this plan asks something narrower and considerably harder to fake: that every such decision have exactly one name against it, and that the name mean something. None of the four priorities invents a discipline the University does not already practise somewhere. Each extends a habit already at work in one part of the institution — a named convenor, an attested custodian, a published register — to the specific and fast-growing case of decisions an AI-assisted tool has helped make. That is a deliberate choice: an institution that already knows how to name someone accountable for a research instrument does not need a new capability to do the same for a rostering flag, only the will to apply the existing one without exception, at a volume the existing one was not originally built for. The remainder of this document sets out the operating environment that makes this commitment necessary, the ambition that follows from it, and the four strategic priorities, their initiatives, and their measures in detail, before closing with the phasing, governance, and review arrangements that will carry the plan through to 2031.

Holistic well-being and success: Provide a comprehensive foundation of support for individuals throughout all stages of their relationship with the university, beginning by attracting and retaining talented students, faculty, and staff who will contribute to a thriving university community. Its people are the [ORGANISATION]’s most important resource. Success in every aspect of the university’s mission is founded on attracting and retaining talented and engaged individuals who will contribute to a vibrant environment for learning, innovation, and discovery. As the university pursues its vision to be the destination of first choice for those seeking a place to grow, learn, contribute, and thrive, the university is committed to nurturing a culture of care and respect within which all feel supported as they work toward their personal and collective goals. The university will chart clear pathways for advancement, celebrate excellence and achievement, and ensure access to holistic well-being and mental health supports. The UI will build on the great advances it has made in existing programs and services to become widely recognised as a campus that cares for every member of its community. A.

Embed well-being and mental health into all aspects of campus culture to better support students, faculty, and staff. 1. Evaluate the effectiveness of and recommend improvements to existing well-being programs, and identify service gaps based on population data. 2. Identify well-being and mental health needs of different groups and evaluate effectiveness of existing programs in meeting those needs. 3. Create a cohesive framework of existing holistic well-being services and resources for students, faculty, and staff to ensure a comprehensive well-being and mental health infrastructure. 4. Increase access to and awareness of mental health and well-being resources. 5. Expand curricular and co-curricular learning for all students that provides foundational well-being knowledge and skills.

A Community of Calibrated Feel Why this matters. Attunement is a capability of people, and it is only an institutional capability when the people who hold it are many, aligned, and renewed. A felt sense that lives in a handful of senior practitioners is a dependency, not an assurance arrangement. The third priority therefore builds the community: accredited practitioners across every school and portfolio, a shared sensibility maintained through deliberate calibration, and a pipeline through which the feel is passed on faster than it retires. What we’ll do. 1. Develop and deliver Foundations of Vibe Literacy, an accredited program through which every continuing staff member acquires the shared vocabulary, calibration practices, and recording conventions of structured attunement. 2. Establish a practitioner accreditation pathway, from foundation through panel ready to senior practitioner, with progression assessed — appropriately — by attunement, and with senior accreditation renewed through participation in calibration convenings. 3. Build calibration into the institutional rhythm, through regular cross-school convenings in which practitioners re-align their reads against shared cases, drawing on the [ORGANISATION] line where an intensive format serves the cohort. 4. Recruit and promote for feel, incorporating demonstrated attunement capability into academic and professional promotion criteria and into selection for institutional leadership roles. How we’ll know. — 10 —

• All continuing academic and professional staff will hold Foundations of Vibe Literacy accreditation by the end of 2029, sustained at 100% of the continuing cohort thereafter. • The community of panel-ready practitioners will at least double over the plan period, with completions across the accreditation pathway in the low thousands. • By 2031, the University will maintain at least 80 strategic partnerships with organisations whose quality cultures it judges, on attunement, to be compatible with its own.

Our ambition for 2030 is to further enhance our impact by strengthening our research position and working with industry to broaden our translational impact and innovation, ensuring we deliver high-quality, world-leading research, which addresses local and global challenges.

Our researchers will benefit from a range of development opportunities to enable them to thrive in their research, advance their careers and reach their potential as future leaders. We will invest in our researchers to develop international excellence from our postgraduate research students, through early career researchers and Fellows, to international research leaders.

PRIORITIES THAT DEFINE AND UNITE [PLACE]Students, teaching and research are our foundation. Like all universities, at our core we are an institution defined by our commitment to education, discovery and the development and mobilisation of knowledge, and to providing a supportive working and learning environment for our students, staff and faculty. Our areas of study and our strengths in research in scholarly activity are vast and all contribute to a better world.

But what makes UVic different? Our community told us about the strengths and priorities that make UVic distinct—and was clear about what should guide us toward building a better tomorrow. UVic is distinct because we prioritise: [PLACE] perspectives. We want to be a community that is open to learning, prioritises being in right relationship with and respecting the rights of all people and things, and deconstructs systemic barriers to the full participation of First Peoples in the university’s life and work. People, places and the planet. From the campus to the global community, we support people’s wellness and ability to thrive, and are addressing sustainability, climate action and the systemic barriers affecting equity, diversity and inclusion in multiple ways. Change and transformation. Through a culture of trust, curiosity and flexibility, we will continuously re-imagine what we do, how we do it and why—being courageous and open to change helps us transform our communities and the world. Partnerships and collaboration. We support collaboration among faculties, disciplines and divisions; between academic and administrative units; between the campus and our community; and between UVic and our international partners, alumni, research institutions, industry and governments. These strategic priorities are what make us Distinctly UVic.

text: The main tactical and strategic risks are identified in terms of probability and impact and then recorded in a risk register with responsibility for monitoring and updating within the organisational unit. Risk management is an ongoing process, which means that continuous attention is required to monitor – and, where necessary, adjust – the risks and control measures. Aided by the risk registers, the organisation ensures the continuous risk management process from which results can also be distilled periodically. By applying this risk and control system, [ORGANISATION] is agile and ready for the future. Specific internal bodies Internal Audit Using a systematic and disciplined approach, Internal Audit evaluates the adequacy and effectiveness of governance, risk management and internal control of all activities and resources, as defined by the EB in line with the Code of Good University Governance. The services of Internal Audit are intended for internal use within [ORGANISATION]. The evaluations, research and recommendations provide [ORGANISATION]’s responsible management with additional assurance and contribute to improvement and change. Internal Audit supports management in analysing, improving and accounting for their operations by contributing to their insights with images, analyses and evaluations. Internal Audit fulfils the third-line role in the execution of its function in accordance with the ‘three lines model’. In doing so, Internal Audit plays an important supporting role for the EB, the deans and the directors of [ORGANISATION], helping them to be in control of implementing, improving and accounting for their activities. Internal audit is an independent position. Audit Committee The Supervisory Board’s Audit Committee advises and supports the Supervisory Board on the effectiveness of the design and operation of the university’s internal risk management and control systems. Sub-goal: Increased interaction between students and researchers The university will encourage more interaction, and include students in research projects to a higher degree. This will develop students’ own competencies, in-depth knowledge in the degree programmes and the students’ ability to participate in research collaboration and research teams, in addition to contributing to students’ academic Bildung.

IMPLEMENTATION AND FOLLOW-UP The 2025 strategy will remain in force for a five-year period. In connection with the development of the strategy, goals, sub-goals and concrete initiatives have been set, just as currently ongoing strategic initiatives and the strategic framework contract have been incorporated into the strategy. The university will monitor the implementation of the strategy closely and draft action plans in collaboration with the faculties, schools and departments. Each year from April to June, the university will follow up on the activities of the previous year, and will then determine the activities for the coming year. In this way, the university will ensure the availability of the necessary resources, administrative support and, not least, local and subject-specific ownership of the strategy. In addition, implementation and follow-up will also provide an opportunity for the university to launch new initiatives, which will enable the university to react appropriately to any changes in its framework conditions, and not least meet new and unforeseen needs on the part of society. In this regard, the university’s goal is to respond with greater agility, thus increasing its contribution to society.

[ORGANISATION]'s values Our fundamental values are described in the Magna Charta of the [PLACE] Universities. We safeguard freedom of research and expression, in addition to individuals’ opportunities to realise their potential. Open dialogue, tolerance and diversity are the very foundation of the university’s vocation. Because we regard the universities as one of the pillars of society, we assume co-responsibility for the development of a democratic, sustainable society.

STRATEGIC PRIORITY: GLOBAL REPUTATION AND PARTNERSHIPS At Queen’s, we will foster an environment where local impact and global ambition pervades all our activities. We will enhance our international reputation as a world-class research and educational institution, communicating our distinctive impact to the world. Through our global reputation, we will also promote the international profile and connectivity of [PLACE].

Offer an international experience We will offer an international experience that attracts and supports exceptional individuals from around the world, making Queen’s a destination of choice for talented students and academics and leading to an enriched learning environment for all. We will identify and invest in opportunities that promote global mobility for our staff and students, sustained research programmes and postgraduate collaborations.

We will focus our efforts on high-quality international partnerships, in areas of strength, which will support our priorities in research and education. We will explore partnerships that allow us to embrace opportunities we could not access alone, with partners who are eager to support initiatives that take us forward in our mission, and in so doing help deliver the growth and global reach of the University.

Lead and shape the agenda on social transformation We will engage in a socially transformative and responsible way. We will provide platforms for debate and policy development on key global challenges and deliver, both at Queen’s and around the world, major public-facing events, focusing on significant societal issues. We will encourage and support our staff to take leading roles in external bodies and learned societies, using our knowledge and expertise to inform policy and influence decision makers.

The third is geopolitical. The strategic environment in which [PLACE] operates has become more contested, more uncertain, and more consequential for the country’s future. [PLACE] universities are increasingly being asked to support a broader, more deliberately diversified set of international partnerships — particularly across the [PLACE], and with [PLACE] partners with whom [PLACE] shares both research traditions and strategic interests. [ORGANISATION] is well placed to lead in this work, but doing so well will require sustained and intentional effort across the plan period.

Within this environment, [ORGANISATION] sits in a particular position. We are the country’s national university, research-intensive at a scale and depth unmatched in [PLACE], and home to research and teaching strengths — across the sciences, humanities, social sciences, and policy domains — that are genuinely globally distinctive. We are anchored in [PLACE], a city whose institutional fabric is closely entwined with our own, and connected through long-standing relationships with peer institutions across the world. This position confers both opportunity and obligation. The opportunity is to make a contribution to the national effort that no other institution can. The obligation is to do so with the seriousness, the focus, and the strategic clarity that the country deserves from its national university. This plan is our response.

Our ambition By 2031, the [ORGANISATION] will be the world’s leading university for the study of [PLACE] and its place in the world — recognised for the depth and quality of its research, the formation of its graduates, and the contribution it makes to the public life of the country and the region. This ambition is deliberate. It draws on the particular history and mission of [ORGANISATION], on the strengths we have accumulated across eight decades, and on a clear-eyed read of the contributions [PLACE] and the world will need from a national university over the decade to come. It is grounded in what we already do well, and oriented toward what we are working to become.

equivalent maturation is more recent and more fragmentary: the institutions have not yet collectively decided what an articulated practice of error and accident looks like for an interpretive or compositional tradition. In the [ORGANISATION], the question becomes acute: the disciplines housed there both produce the generative systems whose failures preoccupy the public and develop the methodological tools through which those failures are studied. And across the University’s professional cohorts, the wider conversation about institutional candour places new demands on the disclosure and learning practices through which the institution governs itself. The University is well placed to lead, but only on the condition that it is willing to organise itself around the proposition that being a research university involves being wrong, often, in particular and disciplined ways. The Plan that follows is the University’s commitment to do so.

What we will become By 2031, [ORGANISATION] will be the [PLACE] university most attentive to its own errors, glitches, and accidents, across teaching, research, and operations. The University will treat these as primary sources of institutional learning rather than departures from a smoother norm. Researchers will publish into a methodological environment in which a substantive false start is a declared element of the work rather than an item edited out before submission; students will graduate from coursework in which the productive uses of failure are part of the explicit curriculum rather than picked up tacitly from a supervisor; and the institution will report annually on its own significant mistakes, near-misses, and corrections at the same cadence and with the same seriousness as it reports on its financial position.

How we’ll know. • A published annual programme of public performance, sustained from 2027, with not fewer than 30 free events per year by 2031 and an attendance baseline established and reported against. • Sustained partnerships with at least 12 cultural institutions, festivals, and [PLACE] cultural organisations across the plan period, with co-produced outputs accruing each year. • A public-performance studio cycle integrated into every flagship undergraduate degree by 2030, with completion attested in the academic record and reported through the annual academic returns.

Foundations for a Sovereign Practice Why this matters. The practice of new instrument-making depends on a constellation of capabilities — fabrication, computing, archive, acoustical, professional — without which the most ambitious ideas remain notional. The plan period asks [ORGANISATION] to underwrite those capabilities for the country, in the same way the country has historically underwritten the foundational capabilities on which national research and cultural life depend. What we’ll do. 1. Consolidate [ORGANISATION]’s instrumental-practice infrastructure into a coordinated precinct, including a fabrication suite, a controlled- acoustic facility, a public facing performance space, a climate- controlled instrument archive, and the digital infrastructure required to sustain them across decades.

2. Establish the [ORGANISATION] Instrumental Practice Archive as a permanent, climatecontrolled, publicly accessible repository for instruments designed and built at [ORGANISATION] and by partner institutions, with curatorial and conservation arrangements appropriate to objects intended to remain playable. 3. Renew the professional support arrangements — workshop staff, archive curators, programme administrators, technicians, and safety officers — without which the foundational capabilities cannot be sustained, with workforce-capability and wellbeing measures tracked publicly across the plan period.

How we’ll know. • The [ORGANISATION] Instrumental Practice Archive operational and open to the public by 2029, with curatorial standards and a published acquisition policy adopted by Council and a published custodial register sustained from opening. • A precinct-wide fabrication and acoustic capability operating at sustained scale from 2028, with audited access, equity-of-access measures, and a published utilisation framework reported on annually. • Renewed professional-staff arrangements in place by 2027, with workforcecapability and wellbeing indicators in the top quartile of comparable [PLACE] research-intensive universities across the plan period.

A distinctive position [ORGANISATION] sits in a particular position. We are [PLACE]’s national university, established by an Act of [PLACE] [ORGANISATION] with a charter to serve the nation. We are research-intensive at a scale and depth unmatched in the country. And we are home to research and teaching strengths — across the sciences, humanities, social sciences, and policy domains — that are genuinely globally distinctive. This vision is ambitious and focused. It reflects our distinctive mission, our particular institutional strengths, and the moment in which we find ourselves. It is grounded in eight decades of demonstrated capacity, and oriented toward the next.

It also gives the University’s research leadership, for the first time, a shared account of how investment decisions across schools and institutes are actually landing, rather than a picture assembled only at each grant round or annual report.

What we’ll do 1. Diversify the University’s research income base across competitive grant funding, philanthropic support, and industry and government collaboration. 2. Expand doctoral training capacity and strengthen the candidate experience across every school. 3. Renew major research infrastructure and align priority investment with capability of recognised national significance.

text: (i) Valuation Inputs, Processes and Relationships to Fair Value for Items Categorised in Level 2 & Level 3 Land and crown lease Land and crown lease (level 2) The land of the University has been classified as level 2. These parcels of land have been valued using the market approach which is based on the condition, location, land area and restrictions on sale or use of the asset (if any). Key observable inputs: Prices of comparable assets sold within a reasonable timeframe of the valuation date. Interrelationship between key unobservable inputs and fair value measurement: The estimated fair value increases (decreases) as the value of comparable assets increases (decreases) based on market forces reflected by analysed sale evidence of comparable assets. Buildings and infrastructure Buildings and Infrastructure (level 3) The most of the buildings of the University are considered specialised assets for which there is no active and liquid market and as such have been valued using the cost approach (depreciated replacement cost). This is based on the current construction costs per square metre to replace the asset. Key unobservable inputs: Current Replacement Cost (CRC) per square metre of a modern equivalent asset was primarily determined by analysis of recently completed projects within the [ORGANISATION], other universities and education/specialised facilities. What we’ll do 1. Move beyond first-generation reconciliation work toward structural transformation, including a renewed [ORGANISATION], sustained investment in [PLACE]-led research, and a long-term commitment to truth telling about the university’s own history. 2. Deepen engagement with the [PLACE] public service, including through expansion of executive education, renewal of long-running partnerships with policy agencies, and a sustained programme of evidence-based contribution to national decision-making. 3. Build durable partnerships with civil-society organisations, primary industries, and the cultural sector, with at least 75 active strategic partnerships of national significance by 2031.

Priority 4: A Capable and Connected Institution None of the above is achievable without renewed institutional foundations. Over the plan period we will invest in the people, the systems, and the working culture on which the university depends — and we will commit to ways of working that match the seriousness of the academic mission they support.

Why this matters The quality of an institution’s work is shaped by the quality of its internal life. Universities make their best contribution when staff have the time, the systems, and the conditions to do work of substance — and when the institution’s own practices honour the kind of careful, deliberative reasoning the academic mission depends on.

What we’ll do 1. Modernise digital infrastructure, including a renewed approach to research data, a contemporary teaching technology stack, and an institution-wide approach to artificial intelligence in education, research, and administration. 2. Renew the conditions under which institutional decisions are made and communicated, with a renewed emphasis on written briefs, working papers, and

structured discussion in place of presentation-led decision-making, so that staff time is spent on argument rather than arrangement. 3. Build a culturally safe and structurally equitable working environment for all members of the [ORGANISATION] community, with clear measures of progress on representation, retention, and career advancement for staff and students from historically marginalised backgrounds.

comfortable rankings outcomes. The production is operating in a tighter house. The Plan accordingly invests its rehearsal time in the numbers most likely to land, rather than spreading the company across a programme so broad that no number can be properly staged. The fourth pressure is epistemic. The sector has drifted, over the previous decade, toward measures of academic productivity that reward throughput over the slower forms of work on which a research university’s reputation is in fact built. The applause that a university most needs is not the kind that follows a flashy opening; it is the kind that follows the eleven o’clock number — the moment, late in the run, when the audience recognises the depth of what the company has been doing all along. The Plan reorients several measures in order to honour that distinction. Read together, these four pressures ask the University to articulate its purpose with the seriousness of a production that intends a long run, rather than the seriousness of a production hoping to survive its previews. The Plan accordingly addresses the dramaturgy of the institution as well as its content: not only what the University intends to do, but how it intends to stage the doing, in a register that the country can recognise and return to.

What we will become By 2031, [ORGANISATION] will be a national university recognised — within the country and in its region — as an institution that has earned its standing ovation. The University will have produced, across the run of this Plan, a set of structural commitments and visible moments that the country recognises as the University’s own work, performed in the University’s own voice. The disciplines will have been cast with care, the ensemble numbers rehearsed, the eleven o’clock numbers delivered. The production will, by 2031, be ready for its next chapter — not as a closing curtain but as the company moving into a second long-running season, on the same stage, for the same audience, with the same seriousness and a deeper repertoire.

Oversight and review How this plan was developed This plan is the product of extended consultation across the [ORGANISATION] community. Over the course of 2025, the executive convened a series of facilitated workshops with academic staff, professional staff, students, alumni, and partner organisations across government, industry, and the cultural sector. The directions set out here reflect the convergence of those deliberations and have been considered and endorsed by Council through its established governance arrangements.

Accountability Council holds responsibility for oversight of this plan. The Vice-Chancellor and the executive are accountable to Council for its delivery, and each strategic priority has a designated executive sponsor with operational responsibility for its implementation. The plan will be reported on annually, both to Council and to the broader university community. The annual report will describe progress against each success measure and will be published openly on the university’s website. Reporting will be candid about what has not yet been achieved as well as what has. A mid-period review will be conducted in late 2028 by an independent panel commissioned by Council. The review will assess progress, recommend adjustments where required, and be considered by Council before any material changes are implemented through the executive.

Looking ahead The decade to 2031 will demand much of [PLACE] and of the institutions on which the country relies. [ORGANISATION] will meet that demand with the seriousness and clarity the moment requires — through the sustained effort of every member of the [ORGANISATION] community, and through the contribution it enables [ORGANISATION] to continue to make to the country and the region. The work begins now.

The mid-period review will be undertaken in late 2028.

Embed (2029-2030) Through 2029 and 2030, the focus will shift from build to embed — from new investment to sustained operational delivery. Programs will be tuned for outcomes; partnerships will deepen; success measures will be tracked publicly and acted on.

text: Safety and Security Safety and Security, together with other security departments, is committed to making [ORGANISATION] a safe environment. It continued to work on Business Continuity Management in 2023, with the aim of minimising the impact of a crisis on key university processes. A system is meanwhile being set up that will allow managers and specialists to self-report on key assets within their management unit, and the associated vulnerabilities. Safety and Security works closely with ICT in this regard. In the past year, a range of climate actions have taken place on campus. Safety and Security assumed the lead in ensuring security around demonstrations and an occupation. The department also worked closely with both internal partners (including Campus Safety) and external partners (the municipality and police). This meant that campus safety was not compromised during the actions. The climate issue, the outcome of the [PLACE] elections, and the violent conflict in Israel and the Palestinian territories were among the issues that stirred debate and emotion on campus. Safety and Security monitors possible polarisation, which may result in an actual or perceived lack of security on campus. Where necessary, the department took action or gave advice for that purpose. Students and staff also travelled abroad a lot in 2023. Safety and Security has provided support to individuals staying in a country where a crisis or disaster occurred on several occasions. The department also gave a large number of travel safety training courses. And it provided security advice to those who wanted to travel to a country with an increased risk profile. Safety and Security has seen an increase in cases of concerning behaviour among students over the past year. The department has organised new workshops on this topic for academic counsellors, psychologists and student counsellors. It also handled a significant number of reports on concerning behaviour. In several complex cases, Safety and Security has provided risk assessments at the request of faculties, with courses of action where necessary. In 2023, the department prepared another security risk profile (SRP).

Priority 1: Research with Public Purpose Why this matters The defining feature of [ORGANISATION]’s research has always been its proximity to the questions that matter for the country and the wider world. Over the plan period we will sharpen that distinctiveness — focusing investment on mission-aligned priorities, renewing our cross-disciplinary capability, and building the partnerships and infrastructure on which our research strength will depend through the late 2020s and beyond.

Concentrate investment in a small number of flagship research programs of international standing, each addressing a problem of clear public significance and each connected to teaching at the postgraduate and research-training level. 2. Strengthen the institutional supports for research integrity, research data, and the responsible use of artificial intelligence in research, so that [ORGANISATION]’s research practice continues to set the standard for the sector. —9—
