text: Planning Without Latency Our position. Sensing a priority early is of no use if the plan then takes three years to record it. The second priority is latency: the interval between a priority’s emergence and its appearance in the live plan, which the University will drive as close to zero as an accountable process allows. This means retiring the fixed planning cycle in favour of continuous ratification — a plan amended in near-real time as priorities are recognised, governed throughout, and never more than a quarter behind the institution it describes. The work is led with the [ORGANISATION], whose scholarship on measurement latency and closed-loop response underpins it. In a working operation, the lag between sensing something and reporting it is the whole problem. A plan updated once every five years has a latency of five years. We can do considerably better than that. Our actions. 1. Replace the fixed five-year plan with a continuously ratified living plan, versioned and published in full, in which a newly recognised priority is incorporated within one ratification cycle of its confirmation rather than at the next scheduled review. 2. Establish a standing monthly ratification sitting of the University Executive, at which priorities surfaced by the [ORGANISATION] are considered for incorporation into the live plan, so that the plan never accumulates a backlog of priorities the institution is already pursuing. 3. Instrument the plan itself: publish, through the [ORGANISATION], a running measure of priority latency for every priority the University holds, defined as the elapsed time between its emergence and its incorporation into the live plan. Our targets. • By 2029, the median priority latency across the University will fall below thirty days, and no priority the institution is observably pursuing will remain unrecorded in the live plan for longer than a single quarter. • The living plan will be re-published in full after every monthly ratification sitting from 2027, and each version will remain permanently and publicly accessible, so that the University’s changing priorities can be audited rather than quietly revised.

Priority 1: Research That Meets the Moment The defining feature of [ORGANISATION]’s research has always been its proximity to the questions that matter for [PLACE] and the wider world. Over the plan period we will sharpen that distinctiveness — focusing investment on mission-aligned priorities, expanding our cross-disciplinary capability, and growing the research income on which the university’s future depends.

Our position A national university is not the sum of its grants and rankings; it is the standing capacity of a country to ask the questions only its national university is positioned to ask. That capacity has to be maintained, and it has to be renewed.

Our actions • Concentrate investment in a small number of flagship research programs of international standing, each addressing a problem of clear national significance and each connected to teaching at the postgraduate and research-training level. • Renew the university’s cross-disciplinary research capability — with particular emphasis on the intersections of computing, the life sciences, and the humanities and social sciences — through shared infrastructure, shared platforms, and shared methodological practice. • Strengthen the institutional supports for research integrity, research data, and the responsible use of artificial intelligence in research, ensuring that [ORGANISATION]’s research practice continues to set the standard for the sector.

Priority 2: Education for a Connected Continent The world our students will work in is being remade. Our educational programs will be redesigned around the dispositions and knowledges that will matter most over the coming decades — with particular attention to inquiry, judgement, plurality of knowledges, and the capacity for substantive engagement across disciplines under conditions of uncertainty.

Our position Education at a national university is not a transaction; it is a decade-long act of trust between the institution and the people who choose to study with us. That trust has to be earned in the design of our programs, the quality of our teaching, and the seriousness with which we treat the question of what our graduates will be ready for.

How we developed this plan This Plan was developed over fourteen months through a process of facilitated consultation across staff, students, alumni, partners, the [PERSON] Family Trust, and the country’s principal [PERSON] scholars. The [PERSON] Family Trust contributed substantively to the working group’s deliberations about the centenary programme and to the preservation arrangements for the archive. The working group also consulted with the curators of the Questacon [PERSON] exhibition (2013) and with the producers of the 2014 ABC documentary series in order to draw on the existing public-facing scholarship. The framing language of the Plan — “the [PERSON] disposition”, “the patient examination of the half-baked”, “the tartan paint line item” — emerged from the consultation rather than being imposed at the outset. Where the language has been retained, it is because participants in the working group returned to it spontaneously across multiple rounds.

Chancellor remains accountable to Council for delivery. Within that frame, three governance moves give the Plan effective traction. First, a [PERSON] Centenary Standing Committee, chaired by a Deputy Vice-Chancellor and reporting quarterly to Council, takes responsibility for the indicator set across all four priorities and for ensuring that the centenary year in 2031 finds the University in the institutional condition the tradition warrants. Second, an Accountability and Review schedule, published annually, sets out which indicators are due for full reporting in which quarter, with no indicator permitted to slip beyond the next quarterly review cycle. Third, Council’s Audit and Risk Committee will, from 2027, treat indicator slippage on the same footing as financial sustainability. Annual reporting against the Plan will be published in full, including instances of indicator slippage, elements of the Plan that have not progressed at the pace this document anticipated, and any element of the [PERSON] Centenary Programme that has been reprioritised or deferred. The reporting will not be selective.

This reset provides us with an exciting opportunity to reflect and refocus, and to ensure that, across the organisation, we are aligned to delivering against our Strategic Framework by empowering our students and staff through the opportunities we create, with the region we are part of being at the heart of what we do. The fundamental principles around our Strategic Framework reset are based on feedback from colleagues around the institution. From this feedback, it is clear we need to simplify the content of our Framework and reposition it to make it accessible and relevant to all, provide greater clarity on what we need to be doing to be successful, and capitalise on our strengths to enable us to meet the challenges and opportunities of the future.

A key element of our Strategic Framework reset is to ensure its accessibility and relevance to all staff, making sure that our strategic ambitions can be aligned to individual and team contributions and performance throughout the organisation. This image sets out the key elements which comprise our simplified representation of our Strategic Framework’s content.

What we do and how we do it through to 2030 is shaped by our Pillars, which set out what we will succeed at to fulfil our overarching Purpose and ensure the University succeeds for its students, staff and region. When our Strategic Framework was launched in 2018, there were three Pillars. Since then, our ability to build on our strengths and capitalise on opportunities has led to the decision to now introduce a fourth Pillar, through which we will lead the way in impact from industry engagement and give greater strategic visibility to this critical element of the [ORGANISATION]’s heritage and future.

Our communities We will strengthen our relationship with communities throughout [PLACE] by ensuring that our activities are relevant and recognisable to people living in the region, working with local groups and stakeholders in a collective initiative to deliver social and economic transformation. We will continue to grow our commitment to [PLACE] culture and the Arts through our teaching and research and our Arts and Innovation centre, Pontio.

ECONOMIC, SOCIAL AND CIVIC IMPACT Supporting a prosperous [PLACE], we envisage an innovation crescent, stretching from the [PLACE] Republic to the Northern powerhouse of [PLACE] West [PLACE] with the University at its heart, driving a place-based innovation agenda. We will support a wealth of civic mission activities – regionally, nationally, and internationally – and recognise these as a fundamental aspect of our core activities.

OUR PRIORITIES Supporting business We will play a lead role in the economic growth of [PLACE] and the UK, influencing and supporting key industrial sectors and their supply chains. We will focus on sectors of regional significance and those with emerging potential for growth, such as health and low carbon energy, working in partnership with public and private organisations to promote resilience and sustainability. We will build on the success of M-Sparc, our Science Park, to support our aspiration for greater employability, start-up, and commercialisation across [PLACE]. We will specifically seek to play a lead role in the growth of a vibrant health and life sciences sector across the region through the development of research in the [PLACE] [ORGANISATION].

Regional skills We will support regional workforce development through our undergraduate and postgraduate provision and the upskilling of the existing workforce through our Continuing Professional Development and professional qualifications programmes. We will lead a shared vision across the education sector in [PLACE] to bridge across statutory, further, and higher education boundaries and provide an alternative offer to established education and training routes through the development of pathways to meet regional skills needs.

text:
UQ is a world-leading, research-intensive university that excels across the pipeline of research and innovation: from Discovery, through Application, Demonstration and Deployment of research. Maintaining our depth of research excellence across a breadth of disciplines will enable us to deliver transdisciplinary solutions to the most compelling challenges of our time.

Our research excellence is enhanced through our commitment to collaboration. We know we that we need to collaborate to address global research challenges. Over the next four years and beyond, we will look for opportunities that will allow us to deliver both mission-driven research and larger scale research initiatives aligned to the priorities of government, industry and the broader community. UQ is committed to investment in areas where new research partnerships can be founded, and where existing collaborations can be deepened. We will actively participate in the development of innovation precincts that enable shared access to state-of-the art research facilities, researchers and co-designing solutions with partners. Through these collaborations, discoveries will be nurtured to deliver tangible, positive outcomes. Above all, we know that our research and innovation achievements are dependent on our extraordinary community of UQ researchers, professionals and higher degree by research students. A talented and diverse research and innovation workforce is an institutional and national asset, and UQ is committed to supporting our people to thrive. Through our research capabilities, our partnering mindset and supporting and developing our people, UQ will deliver worldclass research and innovation to support [PLACE]’s national aspirations and develop solutions for major global challenges. In doing so, we aim to double our industry and philanthropic funding for research, as we continue to be seen as a national leader in research excellence, impact and engagement.

We will raise awareness and promote greater understanding of and engagement with equality, diversity and inclusion issues across our University community through implementing and keeping under review our Equality, Diversity and Inclusion Policy and Strategy. putting in place a comprehensive suite of student support measures and ensuring that our student services are world-class. INSTITUTIONAL SUSTAINABILITY We will put foundations in place to ensure that the University can achieve its growth ambitions by underpinning our strategy with sustainable enabling infrastructure, resources, and services. A culture of excellence, innovation, and a willingness to think differently and to continually review the way we work, will be critical to deliver modern, digital, effective, and efficient services.

OUR PRIORITIES Financial resilience We will increase financial resilience and sustainability, and diversification of income, with a reduced dependence upon public funding. We will ensure all commercial provision provides value for money, considering other delivery arrangements, such as strategic sourcing, where this can enhance value for money. We will plan for a sustainable future, ensuring our operational business plans are aligned to the delivery of our long-term goals and the sustainability goals in the Well-being of Future Generations ([PLACE]) Act.

Marketing and brand We will invest in access to insight and intelligence to enable the University to be evidence-informed in both our portfolio development and marketing and recruitment operations. We will deliver creative marketing and brand building activity in support of our ambition to grow our reputation locally, nationally, and internationally, and to underpin all aspects of University business.

Our Campus We will imagine and deliver an impactful programme of improvements to our physical and digital environments that will animate and activate our campus, driving student experience and success, providing an inclusive, welcoming and safe place for all our community, whilst investing in our learning and research spaces to ensure we meet the needs of a contemporary higher education offer. We will collaborate with the [PLACE] Strategic Partnership priorities, supporting the regeneration of the city of [PLACE], and improving links between the University and the city. The University’s Environmental Management System will continue to support our commitment to environmental sustainability.

text:
This is the environment this plan answers. Not a single new pressure, but the accumulation of many small ones, each asking the University to be more certain, earlier, and for longer, about the trajectories it is prepared to back. [ORGANISATION]’s setting sharpens the point rather than softening it. A university that draws its staff, students, and partners from across a single region carries a longer institutional memory of the commitments it has made there than a larger, more transient institution might; a trajectory backed badly is not easily forgotten by the people around it. Place, in that sense, is not a backdrop to this plan but a discipline on it — the University answers, over the decade ahead, to the same community it commits to, and a commitment that does not hold up under evidence will be noticed close to home before it is noticed anywhere else.

Where we are headed By 2031, no commitment [ORGANISATION] makes will outlive the evidence that justified it. This is a narrower ambition than it first sounds, and a more demanding one. It does not mean the University will commit to less, or more slowly. It means that whatever the University commits to — an appointment, an admitted cohort, a partnership, a continuing career — will carry a live account of the trajectory behind it, refreshed on a published schedule rather than assumed to still hold. A university that can show, at any point across the life of a commitment, the evidence that still justifies it, is a university whose confidence in its own decisions can be checked rather than simply taken on faith. That is the institution this plan builds toward. Reaching it means treating evidence of trajectory as infrastructure rather than paperwork: something built once, resourced properly, and maintained on a schedule the University publishes and keeps to, in the same way it maintains any other system its people and partners rely on.

text: Two years after becoming one of the first private donors to Manaaki Manawa, the Centre for Heart Research at the [ORGANISATION], octogenarian Garth Barfoot became a heart patient himself. In 2021, Garth’s $100,000 donation was used to buy a state-of-the-art ultrasound imaging platform for the newly launched centre. In 2023, a year after having a heart valve replaced, he was back in [PLACE] Shore Hospital having a pacemaker fitted after suffering spells of dizziness caused by bradycardia (abnormally slow heartbeat). Garth’s name is well known through Barfoot & [PLACE], the real estate company his father founded in 1923, but in more recent years, he’s forged a new reputation as a distance runner, completing more than 30 marathons and triathlons. The pacemaker enabled him to fulfil a long-held dream. In November 2024, at the age of 88, he became the oldest finisher in the New York marathon, completing the event in a gruelling 11 hours, 29 minutes and 49 seconds. The achievement had eluded him the year before when he had to pull out of the event because of the cold. The news that the pacemaker technology that assisted him is about to become even better doesn’t surprise Garth, who calls it a “no-brainer”. Garth has talked about the new device with its developer, Professor [PERSON]. “He said that when he was working, they would always look forward to the next model of car, and now, at his stage of life and after what he had gone through medically, he was waiting for the new pacemaker models to come through.” Garth doesn’t have a wish list for a dream pacemaker. “But at 89, as someone who is old enough to have seen the uptake in use of pacemakers by my contemporaries, I know that with the help of researchers like Julian, we will be finding them even more useful in the future.” Private donors like Garth are a vital source of funding for Manaaki Manawa. Others who’ve generously supported Julian’s work include the Kelliher Charitable Trust and the Heart Foundation.

Science, economy, society and politics are facing global challenges: Any solution to pressing issues such as the climate emergency, security, healthcare, migration and technological change can only be international. For universities and higher education this brings both responsibilities and opportunities. In this context it is the task of the internationalisation of universities to enable global learning and research through cooperation, networking and exchange, to help prepare students for the complex challenges of the 21st century1, and to participate in the efforts to find solutions to global problems through science and the humanities. In a globalised world of work, international experience and intercultural competence acquired as part of a university degree or at the doctoral stage (such as the knowledge of global markets) and skills acquired abroad (such as language proficiencies and country-specific qualifications) are gaining in importance for everyday professional life.2 High-tech companies, in particular, consider international experience to be a very important selection criterion for their employees.3 This means that the issue of internationalisation of study programmes and in the doctoral programmes is becoming increasingly important, especially with regard to international mobility and an international campus life.

In this process, digitalisation should be understood as an opportunity. The Covid-19 pandemic has thoroughly changed internation­ alisation. The restrictions of physical mobility and the accelerated trend towards online and virtual teaching and learning have expanded the concept of international mobility. Online teaching and learning open up new opportunities, especially when it comes to “internationalisation at home”. The opportunities provided by virtual mobility contribute to a more inclusive access to inter­ nationalisation activities as they open up new target groups. In this context we are able to rely on established partnerships which are particularly well suited for the creation of virtual mobility. At the same time, students and young academics continue to show a marked interest in face-to-face encounters and stays abroad.4

priorities already in motion, not to issue them from the centre. Direction does not disappear — it is exercised earlier, in the anticipatory work, and distributed more widely — but the plan’s own role becomes ratification: the orderly, accountable acknowledgement that a priority has emerged, been tested, and earned a place in the institution’s record.

Our actions. 1. Redefine the strategic plan, in the University’s governance instruments, as a ratifying record rather than a directive one: inclusion in the plan certifies that a priority has emerged and been pursued, and confers resource, but does not itself originate the priority. 2. Establish a published test for ratification — evidence that a priority has been enacted somewhere in the institution for at least one full cycle — and apply it without exception, so that no priority is written into the plan on the strength of intention alone. 3. Devolve the authority to begin pursuing an emerging priority to schools and portfolios, ahead of ratification, under a standing mandate that treats early, evidenced action as the ordinary way priorities enter the University rather than as an irregularity to be corrected. Our targets. • From 2028, every priority in the live plan will carry a public ratification record showing where and for how long it was enacted before it was included, and no priority will appear in the plan without one.

• By 2030, no strategic priority will be originated by the planning process itself; the University will be able to trace every priority in its plan to an emergence that preceded its ratification, and will publish any case it cannot. • Throughout the plan period, the University will maintain a published register of priorities it began pursuing before ratification, with no entry removed to tidy the record, so that the institution’s anticipatory action remains auditable.

Each of our strategic themes is fundamental to our success, defining our specific approach and the integrated actions we need to deliver. Our themes are complemented by a series of key performance indicators and operational measures. The qualitative goals of our 2030 Strategy are to: § be a leading Education Group recognised for our educational pathways and delivery at scale of innovative approaches to learning § be recognised internationally for our focus in challenge-led research and for the excellence of our research centres § be recognised internationally for the scale and impact of our innovation ecosystem § be recognised internationally for our global presence, profile and reputation. Through our strategic themes, we will enhance our educational offer by expanding our provision and developing our learning pathways from schools, further education, apprenticeships, undergraduate and postgraduate education, through to executive education and continuing professional development. We will improve and increase the scale of our research power and enhance our reputation internationally for challenge-led research; entrepreneurship and innovation; and for the excellence of our research centres.

We will deliver a high-quality education based on where and how our students want and need to learn, what they want to learn, the skills they want to develop and the experience they want to live. Our students are empowered to take control of their educational journey, creating better futures.

Through our research we will deliver significant impact on the economy, public services, the environment, and society at the local, national, and international level. Central to our research strategy is the development of a strong impact culture built upon collaboration. We will consider impact throughout the lifecycle of our research projects and programmes, co-creating impact pathways with the beneficiaries of our research and sharing our knowledge and experience with colleagues and stakeholders. We will engage the public with our research; communicating information on why it is needed; how research is conducted (including the social and ethical implications) and the thematic areas of research within the [ORGANISATION] Group.

• Median time between an asset becoming unavailable and its replacement or repair falls by at least half against the pre-Register baseline. • Register update compliance, a steward’s entry reviewed within its due cycle, holds above 95% every year from 2028 onward. • Every newly named steward completes induction within one month of appearing on the Register, with no backlog carried past a single reporting quarter.

Capability Through Clear Custodianship Why this matters Shared research equipment and actively maintained datasets currently rely on inherited knowledge of who looks after what, passed on informally when a custodian moves between labs or leaves the University altogether. Formal, attested custodianship protects research capability directly: an instrument that is calibrated on schedule and handed on cleanly serves every project that depends on it, not just the one that happened to be running when it was last checked. The University’s research strategy already depends, in practice, on this kind of custody working quietly in the background; this priority simply makes that dependency visible, named, and reviewable rather than trusting it to survive the next round of staff turnover by luck.

1. Assign a named custodian to every item of shared research equipment and every actively maintained dataset, published on the research-infrastructure register alongside the Stewardship Register. 2. Require an annual custodianship attestation, renewed or formally reassigned, with a documented succession protocol triggered the moment a custodian departs. 3. Route every custodian-reported fault directly into the relevant lab’s maintenance queue, closing the loop between a report and its resolution. 4. Publish a lightweight custodianship handbook for each equipment category — calibration cadence, fault-reporting steps, succession checklist — so a new custodian inherits a procedure, not just a name. How we’ll know • 100% of shared research equipment carries an active, attested custodian by 2029. • Average custodian tenure at handover exceeds eighteen months, with a documented successor named within a fortnight of any departure. • Equipment fault-to-resolution time falls year-on-year for the remainder of the plan. • Every equipment category carries a published handbook, reviewed at each custodianship handover without exception.

Education That Shapes the Future Why this matters. The graduates who pass through [ORGANISATION] during the plan period will work for forty to fifty years across fields whose shape we cannot fully predict. The strongest preparation we can offer is not a fixed body of knowledge — though knowledge matters — but the dispositions and forms of practice that allow a person to keep learning, keep contributing, and keep adapting through long working lives in unsettled fields. Education at [ORGANISATION] should equip graduates to do that work well. What we’ll do. 1. Renew the undergraduate curriculum around durable capabilities and forms of practice, including studio-style and ensemble learning formats in which students rehearse the moves of inquiry and collaboration alongside academic content, rather than acquiring content in isolation from the work it is meant to support. 2. Deepen the integration of research into education at every level, so that students at every stage encounter live questions, contribute to ongoing work, and develop the judgement that comes from sustained engagement with real problems. 3. Strengthen postgraduate and professional education as a coherent program of study, including renewed Masters offerings, expanded micro-credentialing in areas of national capability need, and professional pathways that complement the HDR program rather than competing with it. How we’ll know. • Sustained improvement in graduate satisfaction, employability, and destinations, particularly in fields of national capability need. — 10 —

• Growth in postgraduate and professional education enrolments by approximately 25–35% over the plan period, with a corresponding diversification of the student body. • Doubling of the proportion of [PLACE] students across the university by 2031, supported by renewed pathways and sustained institutional commitment.

Roadmap The plan will be delivered in four overlapping phases across the period to 2031. The phases are sequential in emphasis but not in start — each priority will have activity under way from the first year of the plan.

Foundation (2026) In the first year, we will put in place the governance, baselines, and foundational investments needed to deliver the plan. Each priority will have a designated executive sponsor, a dedicated implementation team, and a published baseline against which progress will be measured. Foundational investments — in flagship research programs, in educational redesign, and in the digital and physical infrastructure that supports them — will commence.

Acceleration (2027-2028) Through 2027 and 2028, the major investments and program changes set out in this plan will reach scale. New postgraduate programs will commence; flagship research initiatives will reach operational maturity; the campus precinct refresh will deliver its most visible early outcomes. The mid-period review will be undertaken in late 2028.

Consolidation (2029-2030) Through 2029 and 2030, the focus will shift from build to sustained operational delivery. Programs will be tuned for outcomes; partnerships will deepen; success measures will be tracked publicly and acted on. The cultural and structural changes initiated in earlier phases will be expected to be visible in the lived experience of staff and students.

Legacy (2031) In 2031 we will assess what the plan has delivered, recalibrate where outcomes have not been met, and prepare the strategic direction for the period beyond. The 2031 review will be conducted with the same depth of consultation that produced this plan, and the lessons learned across the period will be carried into the next.

How we developed this plan This plan is the product of an extended period of structured consultation across the [ORGANISATION] community. Over the course of 2025, the executive convened a sequence of facilitated workshops with academic and professional staff, undergraduate and postgraduate students, alumni, and external partners, including representatives of the [PLACE] public service, industry, the cultural sector, and [PLACE] communities with long-standing relationships to the university.

VISION We aspire to be a transformative power. We will be renowned for the exceptional quality of our education and the experiences of our students, our world-class research with far-reaching impact, and the highest standards in [PLACE] in our progressive academic health system. [ORGANISATION] will respond to the needs of a rapidly changing world and shape its future, becoming: • a destination of choice for students • a continuously accelerating powerhouse of impactful research • an employer of choice for our staff • a provider of choice for people engaged with our health enterprise • a community where everyone is valued, included and respected • more deeply aligned with [PLACE] peoples • a nexus for partnership and innovation in [PLACE] and around the world • a place of pride for graduates and alumni • agile in response to the rapidly changing national and global landscape • enduring and sustainable.

A gathering of students and staff with a shared vision of what it means to belong to a university that serves the nation and the world. Our remarkable students and dedicated staff are the lifeblood of an open, ethical and diverse [ORGANISATION] community: • our students and alumni will realise the benefits of both their education and broader experiences at [ORGANISATION] throughout their lives so they might achieve their hopes, dreams and aspirations • for staff, [PLACE] will be a place of professional achievement, satisfaction and belonging in the service of advancing the University • those receiving treatment and support in our health services will find healing, learning and discovery at the heart of all that we do. We will become more internationally leading whilst staying locally relevant by building stronger and more focussed national and international partnerships. This will help us to achieve what we couldn’t do alone, and enable the knowledge and skills gained to be shared with our local community for mutual benefit. Our ambition will be to encourage greater research alliances to enhance research quality, and greater proactivity in proposing new collaborative initiatives at local, national and international levels. We will renew our focus on creating strategic partnerships with business and industry, growing support for innovation and commercial activities within the University.

We will forge international educational alliances with relevant and mutually beneficial expertise, to improve our own provision and the profile of our courses internationally. We will extend our philanthropic activities to embrace new partnerships and initiatives. Closer to home, our new strategy will see the University further develop its civic role and partnerships in [PLACE] and the wider region, by engaging in continuing education, economic development activities, innovation and community engagement.

Our strategy was formed during a global pandemic, with perhaps greater uncertainty about the future than many of us have experienced in our lifetimes. Therefore, our strategy provides a high-level framework setting out what we want to achieve, by what means and in what timeframe, with the flexibility to adapt to a rapidly changing world. The implementation of the University Strategy will be achieved via our ongoing operational planning processes, a range of specific action plans and a programme of institutional initiatives. Implementation will be overseen by the University Executive Board and progress towards achieving our targets will be reported to our governing body, Council, for scrutiny.

[PLACE] communities and scholars, the [PLACE] public service, and members of the international scholarly community all contributed. The process included a series of facilitated workshops, written submissions, partner roundtables, and focused engagements with under-represented voices within the university community. A standing reference group reviewed successive drafts; the academic and professional communities of the university tested the emerging directions; Council deliberated on the plan in successive meetings before adopting the final document. The plan that follows is the product of that process, and the directions it sets out are informed by the evidence and judgement of the many people who shaped it.

Looking ahead The decade ahead will not be a quiet one. [PLACE] universities are operating in a period in which the public, the government, and the international community all expect more substantive contributions than they have for some time, and in which the conditions of that contribution are themselves in flux. [ORGANISATION] is well placed to meet that moment. We are a national university with a particular role, a deep research culture, and a long-standing relationship with the public life of the country. The plan set out here is a description of how we intend to play that role across the period to 2031, and how we will remain open to the evidence of how the decade actually unfolds. The work that follows is the work of an institution that knows what it is for and intends to do that work well. It will require sustained effort across the university and across the decade. The contribution that [ORGANISATION] will make to [PLACE], the region, and the world over the period ahead will be the measure of how well we do it.

[PLACE] universities are operating in a period in which the public, the government, and the international community all expect more substantive contributions than they have for some time, and in which the conditions of that contribution are themselves in flux. [ORGANISATION] is well placed to meet that moment. We are a national university with a particular role, a deep research culture, and a long-standing relationship with the public life of the country. The plan set out here is a description of how we intend to play that role across the period to 2031, and how we will remain open to the evidence of how the decade actually unfolds. The work that follows is the work of an institution that knows what it is for and intends to do that work well. It will require sustained effort across the university and across the decade. The contribution that [ORGANISATION] will make to [PLACE], the region, and the world over the period ahead will be the measure of how well we do it.

Our aspiration By 2031, [ORGANISATION] will be a university recognised — nationally and internationally — as a steward of the conditions under which the deepest forms of inquiry and education are possible. The University will operate within a published institutional carrying capacity. Its disciplines will be tended as a polyculture rather than ranked as a monoculture. Its partnerships will be measured by their reciprocity, not their volume. Its calendar will include fallow weeks in which the institution practises the kinds of pause that —8—

intergenerational scholarship requires. Its capital footprint will be smaller than it is today and its intellectual footprint deeper. Above all, the University will have demonstrated — not asserted — that the long maintain is itself a serious form of national contribution, and one that no other institution in the country is better placed to model.

Our priorities The four priorities below describe how the reorientation of the plan will be made operational. Each priority is introduced by the question it addresses, followed by the structural commitments through which the University will give the priority real purchase. Before the priorities are unpacked in detail, the table below names the shifts in framing that underpin them as a whole. From

Soil Stewardship and the Long Maintain Why this matters. The intellectual, financial, ecological, and relational substrates that have sustained [ORGANISATION] since 1946 cannot be assumed. They are produced — and depleted — by the choices the University makes about what it builds, what it lets go, and what it tends across long cycles. The reorientation this plan describes begins with the soil. Without an honest account of the conditions that make scholarship possible, every subsequent priority risks being read as a slogan. The starting work, accordingly, is the maintenance and improvement of the substrates themselves, treated as a serious institutional discipline rather than the residue left over after planning. What we’ll do. —9—

Strategic pillars Pillar 1: Discovery for the Nation [ORGANISATION]’s research has always been distinguished by purpose, scale, and proximity to the questions that matter for [PLACE]. Over the plan period we will sharpen that distinctiveness — concentrating investment in mission-aligned research priorities, expanding cross-disciplinary capability, and growing our research income through programs that deliver national impact.

Transformation initiatives • Strengthen mission-aligned research in critical and emerging technologies, with sustained investment in three to five flagship programs. • Build the country’s most ambitious cross-disciplinary research initiatives at the intersections of computing, the life sciences, and the humanities. • Grow Category 1 research income through nationally significant programs, with a particular focus on opportunities arising from the National Reconstruction Fund and successor instruments. • Expand sovereign research infrastructure — high-performance computing, secure facilities, and specialist instruments — across the campus and partner sites.

Pillar 2: Education for a Changing World The world our students will work in is being remade. Our educational programs will be redesigned around the dispositions and capabilities that will matter most over the coming decades: deep disciplinary judgement, comfort with technical complexity, and the capacity for inquiry under uncertainty.

Transformation initiatives • Renew the undergraduate experience around inquiry, judgement, and futures literacy, with substantive curriculum redesign across all colleges by 2028. • Build new postgraduate programs in [PLACE] affairs, advanced computing, and public policy, drawing on [ORGANISATION]’s distinctive depth in each area. • Embed work-integrated and placement-based learning across all faculties, with particular emphasis on partnerships with the federal public service and key industries. • Lift HDR completions and reduce mean time-to-completion through redesigned candidature support and renewed supervisory frameworks.

Pillar 3: Engagement and Reconciliation Universities flourish through their relationships with the communities they serve. Over the plan period we will deepen our partnership with [PLACE] communities, sustain our engagement with the federal public service, and build durable industry partnerships in the sectors that matter most for [PLACE]’s future.

Building for the Future In a landmark development for our university and city, we are building a new Library and Learning Commons at the heart of our campus. This purpose-built facility will transform student, staff and public engagement in our learning resources, technologies and academic skills. After 175 years of university education in [ORGANISATION], it marks an exciting new chapter in how we engage with knowledge and discovery. This flagship building will be located beside the city’s Quincentennial Bridge and it will act as a beacon of learning for our university city. It is designed to be an inspirational, welcoming, high-tech space of learning and creativity that brings diverse people and disciplines together. We look forward to it becoming a vibrant scholarly and social space for [ORGANISATION].

By 2035, we will be counted among the Top 200 universities globally in at least one established World University Ranking. This target demonstrates our ambition to be a highly effective organisation, recognised for our high standards of research excellence and global impact.

We will be a university of choice that inspires and supports its students across their learning journey to become outstanding graduates. This target demonstrates our ambition to focus collective effort to improve student progression, academic engagement, teaching excellence, wellbeing and belonging.

Strategy Implementation Together, we have set out an ambitious shared vision for our university in the coming years. Realising this ambition will require institutional focus to ensure that decision-making at all levels supports delivery and that strategic financial planning and revenue growth align with our priorities.

Our Colleges are at the heart of our vision and they are the key drivers of research and teaching excellence. Each of our four Colleges will publish their own College level strategies identifying where and how they will contribute to us achieving our collective vision for the University. Implementation of these actions will be monitored over time through our Colleges’ rolling five-year business plans, and School and Research Institute annual operational plans.

The third signal is the country’s collective unpreparedness. The working group has consulted with senior figures across the public service, the political class, and civil society and has come to the view that the country does not yet have a settled framework for the social, economic, and democratic consequences of the working assumption. The University considers itself uniquely placed to contribute to that framework. The fourth signal is the rate at which graduate destinations are already shifting. The early cohorts entering the workforce in 2025 and 2026 are encountering professional conditions different in kind, not merely in degree, from the conditions their immediate predecessors encountered. The working group has examined the destination data across the previous three undergraduate cohorts and has concluded that the trend is consistent with the working assumption. Read together, these four signals ask the University to articulate a posture that is structurally responsive to the moment. The posture this Plan adopts is, by deliberate institutional choice, more sharply specified than the postures of recent strategic plans. The University is acting on the working assumption, not waiting for it to be confirmed.

Our ambition By 2031, [ORGANISATION] will be a university that has, over the run of this Plan, structurally reshaped itself in light of the working assumption and made a substantive contribution to the country’s preparation for the conditions the working assumption describes. The University will have wound down those of its functions whose continuation is no longer defensible, cultivated the institutional and civic vocations the working group considers least automatable, and contributed visibly to the democratic shaping of the post-cognitive-labour settlement. The University will be smaller in some dimensions and larger in others. It will, by 2031, be the institution the country requires it to be in the conditions the country will, by then, be operating in.

Our actions. 1. Establish the [ORGANISATION] as the University’s primary planning instrument — a public, continuously maintained account of priorities on approach, each entry carrying the date it was first sensed, the evidence for its emergence, and its current standing between sensed and ratified. 2. Commission the [ORGANISATION] to run a standing horizon-scanning program across every school and portfolio, surfacing forming priorities to the University Executive on a monthly cadence rather than at the planning cycle’s convenience. 3. Extend the [ORGANISATION] to every operational area, so that the distance between the University’s stated priorities and its enacted ones is measured continuously and published, and so that a widening gap is treated as an early signal of a priority the plan has not yet caught. Our targets. • By 2028, every strategic priority the University adopts will appear first on the [ORGANISATION] — dated, evidenced, and public — before it appears in any other planning document, with no exception sustained for more than a single review cycle. • The [ORGANISATION] will be reviewed every quarter from 2027, and no priority will be permitted to enter a University plan without a Register entry establishing that it was sensed before it was set. • By 2031, the median interval between a priority’s first appearance on the Register and its independent confirmation as an institutional priority will exceed twelve months, demonstrating that the University routinely senses its priorities a year before it would once have declared them. —9—

Ratification, Not Direction Our position. A plan that records priorities the institution is already pursuing cannot also pretend to be the source of them. The third priority is the constitutional one: to reconceive the University’s planning authority as the power to recognise and ratify — 10 —

Instruments turned inward For most of its life the School has built indicators for other organisations. Over the period it began, deliberately, to build them for itself. The [ORGANISATION] — the shared library the School maintains for its collaborators — was extended with a mirror wing holding measures of the School’s own operation, and the [ORGANISATION], until then largely a demonstration piece, was pointed inward and left running. The count grew quickly, and then kept growing. By the close of the period the School was tracking more indicators on itself than it had ever maintained on any single collaborator, a fact its own instruments were the first to report.

In 2022 the School invited a national statistics agency to help rebuild its selfindicator schema on the standards the agency applies to the national accounts. Associate Professor [PERSON], who led the work through the [ORGANISATION], noted that it was the first time the School had held itself to a measure it had not designed. The schema has governed the School’s internal reporting since, and the agency retained a copy for its own files.

Evaluating our own evaluation The [ORGANISATION] programme was built to study how organisations review their own work. It was inevitable, if awkward, that the programme would eventually be asked to study the School. Over the period the [ORGANISATION] turned its attention to the School’s own review calendar — the rhythm at which its programmes, labs and initiatives return for scrutiny — and found, among other things, that the calendar had drifted from what its own indicators would have set. The Observatory reported the drift to the body responsible for the calendar, which was the Observatory.

Who we are The [ORGANISATION] is [ORGANISATION]’s measurement-andprocess school. It studies how organisations count, evaluate and improve, and, across the period covered by this report, extended that inquiry from paperwork and process to the physical fleet the University now depends on to keep its paths swept and its parcels moving. Its people work across six research themes, anchored by the [ORGANISATION], the [ORGANISATION], the [ORGANISATION] and the always-on [ORGANISATION]. The School teaches the [ORGANISATION] to a cohort each year, runs the [ORGANISATION] for professionals who cannot leave their posts for a degree — [PLACE] the Dashboard chief among them this period — and supervises PhD candidates whose projects are embedded, by design, in the organisations and instruments they study. It traces its origins to the [ORGANISATION]. A School whose subject is measurement inherits, sooner or later, whatever the University measures next. Over this period that turned out to be a fleet of machines, and the wall built to watch them.

In 2022 the School partnered with a metropolitan transit authority whose own control-room fleet dashboards had drawn the same criticism the School had long made of others. Dr [PERSON]’s team reviewed the tile’s design against the authority’s fleet-monitoring interface, recommending the uptime figure carry a visible confidence band rather than a single number. The authority adopted the recommendation; the University’s own dashboard has not, to date.

“Every fleet dashboard we have seen treats ‘not broken’ as the same thing as ‘working’. We said so in our own control room five years ago and have been saying it to everyone else’s ever since.” — Head of Fleet Systems, a metropolitan transit authority

The University’s policies and procedures strictly prohibit all forms of discrimination, vilification, intimidation, violence, and other disrespectful or oppressive behaviours, regardless of cultural background, religion, gender, or political conviction. Where standards are not met [ORGANISATION] acts decisively to uphold these standards. From 2026, all coursework students and Higher Degree by Research (HDR) candidates will be required to complete the [ORGANISATION] Rights, Relationships and Respect online module. This mandatory training meets baseline requirements of the National Higher Education Code to Prevent and Respond to Gender‑based Violence, ensuring that all students receive foundational education on respectful relationships, consent and safety. Also from 2026, [ORGANISATION] will implement the Workplace Gender Equality Agency (WGEA) targetsetting requirements, which require large employers to select, monitor and publicly report on measurable gender equality objectives on a three‑year cycle.

Health, safety and wellbeing [ORGANISATION] promotes excellence in health and safety leadership for staff, students, visitors and contractors. The University maintains a comprehensive work health and safety management system shaped by its operational context and ensures consistent implementation across all campuses, functions and activities to support a safe and healthy working and learning environment.

Engaged Alumni [ORGANISATION] is committed to cultivating lifelong relationships with its alumni. [ORGANISATION] graduates hold influential leadership roles across [PLACE] and around the world, spanning government, business, academia and the not‑for‑profit sector. The University actively seeks to harness this collective expertise and experience to create meaningful opportunities for current students and staff through mentoring, networking and collaborative initiatives. By strengthening these enduring connections, [ORGANISATION] deepens its global community and ensures alumni remain active contributors to the University’s mission, reputation and long‑term success.

Education That Shapes the Future Why this matters — A grade tells the University what a student achieved; it says very little about whether the student was in the room while achieving it. As teaching moves further across lecture theatres, tutorial rooms, and recorded delivery, the University’s ability to say who actually engaged, and when, has not kept pace with its ability to say who eventually passed. This is not a proposal to make attendance compulsory in spirit — it already is, in every unit outline that lists participation as an expectation. It is a proposal to stop treating that expectation as unenforceable simply because the University has not, until now, looked at the record it was already keeping of whether anyone met it.

What we’ll do — 1. Extend swipe-card readers to every lecture theatre and tutorial room by 2028, matching the coverage already standard in professional and research spaces. 2. Instrument the lecture-capture platform with a recurring engagement ping during recorded and livestreamed delivery, logged against the enrolled student rather than the device. 3. Link swipe-derived and ping-derived attendance to scholarship renewal and progression review, alongside — not instead of — academic performance. 4. Publish a unit-by-unit presence comparison across delivery modes, so a fully online unit and a fully in-person unit are held to the same recorded standard rather than exempted from one another. How we’ll know — —9—

• A published Presence Index for every unit of study will track the gap between enrolment and recorded appearance by 2027. • 100% of first-year units will carry a minimum recorded-attendance threshold before a final grade is released by 2029, with no standing exception carried past a single semester. • By 2031, scholarship and progression panels will receive a presence record alongside every academic transcript they review. • The cross-mode presence comparison will publish for every unit of study by 2030, with no delivery mode carrying a lower recorded-attendance threshold than another.

STRATEGIC PLAN COMPOSITION The overall direction of our strategy builds on the achievements of our previous Strategic Plan 2019-2023, Our Future is You. We have sharpened our vision and refined our pillars, goals and priorities to reflect our focus towards genuine accessibility, collaboration and connectedness across education, training and research. [ORGANISATION] Strategic Plan 2024-2028, We Change Lives, is organised by pillars that capture the purpose and vision of the University. Under each of the pillars are strategic goals that identify the outcomes to be achieved. The plan also documents the strategic priorities that will be undertaken to achieve these goals, along with the strategic measures that will monitor our progress.

PEOPLE Our people are our purpose, and their success is our legacy. We recognise that we need to create transformative life opportunities through fostering the talents and enhancing the potential of our students, staff, alumni, and communities. We are committed to creating an environment of lifelong learning where people feel empowered and proud to learn, work and grow with [ORGANISATION]. We will be leaders in providing innovative, accessible, supportive and flexible learning, engaged workplaces and enriched societies.

At [ORGANISATION], we celebrate the incredible diversity of backgrounds, cultures, abilities, perspectives, and talents found amongst our staff. We recognise that this enables us to support the same rich diversity found within our student cohorts and communities as well.

1.4 Equality, Diversity and Inclusion: Create an environment that brings out the best in our staff, strengthened by a culture of equality, inclusion, flexibility and innovation so our staff are inspired to achieve and excel, and so they are held in the highest regard nationally and globally.

A Connected and Accountable Campus Why this matters Committee minutes and process action items too often close without anyone clearly responsible for carrying them forward, and a good decision that dissolves into an unowned action item is functionally indistinguishable from a decision never taken at all. Naming an owner at the point of minuting connects governance to delivery, and connecting the Stewardship Register to the [ORGANISATION] means an asset’s steward and its live status are always read from the same published record. A campus that is well connected on paper — a register here, a dashboard there, a committee structure that maps neatly onto both — is only actually accountable if the same name can be followed from one system to the next without a gap. What we’ll do 1. Require every committee and working-group action item to carry a named owner and a review date at the point it is minuted, with no “for information” placeholder standing in for an owner. 2. Publish an escalation ladder naming who inherits an action when its owner is unavailable, rather than leaving it to whoever next reads the minutes. 3. Integrate the Stewardship Register with the [ORGANISATION] so an asset’s steward and its live status sit on the one published record. 4. Review every standing committee’s terms of reference to confirm it names an owner for each of its recurring outputs, not only for one-off decisions. How we’ll know

• The proportion of action items closed by their originally assigned owner exceeds 90% every year of the plan. • Median time from an escalation trigger to a named successor being confirmed falls to under one week by 2029. • 100% of [ORGANISATION] entries carry a visible, linked steward by the close of the plan period. • Every standing committee’s terms of reference names an owner for each recurring output by the end of 2028.

Education for an Uncertain Decade Why this matters Graduates who leave [ORGANISATION] in 2031 will enter a labour market substantially reshaped from the one their degree was designed against; this pillar exists to keep the curriculum, and the judgement behind it, moving at the same pace as the world it prepares people for. It is also the pillar most exposed to the pace of external change, since the tools and expectations shaping graduate work in 2031 are, in large part, not yet invented.

What we’ll do 1. Renew core curricula across every degree to build durable capability rather than tool-specific skill. 2. Expand work-integrated learning so that every undergraduate program carries a substantial applied component by 2029. 3. Build AI-fluency and assurance literacy into every program, so graduates understand not only how these systems work but how they should be governed.

Place, Partnership, and Belonging Why this matters A university’s standing in its region and its community is not a pillar that can be delivered from a dashboard; it is built through the ordinary, cumulative work of partnership, presence, and welcome, and this pillar exists to keep that work central to the plan even as the other three pillars grow more instrumented around it. Its success is measured less by a single indicator than by whether the people closest to the University — students, staff, and neighbouring communities — recognise the change described here in their own experience of the place.

What we’ll do 1. Deepen partnerships with regional government, industry, and community organisations across the University’s campuses. 2. Extend student and staff belonging programs, with particular attention to those newest to the University. 3. Improve the accessibility and openness of University spaces, on campus and online, for the communities the University serves.

Between 2023 and 2025 the School asked a [PLACE] evaluation agency to evaluate the [ORGANISATION] programme itself. Dr [PERSON]’s [ORGANISATION] supplied five years of its own review logs; the agency returned findings, which the Observatory then reviewed and returned in turn. Both sides recorded that the exchange could, in principle, have continued without end, and closed it by agreement rather than by conclusion. “The [ORGANISATION] is the only research unit we have assessed that asked us to assess our assessment of it. We stopped, on the third pass, for reasons of budget rather than of principle.” — Senior Assessor, a [PLACE] evaluation agency

What the dashboard changed The [ORGANISATION] was intended as a tool for watching the School’s work. Over five years it became, quietly, a tool that shaped the work it watched. Staff arranged their weeks around the measures the wall made visible; measures the wall did not carry drew less of everyone’s attention, whatever their importance. The School studies this effect in other organisations under the heading of data cultures, and was not surprised to find it at home. What it had not anticipated was the speed. Within eighteen months the share of the School’s measurement effort directed at itself had doubled, and it has not since fallen back. When a state audit office examined the [ORGANISATION] in 2024, it observed that ninety-four per cent of the measures staff consulted daily had been added in the previous eighteen months, and that the single oldest indicator still on the wall was the one recording how quickly new indicators were added. The office recommended the School retain that indicator on historical grounds. The School’s Dashboard Residents recorded the recommendation on the dashboard.

Sub-goal: Development of the continuing and further education of the future The university’s goal is to contribute to meeting society's increasing demand for the continuing education of the workforce through research-based further and continuing education, for example in connection with the increased digitalisation of society. The existing continuing and further education models are currently under pressure. To this end, the university wants to work with new models that can meet the need for new competencies on the part of both graduates and the labour market, now and in future. Establishing links between students and the labour market Sub-goal: More career-oriented elements in the degree programmes The aim is to give all students the opportunity to collaborate with relevant employers as part of their degree programme. This will allow students to establish links to the labour market before graduation, and will contribute to maintaining the high employment levels of university graduates taken as a whole.

The PhD degree programmes Sub-goal: Increased internationalisation of PhD degree programmes The university will attract more international talents to its PhD degree programmes and increase the international mobility of the university's own talents. During the strategy period, the university will bolster the internationalisation of its PhD programmes by cooperating with the university's international alliance partners. This will enhance PhD students’ international networks and their opportunities for pursuing a successful career, either within academia or in other sectors.

Sub-goal: Earlier career clarification A PhD degree can either lead to an academic career or a variety of alternative careers in the public and private sectors. Society’s demand for highly qualified knowledge workers is increasing, a demand which PhD graduates meet. The university will take steps to introduce career clarification earlier in the PhD programmes to put graduates in the best position to make career choices. Research integration Sub-goal: More immersive modules in degree programmes The immersive modules will serve to further the university’s ambition of increasing research integration in the degree programmes in order to achieve an even higher academic level.

Executive summary This plan sets out five strategic priorities that will shape the work of the [ORGANISATION] through to 2031. Together they describe a coherent ambition: that [ORGANISATION] will become the country’s most consequential site for the integrated study of energies — historical, material, somatic, and planetary — and the most reliable institution for the cultivation of an energetic imagination across the disciplines on which [PLACE] public life depends.

The priorities are interlocking. None can be fully realised in isolation, and the plan is best read as a description of the university we are working to become over the plan period: attentive to the conditions on which institutional life rests, accountable for the energies it draws on and the energies it produces, and recognisably [ORGANISATION].

The remainder of this document sets out, for each priority, the transformation initiatives we will pursue and the measures by which we will track our progress. It also describes the implementation phases that will deliver the plan and the governance arrangements that will hold us accountable to the directions set out here.

transformations are reshaping the operating environment for the university, and each interacts with the others in ways that demand a coordinated institutional response. The first is the maturation of the planetary energy transition. The decade ahead will see substantial decarbonisation of the country’s energy infrastructure, the recomposition of major industrial sectors, and the renewal of the cultural and political settings within which those shifts will be undertaken. Universities sit at the intersection of those shifts — as producers of the knowledge on which the transition depends, as educators of the workforces that will deliver it, and as institutions whose own operations are themselves part of the transition.

A metropolitan transit authority invited Lecturer and Convenor [PERSON]’s team to review the customer-satisfaction tile mounted in its central control room — a single number, refreshed quarterly when the tile first went up, that operations staff had come to check the way they check the time. The team found the figure had not refreshed in over two years; the survey instrument behind it had been discontinued, its contractor reassigned, and nobody in the control room had noticed, because the number on the wall had never stopped looking current. Staff described adjusting rostering and complaint-escalation decisions around a figure that, for the better part of two years, had simply been sitting there. “Nobody lied to us about the number. It just stopped being anyone’s job to keep it honest, and the wall never said so.” — Control Room Supervisor, a metropolitan transit authority

What a number is asked to keep meaning The [ORGANISATION] exists to trace how a piece of research effort becomes counted, valued, and eventually cited work — the usual pathway runs forward, from a finding to its recognition. This period Senior Research Fellow [PERSON]’s team ran the Atlas’s method in reverse on a single class of object: a customer-facing score, taken once for a specific purpose, and asked by everyone downstream to keep meaning the same thing indefinitely.

A national telecommunications carrier had first measured a customer-trust score for a single marketing campaign in 2022, using a bespoke short-form survey run once, to a sample of respondents who saw one advertisement. Four years on, the same figure was still appearing in board papers, investor briefings, and a customer-facing trust page on the carrier’s website — each new citation treating the score as if it had just been taken, none of them noting the year, the sample, or the campaign it was built to evaluate. The Atlas team’s pathway map showed the score picking up eleven distinct downstream citations, only one of which linked back to the original survey instrument.

Introduction from Vice Chancellor. Professor [PERSON] I arrived at the [ORGANISATION] in the Summer of 2022, I was welcomed into an institution that has been transforming lives for decades. What began as [PLACE] Technical College in 1924 has evolved into the county’s only seat of Higher Education, enriching knowledge through research and building a better future for thousands of people in the UK and around the world. I am incredibly proud to be the Vice Chancellor of the [ORGANISATION], and the custodian of its legacy. In uncertain times, our polestar is the positive impact we can make, and the steps we must take to achieve our ambitions and enable others to achieve theirs.

This strategy will be our guide and has been developed in close consultation with the people most affected by it – our staff and student community. Their commitment to their University is on each page, and I thank them for their guidance and counsel. Now it is time for us to rise to their challenge and work together to deliver the [ORGANISATION] they have envisioned. I am looking forward to every step of that journey and invite you to join us.

This strategy has been developed through a process of co-creation. Vice-Chancellor’s introduction This Strategic Plan articulates the direction of the [ORGANISATION] across the period 2026 to 2031. The Plan does so through a framing the working group settled on early in the drafting process and held throughout: that an institution of [ORGANISATION]’s complexity is best understood as a production — a long-running production with an overture, character arcs, ensemble numbers, and a closing standing ovation that the institution intends to earn rather than expect. The framing is not metaphorical decoration. A long-running production has the same operational characteristics as a long-running national institution. It requires a script that the company believes in. It requires rehearsal time that the schedule must protect. It requires a producer’s discipline about which numbers are working and which are not. And it requires an honest assessment, at the end of each season, of where the production is on its run.

This Plan describes how the University will run its production over the next five years. It describes the kinds of standing-ovation moments — the showstoppers, the eleven o’clock numbers, the encores — that the institution intends to earn, and it describes the kinds of supporting work, often invisible from the stalls, that those moments require. We commend the Plan to the University community in the conviction that a national university which understands its own staging is a national university more likely to do its work well. Strategic priorities The Three-Year Horizon and the Wind-Down of Cognitive Labour Premise. The working assumption set out in the foreword has particular implications for those institutional functions whose continuation, on the working assumption, is no longer defensible. The Plan addresses those functions honestly, in the conviction that a national research university owes the staff, students, and country it serves a structured, dignified, and well-supported wind-down rather than a gradual erosion under conditions of denial. Initiatives. 1. Establish the AI Transition Office, chaired by a Deputy Vice-Chancellor and reporting directly to Council, charged with identifying institutional functions for structured wind-down and supporting the people whose work the wind-down affects. 2. Publish, by the end of 2026, an Honesty Statement on the AI Transition, addressed to current students and reviewed annually, setting out the working group’s best assessment of the conditions graduates of each degree will encounter on entering the workforce. 3. Convene a quarterly Three-Year Horizon Review, chaired by the Vice-Chancellor and attended by the Deputy Vice-Chancellors, examining the current state of the working assumption and the University’s structural response. Measures. 1. By the end of 2026, the Honesty Statement on the AI Transition will have been published and made accessible to every current student of the University. 2. By 2029, the AI Transition Office will have completed structured wind-down assessments of every institutional function nominated for review by the Three year Horizon Review.

Custodianship of the Last Human Vocations Premise. The working assumption does not bear uniformly across the institution’s functions. Several vocations — pastoral, contemplative, ceremonial, embodied, and place-based — are considered by the working group to be substantially less automatable across the plan period. The University proposes to identify, protect, and patiently cultivate these vocations as a substantive institutional commitment. Initiatives.

Acknowledgement of Country We acknowledge and pay our respects to the First Peoples, the Traditional Custodians of the lands and waterways. We recognise their spiritual and ongoing cultural connection to Country. We respectfully acknowledge Elders past and present and thank them for their wisdom and guidance as we walk in their footsteps.

Our education will enrich lives, embrace technology and stimulate minds. We will stand up for people in need and for causes that matter to a better common future for humanity. We will nurture ethical leadership, guided by the principles of respect, honesty, courage and sustainability. Our research quality will be without compromise, focused and embedded. We will cultivate a vibrant academic life and dynamic campus experience. We will be deeply engaged with industry and society, tackling big questions to create tangible results. As a Catholic university, we will strive to be a university for the people, both individually and collectively. We will reflect the diversity of our communities. We will embed our commitment to reconciliation and sharpen our efforts toward sustainability. Ours is a vision to make new, to break down barriers and to look on the totality of our endeavours with hope, faith and reason.

Our focus is to enrich lives through learning and knowledge. We create opportunity and stand for those in need. We believe society is enriched through education, and that everyone should be treated with dignity. We aim to inspire and connect people, and act with empathy and courage. We foster a vibrant intellectual life for students and staff, and seek new knowledge which has a tangible impact on real world challenges.

Through our education, research, and the way we operate as a large organisation, we recognise our significant responsibility in addressing sustainability as one of the greatest challenges of our time. We consciously align our activities to the United Nations [[ORGANISATION]] (SDGs) and actively seek to shape a sustainable future.

We forge valued relationships with a variety of organisations to help fully unlock the University’s positive impact on the world, from small and medium enterprises to large public and private sector, nationally and globally significant organisations. Our aim is to be recognised as a partner of choice that is straightforward to work with and has a reputation for quality and reliability.

We will be increasingly proactive in our approach to strengthening and broadening existing strategic relationships, and identifying, building, and embedding new ones. This will be guided by a clearly defined set of priorities that reflect our academic and functional strengths and leverage the University’s key assets.

1. Leadership in sustainability, meaning we embed sustainability in all strategies and decision-making, raising awareness, and improving performance. 2. Academic innovation and impact, equipping students and staff with sustainability knowledge and skills, and delivering world-leading research aligned to the SDGs. 3. Sustainable campus and practices, aligned with the city and region’s intent to reduce carbon emissions to net zero carbon and to embed services and systems that support and enable sustainable behaviour. 4. Engagement and partnerships, amplifying impact through local, national, and global collaborations.

Our partnerships will span multiple sectors, both in the UK and globally, supporting our strategy in multiple ways. This will include further developing collaboration to deliver strong graduate outcomes, such as work-integrated learning and embedding employer perspectives in our curriculum, along with partnerships that help to achieve research income, impact and recognition of the University’s academic excellence.
