text:
Assurance Beyond Measurement Why this matters. The University cannot ask its community to carry assurance through attunement while simultaneously requiring it to feed the instrument estate that attunement replaces. Dual running would double the burden and halve the trust. The second priority is therefore an orderly withdrawal: instrument by instrument, documented, sequenced behind demonstrated attunement capability, and irreversible only in the sense that a retired instrument returns solely by decision of Council. The [ORGANISATION], whose scholarship established why the estate must shrink, will steward the shrinking.

Every instrument we maintain teaches the institution to perform for it. The felt sense of a well-run course is the one indicator we have never had to correct. What we’ll do. 1. Establish the Register of Retired Instruments, a published record of every rubric, checklist, standing dashboard, and acquittal template withdrawn from service, with the date of retirement and the attunement arrangement that assumed its load. 2. Sequence retirements behind capability, so that no instrument is withdrawn before the relevant Attunement Panel has demonstrated, over two consecutive convenings, that its read is stable without the instrument in the room. 3. Replace cyclical internal audit with ambient assurance: a standing, low-intensity attunement presence across the University’s operations, convened by the [ORGANISATION], through which concerns are felt and raised continuously rather than discovered retrospectively. 4. Engage external partners, accreditors, and reviewers early in the plan period, so that the University’s attunement-based evidence is understood, and where possible recognised, in the terms in which it is produced. How we’ll know. • By 2030, the Register of Retired Instruments will record the retirement of the majority of the University’s standing quality instruments, and no retired instrument will have been returned to service other than by decision of Council. • Research income across the plan period will exceed $600 million, assured throughout by ambient rather than acquittal-based processes. • From 2029, the University will accept no external quality finding that its senior attunement practitioners cannot, sitting as a panel, independently feel; divergences will be published together with the panel’s read.

Energy, System, and Substrate Premise. The systems on which the university’s research and educational work depend — compute, lab, fabrication, building, transport — sit on a substrate of energetic conditions that historically have been treated as external to the work itself. The plan period asks [ORGANISATION] to bring those conditions into structured contact with the work, to account for them explicitly, and to act on what that accounting reveals. Initiatives. 1. Establish an institution-wide Energetic-Impact Assessment Framework applied to every major research grant, capital project, building decision, and curriculum review, adopted by Council in 2027 and reported on annually across the plan period. 2. Build sovereign capability for energetic accounting across the disciplines, including measurement, modelling, and reporting tools applicable across the research and educational enterprise, made available to candidates, staff, and partner institutions through a published methodology and a sustained training programme. — 10 —

KPIs. • An institution-wide Energetic-Impact Assessment Framework adopted by Council in 2027, applied to all major institutional decisions, with audited compliance reported publicly each year. • A published Energy Practice Register, sustained from 2028, listing every active research project’s energetic premise, footprint, and implications, custodially maintained at the institutional level and open to the wider research community. • Net-zero direct emissions across all research and operational facilities by 2034, with a credible decarbonisation pathway sustained from 2026 and reported on publicly each year. • Sustained reduction in the embodied energy of new institutional investments across the plan period, with reduction targets adopted by Council in 2026 and reviewed annually.

We are committed to responsible and open research as well as to the open assessment of researchers and research. We are pioneers in the development of researcher careers. Our involvement in international scientific networks and research collaboration has increased, giving us visibility and a strong standing. We are one of [PLACE]’s leading universities in acquiring EU research funding. We work openly in regional, national and international networks and with stakeholders. Our collaboration is responsible, reciprocal and goal-oriented. We actively contribute research-based knowledge to the public debate. Our financial flexibility has become stronger. Our thriving community is committed to common goals. We offer a wide range of opportunities to develop expertise and leadership. Our welcoming campuses and functional facilities meet the changing needs of teaching and research, and the requirements of sustainability. We effectively use the opportunities provided by automation and artificial intelligence.

An open dialogue, both within our community and with the wider society, is of particular importance to us. Openness supports the production of new knowledge and sharing it with society. We are committed to the principles of open science.

For us, responsible criticism is a constructive debate based on researched information and respect for the diversity of opinion. We strengthen the ability of the members of our University community to analyse issues independently and objectively.

Our diverse and flexible curriculum allows for choosing interesting and individual study paths. By anticipating changes in the operational environment, we ensure that our education is upto-date and adapts to the changing world. The latest scientific knowledge guides our teaching.

We are a notable player in the [PLACE] education area, and internationality is a central part of our education. We strengthen our international education selection and multicultural competence that prepare students and teachers to operate fluently in a global environment. Collaboration with the higher education institutions in the [ORGANISATION] region creates new opportunities for students to engage in international networking.

text: In this strategic plan, we set out a programme of consolidation. Rather than attempting to define or direct the academic life of the university, this plan for institutional-level activity focuses on reworking the structures on which our academic success depends, and which will help staff and students to thrive at [ORGANISATION]. The Strategic Plan sets out plans for investment in our programme of [ORGANISATION] to enhance our institutional impact, both externally and internally; to ensure transparency in our decision-making, including investment for the future; to drive change in education, simplifying where possible in the interests of staff and students; and to prioritise a comprehensive programme of service improvements to create a high-quality environment for our world-class research and education. Rethinking our ways of working seemed necessary when we began the consultation process at the start of the 2021-22 academic year. Against a backdrop of rising inflation, financial uncertainty and geopolitical instability, it is now urgent. Like other organisations facing a period of deep, externally driven change, we must use our considerable resources wisely to put us in the best possible position for the long-term. By focusing on a smaller number of priorities and being as efficient as possible, we can free up resource for what matters most: supporting staff and students so they can do their best work. This will require a new mindset and a shared approach to change, with deep cooperation between local academic units and university-wide services, close attention to local needs (especially those of academic staff and students), and a whole-institution approach to efficiencies of scale. It will also require a robust financial strategy and an estates strategy that is agreed and understood widely across our community. Our institutional values must underpin the delivery of this strategic plan. By changing how we are organised and how we work together, we aim to create an environment that enables academic rigour and intellectual innovation to thrive and where our staff and students feel supported to learn and work as part of a dynamic and mutually respectful community.

We will seek leadership in academia and public debate through critical reflections on key issues and expert solutions. We will consistently implement forms of expert participation in the formation of the state policy. By contributing to overcoming the current challenges, we will create an interdisciplinary research and study environment focused on the implementation of the sustainable development goals – health and well-being, high quality education and climate change prevention. In parallel, we will further the research of [PLACE] studies as a scientific knowledge of the totality of [PLACE]. Another important dimension of our responsibility to the society is scientific communication, which shapes the public opinion on the basis of a solid and reliable knowledge. We will realise the need to not only persuasively inform about the works of scientists, but also to strengthen the public understanding that a scientific knowledge and critical reflection are fundamental and its practical value is tangible. We will use the principles of open science and various forms of dissemination for the availability of research results. We will strengthen our international reputation in order to establish [ORGANISATION] as a place of science and studies on the [PLACE] and global university map. By attracting motivated students, we will expand activities with schools and encourage the active choice of studies as a path of personal development based on a scientific knowledge. For postgraduate students, we will provide more opportunities to transform a deep scientific knowledge into ambitious professional goals.

With two national teacher training centres in [PLACE] and [PLACE] implementing their academic potential and with subject faculties getting involved in teacher education, we will implement our national leadership in pedagogical research and studies, assuming ideological responsibility for the development of education in [PLACE] and creating preconditions for a 21st century school – an educational process that meets the needs of the future society. We will implement the concept of teacher training, improvement of their competencies and development of professional qualifications based on international research and the experience of advanced education systems.

A plan written for a turbulent decade has to do something a stable plan does not: it has to take the next contribution seriously, whatever shape it arrives in, and it has to keep building on what is working rather than quietly setting it aside. The directions that follow have been chosen with that disposition in mind.

The plan reflects extensive consultation with our staff, students, alumni, and partners over the course of 2025, and structured deliberation by Council and the executive across the same period. The directions it sets out are deliberate. They will require sustained effort, candid review, and a willingness to revise where evidence requires it. I commend this plan to the [ORGANISATION] community. The work that follows is ours to do together, and I am confident in the contribution that [ORGANISATION] will continue to make to [PLACE], the region, and the world over the period ahead. Vice-Chancellor and President

Executive summary [ORGANISATION] is a national institution with a distinctive purpose: to conduct research, deliver education, and contribute to public life in ways that serve [PLACE], its region, and the broader international community of scholarship. This plan describes how we will sustain and renew that purpose over the period to 2031. Four strategic priorities organise the work of the plan period. Each is developed in detail in the body of this document, with a premise, a set of transformation initiatives, success measures, and an indicative phasing for delivery.

These priorities are interdependent. None can be fully realised in isolation, and the plan is best read as a description of the university we are working to become over the period ahead: ambitious about what universities are for, honest about the work required, and recognisably [ORGANISATION].

The second is the repositioning of the body within knowledge work. The postures, attentions, and conditions on which scholarship and teaching depend have, for a long time, been treated as external to the work itself. The plan period asks the institution to bring those conditions into the work — to recognise that the energetic conditions of academic and professional labour are themselves part of the institutional fabric, and that a research-intensive university that fails to attend to them will not sustain the conditions of its own future flourishing. The third is the rise of energetic accounting in institutional life. What was once an externality — the energy a building consumes, the energy a research programme draws on, the energy embodied in the materials of teaching — is increasingly an object of structured attention, with frameworks for measurement, reporting, and acting on what those frameworks reveal. A research-intensive university that takes that accounting seriously is one that the country can trust to lead the wider transition that comes with it.

[ORGANISATION] sits within this context with particular advantages and particular obligations. We are a research-intensive national university with depth across the disciplines on which the field of inquiry draws — the sciences, the engineering disciplines, the humanities, the social sciences, the creative arts — and a national charter to take seriously the questions on which the country’s public life depends. We are located in the country’s capital, deeply integrated with the institutions of national policy life, and within walking distance of the country’s foremost cultural and collecting institutions. The strategic choices in this plan reflect both that position and the work the period demands.

Embed (2029-30). The third phase is concerned with embedding the reorientation into the operational rhythm of the University. Two fallow weeks per year are in routine operation from 2027, and by 2029 they have become a stable feature of the calendar. The Mycelial Forum has met often enough by this phase that its conventions are settled. Carrying-capacity caps are in force across every coursework programme. The Five-Substrate Audit is published in 2029. Renew (2031). The final year of the plan is given over to a structured renewal of the plan itself. Council receives a formal account of the period, with the Soil Health Index trends, the Reciprocity Register reciprocity ratios, and the carrying-capacity adherence reported in full. The next strategic cycle is designed in the light of the period’s findings, with an explicit expectation that the language and indicators of the current plan will themselves be subject to composting before being carried forward. The phases are scheduled rather than time-locked. Indicators that flourish ahead of phase will not be artificially held back; indicators that lag will not be artificially accelerated.

How we developed this plan This plan was developed over fourteen months through a process of facilitated conversations across staff, students, alumni, partners, and [PLACE] colleagues. Where conventional consultation would have aggregated views into a synthesis, the working groups instead practised pluri-vocal layering — surfacing dissonance rather than resolving it, and returning to the same questions across three successive rounds rather than treating early responses as settled. The framing language — soil, polyculture, mycelium, fallow, steady state — emerged through this process rather than being imposed at the outset. Where the language has been retained in the final plan, it is because participants in the working groups returned to it spontaneously rather than because the executive selected it. The plan has, in this sense, been composted into shape rather than pushed into form.

As a public institution, [ORGANISATION] is committed to providing learners with access to high quality education and supporting the social, cultural, and economic needs of Alberta and its people. With Alberta’s younger, diverse population projected to grow well into the 2030s, and Calgary serving as a key area of population concentration, we must take steps to accommodate the projected demand for a [PLACE] education.

To meet the learning needs of students, [ORGANISATION] is committed to providing more flexible course delivery options that complement traditional methods of course delivery and scheduling. As we work to supplement in-person course delivery with options such as block week, hybrid, blended, and online delivery, we remain committed to ensuring students can develop relationships with their professors and have high-quality learning experiences. Going beyond traditional scheduling, we will strategically provide more course-taking options for students throughout the academic year.

While we are dedicated to growing with the province, we recognise that increasing access to learners seeking a [PLACE] education must not compromise the quality of education we provide. Embracing the challenge to meet learner demand means we must manage growth carefully and consider the University’s personnel capacity, infrastructure limitations, and financial resources.

As we explore ways to optimise course delivery options, we realise the importance of investing in technologies that support faculty’s ability to adopt innovative and creative teaching methods into their courses. We will support faculty to integrate these technologies into their classes to give students the best learning experience possible regardless of the course delivery method. We recognise that students have various goals for attending university. While many students come to [PLACE] to prepare for a particular job or career, others see their education as a pathway to further studies or a means to make a positive difference in society. To meet students’ diverse educational goals, we will leverage our strengths to develop new programs or modify existing programs by investigating programming options such as after-degrees, five-year combined degrees, and credentials with laddering options.

The University’s own experience over the current planning period bears this out. Work already published from within our schools has found that a system recolouring a shared kitchenette’s compost-bin lids changed remarkably little about what actually went into them, and that a fault-reporting instrument installed to replace a handwritten log measured its own uptime more confidently than it measured the thing it was installed to track. These are not failures of any single instrument. They are what happens when a great deal of institutional attention goes into measuring and anticipating, and comparatively little goes into the plainer question of who is holding the thing steady in between. This plan sets out to close that gap directly, deliberately, and by name.

Our ambition By 2031, every asset, process, and shared resource the University holds will carry a single named, accountable steward, published on a register anyone in the University community can check. That ambition is deliberately narrower than “improve accountability” and deliberately broader than any one School’s remit. It asks nothing exotic of the University — only that the habit already practised in its most visible instruments, the [ORGANISATION]’s named convenor, the [ORGANISATION]’s named custodians, extend all the way down to the smallest shared thing the University holds. An institution that can name who is —7—

answerable for its research strategy should be equally able to name who is answerable for its noticeboards. We do not expect this ambition to be comfortable. Naming a steward for something previously held in common surfaces, immediately, how little upkeep some things have actually been receiving. That discomfort is not a reason to soften the ambition; it is the ambition working as intended, in year one, before a single new instrument has been built.

Priority 4: A Capable and Durable Institution None of the above is possible without renewed institutional foundations. Over the plan period we will invest in the digital, physical, and human infrastructure on which [ORGANISATION] depends, and we will work toward an institutional culture in which every member of the community can do their best work.

Our position A university is, in the end, an apparatus for sustaining intellectual work over decades. The settings of that apparatus — the buildings, the systems, the cultures of the people who make it run — have to be tended deliberately if the work is to continue.

• Refresh the campus precinct as a working environment fit for the next twenty-five years, with sustained investment in heritage assets, contemporary teaching spaces, and student amenities. • Build a culturally safe and structurally equitable working environment for all members of the [ORGANISATION] community, with clear measures of progress on representation, retention, and career advancement for staff and students from historically marginalised backgrounds.

Set in motion (2026) In the first year, we will put in place the governance, baselines, and foundational investments needed to deliver the plan. Each priority will have a designated executive sponsor, a dedicated implementation team, and a published baseline against which progress will be measured. Foundational investments — in digital infrastructure, in flagship research initiatives, and in educational redesign — will commence.

Deepen (2027-2028) Through 2027 and 2028, the major investments and program changes set out in this plan will reach scale. New postgraduate programs will commence; flagship research initiatives will reach operational maturity; the campus precinct refresh will deliver its most visible early outcomes. The mid-period review will be undertaken in late 2028.

Ahead-of-Its-Time Research and the [PERSON] Method Premise. The research character of the University has, since [PERSON], been distinguished by a willingness to undertake work whose immediate application is unclear and whose ultimate value depends on the patient unfolding of what later commentators have called the [PERSON] Method: the discipline of taking the halfbaked idea seriously, examining it in its half-baked state, and following it through the patient sequence of testing, recasting, and packaging by which [PERSON] produced, among other things, the wooden magnet, the boxed spark plug sparks, and the celebrated dehydrated water pills. The Plan extends the Method into a structured contemporary research posture.

Initiatives. 1. Establish the [PERSON] Method Fellowship: a ten-year research fellowship scheme for early-career researchers prepared to commit to work whose applications are unlikely to be visible within the term of the fellowship, with a published carrying capacity for the scheme set at two cohorts at any one time. 2. Convene the Wooden Magnet Working Group, named for one of [PERSON]’s signature investigations, charged with identifying research directions the University considers fifty years ahead of their time and protecting them against the funding cycle’s ordinary impatience. 3. Maintain and expand the [PERSON] Collections held at the Menzies Library, including the original sketches, working papers, and surviving prototypes, with the collection made progressively available for direct consultation by researchers across the [PLACE] region. Measures. 1. By 2031, the [PERSON] Method Fellowship will be funding two active cohorts, with the first ten-year cycle settled and an open call for the next. 2. The Wooden Magnet Working Group will have met quarterly from 2026 onwards, with minutes published in full. 3. By 2028, the [PERSON] Collections will have been fully digitised and made publicly accessible, with a published cataloguing standard shared with comparable national archives.

This new facility will set the stage for new levels of fundraising and alumni engagement throughout the next decade. This Strategic Roadmap for a Distinctive [PLACE] State capitalises on the rising trajectory and momentum of [ORGANISATION]. We are committed to becoming an exemplar of the new public research university with a distinctive blend of teaching, research and creative excellence. Beverly Warren President

text: For [ORGANISATION], the implications cut across the four colleges. In the humanities and social sciences, the question of how a text is composed — which tools, which prompts, which editorial passes, which review — is no longer separable from the question of what it argues. In the natural sciences, the production of figures, the formatting of code, the choice of analytic pipeline, and the resolution at which an image is rendered each shape the claim being made. In engineering and computing, the disciplinary self-account has long included the apparatus, but the apparatus itself is now changing on a timeline shorter than the duration of an undergraduate degree. In the [ORGANISATION], the methodological audit trail has medico-legal as well as scholarly weight. A second shift compounds the first. The [PLACE] higher-education sector is moving, under federal direction, toward greater public declaration of how its work is funded, conducted, and reviewed. The technical processes through which research is produced sit squarely within the scope of that declaration. Universities that develop a coherent, articulable account of their compositional apparatus will move with the direction of policy; those that do not will find the account written for them. A third shift is intergenerational. The cohort entering [ORGANISATION] in 2026 has grown up inside a media environment in which the boundary between human composition and machine composition is porous by default. They will arrive expecting an institution that has formed a settled position on what writing is, what depiction is, what attribution means, and what craft now consists in. They will not be served by ambivalence. The Plan that follows is [ORGANISATION]’s response. It commits the University, across the period to 2031, to a coherent posture toward the technical conditions of its own scholarly

text: Where we stand The sector we work within increasingly expects an institution to be able to account for a specific decision, not simply to gesture at a governance framework that covers decisions in general. [ORGANISATION] welcomes that expectation. It sits close to work this University has pursued for years, across the [ORGANISATION]’ anticipatory-capability agenda and the [ORGANISATION]’s evaluation-ecosystem agenda, and it gives that work a sharper edge to press against. Internally, the number of workflows in which an AI-assisted tool contributes to a decision affecting a person’s standing has grown faster than the University’s capacity to review each one in full. Admissions triage, grant-round shortlisting, shift rostering, procurement exception flags, and a growing list of smaller decisions besides now arrive at a human desk already carrying a recommendation. In most of these workflows, a human is still formally the one who decides. What has grown much less certain, as the volume has risen, is how much of the recommendation that human actually reads before they sign. Other institutions across the sector report the same trajectory, in broadly similar terms: an AI-assisted contribution that began in one or two high-visibility workflows, then spread, workflow by workflow, faster than any single governance framework was drafted to anticipate. Most respond by strengthening the framework. Fewer ask the narrower question this plan starts from — not whether a framework exists, but whether the specific person it names to apply it still has the time to do so. [ORGANISATION] does not regard that gap as a failing unique to us. We do regard it as the gap most worth closing first, precisely because it is the one a framework, on its own, cannot close.

Ambition: [ORGANISATION] will be at the international forefront when it comes to knowledge and competence about and for the Artic and High [PLACE]. We will be at the forefront of understanding natural and societal changes in the [PLACE] and the High [PLACE], and the effects of these. We will be an attractive place to study that utilises and values the closeness between disciplines, people and practice. We will translate challenges and opportunities in the High [PLACE] into research questions and explore them in collaboration.

2. The major societal challenges Major societal challenges covering climate and environment, food security, demography and health show that modern society is vulnerable. These challenges demonstrate that global interaction, democracy and mutual trust between people are important. Society needs academic environments that can develop research questions and methods aimed at providing the basis for challenging decision-making processes in the short and long term. Our academic breadth and closeness to nature and society make [ORGANISATION] uniquely suited to contribute knowledge and competence to transformation and adaptation processes and future-oriented solutions across disciplines, trade and industry and civil society. Ambition: [ORGANISATION] will contribute to developing innovative, democratic and sustainable solutions for major societal challenges. We will take responsibility for basic research in our disciplines and contribute to global knowledge production. We will take special responsibility for knowledge and competence needed for environmentally, socially and economically sustainable development. We will share and make available our research and education and facilitate innovation and co-creation internally and with the wider community. Students and staff at [ORGANISATION] will be characterised by their ability to think critically, gain a head start on ideas and dare to challenge established practices.

Our Education [ORGANISATION] has a distinctive, flexible curriculum that encourages students to grow as independent learners. True to our roots as an ancient [PLACE] university, our degree programmes combine breadth and depth, and draw their strength from the quality of our research. We believe in the interconnectedness of research and teaching, and will create new interdisciplinary pathways for study as we address global challenges. Students and the Students’ Association will work together with staff to ensure that our curriculum and our student experience are among the very best in the world.

We will prepare our graduates to thrive in the diverse workplaces of the future by working with external partners and alumni. We will develop more challenge-led teaching, which enables students to learn by tackling real-world problems. We will provide more work-based learning, through placements and volunteering. We will make innovative use of digital technology to enable learning, and equip our graduates with digital skills. We will foster their intellectual development, creative thinking, innovation and entrepreneurship. Our students will grow in confidence and understanding, so that they can be change-makers across the globe. Our education is open to all. We will provide an environment in which all students can achieve success, whatever their background or personal characteristics. We will support our students through effective teamwork across the university. We will set ambitious targets for widening access, working with our education partners to support aspiration and attainment. We will expand learning on demand and continuing professional development. Our education will be available to people wherever they wish to learn with us, and at any stage in their career journey.

Our values The values below emerged through consultation as the dispositions that participants returned to most often when describing the kind of institution the Plan is asking [ORGANISATION] to become. The accompanying glosses preserve the language in which the values were spoken. Set — The conditions of the encounter shape the encounter. The University attends to the mindset, intention, and preparation with which it approaches its work. Setting — The container is part of the work. The University attends to the physical, relational, and temporal conditions in which inquiry is held. Integration — Without integration, the insight disperses. The University takes seriously the slow work of embedding what its inquiry has surfaced. Dose — The right dose for the right purpose. The University calibrates the intensity of its interventions to the durable change they intend to produce. Container — That which holds, holds itself. The University maintains the structural conditions that allow significant work to be undertaken without dispersal.

The world in 2026 The conditions in which [PLACE] higher education now operates are unlike those that shaped the institutional patterns of the previous forty years. Four converging pressures bear most directly on a national university of [ORGANISATION]’s character, each of which informs the framing of this Plan. The first is the intensity of the operating environment itself. Universities are being asked to undertake research and teaching on questions of increasing magnitude and pace — climate, sovereign capability, the rapid development of artificial intelligence, intergenerational equity — under conditions in which the institutional container of the previous decade was not designed to hold them. We will: • Develop a framework for graduate employability based on an approach of joint endeavour, working across the University and with stakeholders to enhance students’ skills, attributes and abilities to secure the outcomes they seek and manage their onward careers with confidence. • Provide clear and responsive oversight of the careers and employability provision, enabling the University to assess and respond to the fast-moving skills and employability agenda. • Align programme and curriculum developments with the changing skills requirements of our students and external partners.

• Ensure every student is provided with opportunities to gain work-based and/or work-orientated experience and ensure effective governance of such activity. • Effectively monitor progress and impact of the framework, including mapping of the levels of work experience, and ensuring the appropriateness and quality of career decision-making skills. • Devise and implement an action plan to support graduating students in the job market and ensure that students recognise what opportunities exist and are confident in what they can offer to prospective employers.

We will: • Develop a digital strategy that sets the future direction for learning and teaching and drives forward our capability and capacity to deliver a blended online and face-to-face learning approach. • Jointly develop high-quality, technology-rich services, co-designed with students and staff. • Develop and implement truly inclusive services, processes and staff development activities that are fit for purpose and facilitate a personalised university experience. • Enhance the student experience through active learning environments, allowing students to connect with information and knowledge in inclusive personalised digital spaces, bridging the physical and the virtual. • Create a fully online offer for a number of Masters courses.

This in no way diminishes our emphasis on wider UK and global engagement, which remains vital to our academic, reputational and financial success. Indeed, these are more important than ever, and our national and international reach brings important economic and cultural benefits to our local region. We have partnerships, campuses and relationships in almost every part of the country and the world. As the UK negotiates its place in the international community, we must continue to lead by example and demonstrate the value of being welcoming and outward looking. It is also important that, where we have a physical presence overseas, we consider how to engage with those local communities and how we can reflect our values in doing so. Nurturing these partnerships takes time and commitment and we recognise that the return on this investment may take time, and that the benefits can be social, intellectual and cultural as well as financial.

Implementation of this strategy requires the collective effort of all members of our University community. Each of us has responsibilities that we must meet and expectations that we are entitled to have of each other. The 3Rs Framework, developed by our People Plan Board based on staff survey feedback, sets out three tenets of leadership for the [ORGANISATION]: Resourceful, Responsible and Respectful. It is underpinned by a conception of leadership that is about more than management or seniority. It understands that each of us can demonstrate leadership in our own area of activity, expertise and influence. These 3Rs, and the conceptual and analytical structures that sit below them, will provide the basis by which we can turn our four principles into action. OUR STUDENT COMMUNITY

A further description of our responsibilities for the audit of the financial statements is located on the Financial Reporting Council’s website at [[ORGANISATION]] This description forms part of our auditor’s report.

These financial statements have been prepared in accordance with the Statement of Recommended Practice: Accounting for Further and Higher Education 2019 (SORP 2019), [ORGANISATION] Regulatory advice 9: Accounts direction, and in accordance with Financial Reporting Standard FIRS 102. [ORGANISATION] is a public benefit entity and has therefore applied the relevant public benefit requirements of FIRS 102. The financial statements are prepared in accordance with the historical cost convention, modified by the revaluation of investments. The financial statements are presented in pounds sterling ($) and rounded in millions to the nearest one decimal place.

A reverse stress test has also been undertaken to understand the conditions necessary for a breach of the financial covenant to occur. The reverse stress test shows operating cashflows in the base case would need to reduce by 90% in 2026 or 90% in 2027. Given the significance of these conditions, the reverse stress test is considered remote and outside the most severe downside scenario.

Based on the assessment performed, Council considers that the Group has adequate resources to continue in operational existence for the foreseeable future, being a period up to at least 31 July 2027. For this reason, the Group and University continue to adopt the going concern basis in the financial statements. No material uncertainties exist.

Council undertakes a going concern assessment by reference to the approved multi-year budget for the period to 31 July 2030, which encompasses the going concern period to 31 July 2027, which was approved by Council in July 2025. The approved budget is designed to support delivery of [ORGANISATION]’s strategic priorities as set out in the Strategic Plan 2022–27, to enable investment in people, buildings and technology, and to ensure long-term financial sustainability.

How do we create equitable and resilient local and global economies to lead us into the future? Technology is transforming the economy and the world of work with the rise of remote and hybrid workers, increased automation and artificial intelligence. New technology can increase efficiency and flexibility, but the workforce must keep up with new systems. Life-long learning will become increasingly important as individuals need to upskill, reskill and reimagine their careers in addition to benefits for personal growth and enlightenment. At the same time, labour shortages, disruptions to supply chains, and geopolitical and digital threats have shown us the vulnerabilities and risks inherent in our economy. [PLACE] faces serious challenges with productivity growth, and without a significant change in course we will not have the resources necessary to advance these futures and the challenges ahead. We have the foundation to shape innovative ecosystems and develop talent to help create more equitable, resilient and future-proofed economies. Already a leader in work integrated learning, we can expand our mandate to support learning-integrated work to help organisations and individuals keep pace with technology and the changing world of work. We can grow our business and entrepreneurial education strengths to include leadership in social entrepreneurship and innovation targeting the public good.

OUR JOURNEY TO 2057 Where are we going and how will we get there? We have bold ambitions for the impact we want to make on the world. To enable these goals, we need to look inward to focus, organise and forecast into the future how we work and create the right environment for our community to thrive.

A message from the ViceChancellor This Strategic Plan articulates the direction of the [ORGANISATION] across the period 2026 to 2031. The Plan is also, by deliberate choice, a document that takes more care than is usual with the language in which institutional intent is set down. There is a saying that returned to the working group across many drafts: one cannot polish a river. The Plan does not aspire to polish what was already a river. It does aspire to follow that river with attentiveness. What we have learned, across consultation with staff, students, alumni, partners, and [PLACE] colleagues, is that a national university’s voice is one of its most durable assets — and one of the most easily flattened by the standard registers of strategic planning. We have accordingly attempted to speak in our own voice across these pages, even where that voice gathers its strength from sources outside the contemporary sectoral idiom.

The blacksmith’s hammer asks no questions of the anvil: this Plan, similarly, makes its commitments without apologising for the unusual grammar in which it sometimes makes them. Across the five priorities that follow, the substance is recognisably the substance of a national university plan — research, education, place, partnership, and institutional capability. The framing is, in moments, less recognisable. We commend the Plan to the community in the conviction that the goat does not weep at the herder’s wedding — that the relations which sustain an institution over a long period are worth tending with whatever language carries them best. Vice-Chancellor and President

In the last year, we have significantly increased our international alumni activity, supporting 47 active global alumni groups and co-ordinating and delivering 113 events. These included piloting send-off events across the [PLACE]and China which were attended by nearly 400 individuals in 10 different cities, three alumni receptions in China where over 200 alumni attended, and a bespoke flagship event held at the Henderson hotel in Hong Kong in collaboration with [ORGANISATION]’s donors Cathy and Martin Lee. We are also engaging corners of the world that have previously seen little to no alumni engagement – this includes organising an alumni reception at the [PLACE] Embassy in Copenhagen as well as an inaugural alumni gathering in Chile, which saw over 120 alumni registered.

Throughout the year, regular donor visits, tours and events provided the opportunity for donors to see first hand the impact of their giving, and to connect with the research community whose work they are supporting. All donors receive the annual Philanthropy Impact Report, while project reports provide timely updates to donors giving to targeted areas of our work throughout the year. Individuals who have made the generous decision to leave [ORGANISATION] a gift in their will were invited to a celebratory event at the [ORGANISATION] in September, to thank them and to share more information about the museum and its collection. They had the opportunity to hear from artist Sarah Macdonald, an alumna of the [ORGANISATION] Slade School of Fine Art, who received life-changing support funded by a gift left to [ORGANISATION] in a will.

We also delivered a successful mentoring programme for 100 students and will double our students and alumni in 25/26. The [ORGANISATION] Connect professional development event series now regularly reaches 1,000 registrations from alumni, a 300% increase on three years ago. We’ve piloted exciting new student enrichment programmes such as AlumniStudent Chats which generated 80 successful mentoring matches, as well as an alumni work-shadowing scheme which supported 20 students to get exposure to real-life workplaces in term three.

The University sits on [PLACE] and [PLACE]-[PLACE] Country, in the federal capital, in a city whose lake, hills, and weather are part of the institutional formation of every cohort that passes through. The lake does not apologise for its depth. The Plan attends to place not as a backdrop but as a constitutive element of the University’s distinctiveness, and one which will, across the period covered by this Plan, be more deliberately tended than it has been over the previous several planning cycles. Read together, these five contexts ask the University to articulate its purpose in a register that is more deliberately particular than the sectoral norm. The framing this Plan adopts — including the occasional reach for sayings that have come up across consultation and that participants returned to spontaneously — reflects a working conviction: a borrowed shadow does not cool the borrower. The University will speak in its own voice across the period of this Plan.

Where we are headed By 2031, [ORGANISATION] will be a national university recognised — within the country and in its region — for the depth of its scholarship, the quality of its teaching, and the unmistakable character of its institutional voice. We do not lend the well its own water: the University’s contribution to public life in 2031 will draw on the deep, particular resources of the institution rather than on the borrowed forms of the moment. The Plan describes how that voice will be cultivated across research, teaching, partnership, place, and institutional capability over the period 2026 to 2031. Even the salt remembers the sea: the University, in 2031, will recognisably be the institution it has long been, in better condition than it received itself, and oriented toward the long century ahead.

Translation, Provenance, and the Crossing Premise. The work of moving between analogue and digital substrates — the digitisation of a physical archive, the printing of a generative work, the encoding of a field instrument, the materialisation of a simulation — is itself scholarship that the University has rarely articulated as such. [ORGANISATION] will treat translation across the crossing as a primary scholarly object. Initiatives. 1. The [ORGANISATION] Translation Office will be established, reporting to the Deputy ViceChancellor (Research), to maintain the institution’s register of analogue-digital translations and to convene methodological renewal across the disciplines that practise them. 2. The University will publish, annually, the [ORGANISATION] Provenance Standard for analogue digital translation, intended for institutional use and made openly available to the broader [PLACE] higher-education sector. Measures. • One hundred per cent of [ORGANISATION] institutional digitisation projects initiated from 2027 will comply with the [ORGANISATION] Provenance Standard, with no exception sustained for more than a single audit cycle. • The Translation Office will release a Translation Inventory annually from 2028, including custodianship, intended-use envelope, and provenance metadata per entry. • A published five-year audit of analogue-digital translation practice across the four colleges, released in 2031 to inform the strategic cycle that follows.

Phasing Delivery proceeds across four phases spanning the period 2026 to 2031 contiguously. Each phase carries a defined posture and a defined relationship to the five strategic priorities. Foundation 2026. The Hybrid Substrate Institute, the three Crossing Studios, the Computational Literacy Programme, the Computational Companion fellowship scheme, and the Translation Office are stood up across the first year of the Plan. Inaugural directors are appointed; foundational frameworks (the Material Reasoning Capability Framework, the Computational Literacy Framework, the [ORGANISATION] Provenance Standard) are released in draft for community consultation; the inaugural Hybrid Substrate Convention is scheduled for 2027 and partner institutions are confirmed.

Dance stories “Choreography tells a story,” says Kisha September. “At the base of every powerful dance is a deep and resonant story that is brought alive and played out through the artistry of movement.” Collaboration is an essential element, she adds. Kisha, who is Head of Dance at Excel School of Performing Arts, is a PhD student in Dance Studies at the [ORGANISATION] and in 2025 became the first-ever recipient of the new Buchanan Dance Research Residency Award. Kisha’s PhD research centres on “conversations about choreography” – especially the question of how “to strip back the process of creating it and handing it on to others”. She is constructing a set of tools to be used by other practitioners, which are designed to open new creative possibilities.

Another transformational advance is wireless charging, being developed at the University’s [PLACE] Bioengineering Institute by a team led by Associate Professor [PLACE] Budgett and Dr [PERSON]. This allows pacemakers to be recharged after implantation and provides the energy for them to co-ordinate their activity with other devices in the body. When it’s time to recharge, electrodes are put on the body surface and small electrical currents pass near the pacemaker which captures energy to store in its battery. With wireless charging, the devices can be smaller and smarter: conventional pacemakers need to be surgically replaced to swap out the battery every 10 years or so. The devices will establish a new standard for “lifelong pacemakers”. Vitally, their tiny size

allows them to be located inside the chambers of the heart, delivered through blood vessels using simple surgery. The availability of power means they can communicate with each other to synchronise pacing at multiple sites, which is essential for 70% of pacemaker recipients.

text:
The conscious cultivation of rationality: A sharp, analytical mind protects creativity from randomness. Those who are driven solely by emotions and external stimuli cannot systematically create something new. This is why fostering reflection, critical thinking, and intellectual discipline is essential.

Why is this particularly important for a technical university? Technical universities are often associated with precise solutions and clear methodologies. However, some of the greatest innovations in technology have emerged from creative breakthroughs – driven by individuals who dared to think beyond existing systems. 

From problem formulation to solution: In science, we often face questions that we cannot yet clearly define. Creativity is essential for transforming initial observations into new research questions, which in turn lead to groundbreaking discoveries.

Technological development is unpredictable: What seems like an ambitious idea today may become the standard tomorrow - or turn out to be a dead end. Creativity enables us to deal productively with this uncertainty and discover new approaches.

Interdisciplinary challenges require new ways of thinking: Many of today‘s most pressing issues – such as climate change, digitalization, sustainable cities - cannot be addressed with rigid disciplinary boundaries. A creative university promotes exchange across disciplines and creates spaces where new approaches can emerge.

Innovation extends beyond research: Creativity is not only reflected in scientific breakthroughs but also in teaching, the organisation of knowledge processes, and the way a university interacts with its environment. Administrative processes, service units, and internal structures also benefit from creative solutions.

However, all of this can only happen in an environment that recognises the importance of rational thinking. Universities must take a leading role in this, as they are the last bastions of enlightenment in an increasingly irrational world. Creativity is not something we only promote in certain research areas - it is a fundamental prerequisite for excellence in science and teaching. By living this aspiration together and at the same time maintaining a space of rationality, we lay the foundation for [ORGANISATION] to remain a place of progress and innovation.

Writing as Engineered Practice Context. Writing at the University — student, scholarly, professional, administrative — is increasingly co-produced with technical systems whose contribution is rarely articulated. [ORGANISATION] will treat the writing apparatus of the institution as scholarship, not infrastructure, and will articulate it for use by the University community and for the broader sector.

Commitments. 1. The University will stand up the Centre for Composition Studies, anchored in the School of Literature, Languages and Linguistics with cross-appointments held jointly across the School of Computing and the [ORGANISATION] & [PLACE]. 2. A “Writing Apparatus” elective stream will be developed and made available to every undergraduate degree program, with a minimum of three sequenced units offered each semester from 2028. 3. The University will establish the [ORGANISATION] Editorial Stack: an institution-wide articulation of accepted, declared, and prohibited writing tools by use class, published openly and revised at twelve-month intervals. Indicators. • One hundred per cent of taught course work at 2000 level and above will publish a “writing apparatus” disclosure to students alongside the standard course outline by 2029. • Three peer-reviewed monographs per year will be published through [ORGANISATION] Press in the Composition Studies series by 2029, sustained through the remainder of the plan period. • An annual [ORGANISATION] Composition Prize, awarded in three categories (drafting, revision, machine-assisted composition), each with a published methodological declaration as a condition of submission.

Visual Composition in Hybrid Media Context. The visual artefacts produced by the institution — figures, diagrams, posters, slides, video, generative output, exhibition materials — pass through compounding technical stacks whose contribution to the eventual artefact is generally invisible to the reader or viewer. [ORGANISATION] will own the visual stack as a site of scholarship and craft.

[ORGANISATION]’s place in the national interest has never depended on the size of its ambitions but on the University’s willingness to be specific about them, and to be answerable when a trajectory it backed does not arrive. This plan is that answerability, written down in advance. — Vice-Chancellor and President

Executive summary This plan commits [ORGANISATION] to a single working principle across the decade ahead: no commitment — to a person, a cohort, or a partner — is made, or continued, without evidence of the trajectory that justifies it. Four strategic pillars carry that principle from the moment an offer is drafted through to the moment a portfolio of evidence is finally retired.

Together, these pillars close a gap the University has lived with for longer than it has been comfortable admitting: that a trajectory, once backed, was rarely checked again. By 2031, evidence of trajectory will accompany every commitment [ORGANISATION] makes and every commitment it renews, reviewed on a cadence the institution publishes and holds itself to.

Other institutions have reached for the same instinct without the same discipline, and the difference shows. A screening step added in response to a single bad outcome, then never revisited, is not evidence practice; it is sediment. [ORGANISATION]’s contribution to this moment is to treat the evidence itself as something to be designed, resourced, and eventually retired — not simply accumulated each time a panel or committee decides it wants to know more before it commits.

text:
Renewing society by art, creativity and design Art, design and creativity drive innovation and entrepreneurship. These concepts radically question and challenge our society and culture. They generate new knowledge and understanding and create value by leveraging humane designs and viable solutions. To reap such rewards, we will develop and promote art-based activities across the boundaries of diverse disciplines, knowledge frameworks and communities.

Educating game changers Grand challenges call for the education of professionals with the knowledge and capabilities to build a sustainable society and to increase wellbeing through disruptive change. These capabilities need to be rooted in disciplinary excellence augmented by art, creativity, multidisciplinary collaboration and entrepreneurship. The development of programs toward integrative thinking and practices to engage students in societal challenges will improve the relevance of our education. We will increase the international exchange opportunities for our students.

Transforming our campus into a unique collaboration hub Our open and experimental collaboration ecosystem will attract students, faculty, staff and partners worldwide. The campus, with its state-of-the-art research and learning environment, is recognised for optimally supporting the production of new knowledge and innovation. We will build a vibrant campus centre that offers attractive opportunities for partnering, collaboration and sharing ideas and experiences.

Excellence in advancing and supporting our core goals Enabling the core academic mission of the [ORGANISATION] community is our first priority. To compete globally for the best faculty, students, staff, partners and other stakeholders, we need to develop world-class conditions and an environment for research, art, education and collaboration. We will invest in sustainable, long-term resourcing of our strategic priorities, build practices to recognise achievement and develop streamlined support service solutions facilitating academic excellence.
